### Description

When using the `post_model_hook` in `create_react_agent` the injection of state/store into the tool calls is not performed.
Any reliance on state in a tool for such an agent will fail the pydantic input args validations.

Cause of the problem is here:
In langgraph/prebuilt/chat_agent_executor.py
The code of [`post_model_hook_router`](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/2553ae0b877c58beb8947db70336c008d7c7ea23/libs/prebuilt/langgraph/prebuilt/chat_agent_executor.py#L709) decides if a tool execution is required, and will use `Send` to route to the tool node like so:
```python
return [Send("tools", [tool_call]) for tool_call in pending_tool_calls]
```

Comparing that with the [`should_continue`](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/2553ae0b877c58beb8947db70336c008d7c7ea23/libs/prebuilt/langgraph/prebuilt/chat_agent_executor.py#L632) implementation, When there is no "post_model_hook" setup it will `Send` to the tools node like so:
```python
tool_calls = [
    tool_node.inject_tool_args(call, state, store)  # type: ignore[arg-type]
    for call in last_message.tool_calls
]
return [Send("tools", [tool_call]) for tool_call in tool_calls]
```

So, when the hook is setup you get the flow:
agent -> should_continue -> post_model_hook -> post_model_hook_router -> tools
And without you get:
agent -> should_continue -> tools

The first, will neglect to inject a state/store and the latter will.
I believe this is a bug.
Ideally, there will be a single "send to tools" implementation which both routers should use.

Hi @tangent2018 - OpenAI’s Chat Completions API does not stream token usage statistics by default. To recover token counts when streaming with ChatOpenAI or AzureChatOpenAI, set `stream_usage=True` as an initialization parameter or on invocation. This is documented here: [ChatOpenAI: Streaming usage metadata](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/integrations/chat/openai#streaming-usage-metadata).
```python
model = ChatOpenAI(
    model_name="gpt-4o-mini",
    stream_usage=True,
)
```

title: Make state access for subgraphs easier from parent graph
body:
### Checked other resources

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. For questions, please use GitHub Discussions.
- [x] I added a clear and detailed title that summarizes the issue.
- [x] I read what a minimal reproducible example is (https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example).
- [x] I included a self-contained, minimal example that demonstrates the issue INCLUDING all the relevant imports. The code run AS IS to reproduce the issue.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Literal

from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableConfig
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
from langgraph.graph import END, START, MessagesState, StateGraph
from langgraph.types import Command, interrupt
from pydantic import BaseModel
from rich import print



class State(BaseModel):
    messages: list[str] = []


def node_builder(name: str, type: Literal["normal", "interrupt"]):
    def node(state: State):
        print(f"{name} node", state)
        return {"messages": state.messages + [f"{name} node"]}

    def node_interrupt(state: State):
        print(f"{name} interrupt", state)
        value = interrupt("enter interrupt")
        return {"messages": state.messages + [f"{name} interrupt"]}

    if type == "normal":
        return node
    elif type == "interrupt":
        return node_interrupt
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid type: {type}")


def subgraph_builder(name: str):

    def build():
        graph = StateGraph(State)
        graph.add_node(f"{name}1", node_builder(f"{name}1", "normal"))
        graph.add_node(f"{name}2", node_builder(f"{name}2", "interrupt"))

        graph.add_edge(START, f"{name}1")
        graph.add_edge(f"{name}1", f"{name}2")
        graph.add_edge(f"{name}2", END)
        return graph

    return build


def main():
    memory = MemorySaver()
    thread_id = "123"
    config = RunnableConfig(configurable={"thread_id": thread_id})

    graph = StateGraph(State)
    graph.add_node("node1", node_builder("node1", "normal"))
    subgraph = subgraph_builder("node2")()
    compiled_subgraph = subgraph.compile(checkpointer=memory)
    graph.add_node("node2", compiled_subgraph)

    graph.add_edge(START, "node1")
    graph.add_edge("node1", "node2")
    graph.add_edge("node2", END)
    graph.compile()

    compiled_graph = graph.compile(checkpointer=memory)
    for chunk in compiled_graph.stream({"messages": []}, config=config, subgraphs=True):
        # print(chunk)
        pass

    state = compiled_graph.get_state(config=config, subgraphs=True)
    print("state", state.values)

    compiled_graph.invoke(Command(resume=True), config=config, subgraphs=True)
    print("resume")
    state = compiled_graph.get_state(config=config, subgraphs=True)
    print("after resume state", state.values)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

I am using subgraphs and interrupts. When my interrupt happens inside a subgraph, I can't get latest state by `get_state` API. Only after interrupt is resumed, I can get full state.

```
resume
```

comments.body:
Hey folks! This is actually the expected behavior. You're getting the state off of the parent graph, so the state hasn't yet been updated because the subgraph node (your subgraph) hasn't completed execution.

In the short term, you can access the subgraph state via something like:
```py
parent_state = parent_graph.get_state(config=config)
sub_state = top_state.tasks[0].state
```

```python
        input=human_input, config=config, stream_mode=["updates", "messages"], subgraphs=True
```

Class RemoteGraph check if its input is Command Instance or not. However, if using it as a sub-graph, Input Command Instance is not sent to it.

I think one way to handle this problem is: fix CompiledStateGraph.stream() and CompiledStateGraph.astream() functions with input as Command Instance.

However I don't see the logic for handling Command Instance in the CompiledStateGraph class.

Does someone have any suggestions?

### Issue with current documentation:

https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/low_level/#node-caching

Does `langgraph.prebuilt.chat_agent_executor.create_react_agent` support CACHE?

### Idea or request for content:

comments.author: YassinNouh21
comments.body:
@khteh 
TL;DR: Yes,`create_react_agent` supports caching at the graph level, but does not expose caching in its function signature directly.

Use Caching with `create_react_agent`. Since `create_react_agent` returns a CompiledStateGraph, you would need to manually configure caching by:
- Creating a custom graph instead of using the prebuilt function if you want node-level cache policies
- Using the cache at the execution level by calling methods on the compiled graph that support caching

```python
import os

from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, MessagesState

from langchain_core.messages import convert_to_messages


def pretty_print_message(message, indent=False):
    pretty_message = message.pretty_repr(html=True)
    if not indent:
        print(pretty_message)
        return

    indented = "\n".join("\t" + c for c in pretty_message.split("\n"))
    print(indented)


def pretty_print_messages(update, last_message=False):
    is_subgraph = False
    if isinstance(update, tuple):
        ns, update = update
        # skip parent graph updates in the printouts
        if len(ns) == 0:
            return

        graph_id = ns[-1].split(":")[0]
        print(f"Update from subgraph {graph_id}:")
        print("\n")
        is_subgraph = True

    for node_name, node_update in update.items():
        update_label = f"Update from node {node_name}:"
```

```python
    pretty_message = message.pretty_repr(html=True)
    if not indent:
        print(pretty_message)
        return

    indented = "\n".join("\t" + c for c in pretty_message.split("\n"))
    print(indented)

    is_subgraph = False
    if isinstance(update, tuple):
        ns, update = update
        # skip parent graph updates in the printouts
        if len(ns) == 0:
            return

        graph_id = ns[-1].split(":")[0]
        print(f"Update from subgraph {graph_id}:")
        print("\n")
        is_subgraph = True

    for node_name, node_update in update.items():
        update_label = f"Update from node {node_name}:"
        if is_subgraph:
            update_label = "\t" + update_label

        print(update_label)
        print("\n")

            messages = messages[-1:]

            "content": f"Successfully transferred to {agent_name}",

            "tool_call_id": tool_call_id,

        return Command(
            goto=agent_name,  
            update={**state, "messages": state["messages"] + [tool_message]},  
            graph=Command.PARENT,

    return handoff_tool
```

comments.author: ccurme
comments.body:
Hello, what model are you using with Bedrock?

I'm unable to reproduce the issue using `langchain-aws` with Claude (I see you are using a custom chat model):
```python
from langchain_aws import ChatBedrock

llm = ChatBedrock(model="anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620-v1:0")
```

From your description, it sounds like the underlying model errors when the message sequence ends with an AIMessage. This is consistent with how the prebuilt react agent works when `response_format` is specified. I think there are a few options here:

1. You could use a [post-model hook](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/reference/agents/?h=hook#langgraph.prebuilt.chat_agent_executor.create_react_agent). For example, if there are no tool calls, you could generate an artifical HumanMessage in this node (e.g., "Reformat the response") prior to the structured output node. Or, you could implement a custom structured output node.

2. You could modify your custom chat model to process message sequences ending in AIMessage, though it's not immediately clear to me what logic you'd want to implement there.

Still, Anthropic / Claude should be able to handle those message sequences ending in AIMessage, so I'm curious what model you're using— see example trace: https://smith.langchain.com/public/eee3132b-ae64-4541-a0c8-456cc8ea0240/r/97e33a8d-7e22-476a-a5a3-f337c29f2fa9

I am using `anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022-v2:0` model that's accessible via our internal aws service endpoint. Which is why I have created a Custom chat model to interact with that endpoint.

I will try your suggestions and see if it helps. I will respond with an update here. Thanks!

comments.body:
Hi @ccurme, I tried the post model hook option, but that didn't help. Since the graph execution calls the post model hook after every llm_call.

My original goal is to have a structured response for agent's final response. So I implemented the `response` node, which invokes agent with Human message - reformat the response - and attached it before the `__end__` node so that agent's final response gets formatted into structure before the graph ends.

I initially thought the `create_react_agent()` would work that way.

cc @ccurme, could you take a look at this one?

Hello, what model are you using with Bedrock?

I'm unable to reproduce the issue using `langchain-aws` with Claude (I see you are using a custom chat model):
```python
from langchain_aws import ChatBedrock

llm = ChatBedrock(model="anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620-v1:0")
```

From your description, it sounds like the underlying model errors when the message sequence ends with an AIMessage. This is consistent with how the prebuilt react agent works when `response_format` is specified. I think there are a few options here:

1. You could use a [post-model hook](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/reference/agents/?h=hook#langgraph.prebuilt.chat_agent_executor.create_react_agent). For example, if there are no tool calls, you could generate an artifical HumanMessage in this node (e.g., "Reformat the response") prior to the structured output node. Or, you could implement a custom structured output node.

2. You could modify your custom chat model to process message sequences ending in AIMessage, though it's not immediately clear to me what logic you'd want to implement there.

Still, Anthropic / Claude should be able to handle those message sequences ending in AIMessage, so I'm curious what model you're using— see example trace: https://smith.langchain.com/public/eee3132b-ae64-4541-a0c8-456cc8ea0240/r/97e33a8d-7e22-476a-a5a3-f337c29f2fa9

Thanks @ccurme for your response. To answer your question:

>what model are you using with Bedrock?

I am using `anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022-v2:0` model that's accessible via our internal aws service endpoint. Which is why I have created a Custom chat model to interact with that endpoint.

I will try your suggestions and see if it helps. I will respond with an update here. Thanks!



Hi @ccurme, I tried the post model hook option, but that didn't help. Since the graph execution calls the post model hook after every llm_call.

My original goal is to have a structured response for agent's final response. So I implemented the `response` node, which invokes agent with Human message - reformat the response - and attached it before the `__end__` node so that agent's final response gets formatted into structure before the graph ends.

I initially thought the `create_react_agent()` would work that way.

title: DOC: Pregel constructor has too many parameters
body:
### Issue with current documentation:

The `Pregel.__init__` method currently takes 24 parameters, which makes it pretty unwieldy to use and maintain. While all these config options are useful, having this many parameters in a single constructor is a code smell.

**Current state:**
```python
def __init__(
    self,
    *,
    nodes: dict[str, PregelNode | NodeBuilder],
    channels: dict[str, BaseChannel | ManagedValueSpec] | None,
    auto_validate: bool = True,
    stream_mode: StreamMode = "values",
    stream_eager: bool = False,
    output_channels: str | Sequence[str],
    stream_channels: str | Sequence[str] | None = None,
    interrupt_after_nodes: All | Sequence[str] = (),
    interrupt_before_nodes: All | Sequence[str] = (),
    input_channels: str | Sequence[str],
    step_timeout: float | None = None,
    debug: bool | None = None,
    checkpointer: BaseCheckpointSaver | None = None,
    store: BaseStore | None = None,
    cache: BaseCache | None = None,
    retry_policy: RetryPolicy | Sequence[RetryPolicy] = (),
    cache_policy: CachePolicy | None = None,
    config_type: type[Any] | None = None,
    input_model: type[BaseModel] | None = None,
    config: RunnableConfig | None = None,
    trigger_to_nodes: Mapping[str, Sequence[str]] | None = None,
    name: str = "LangGraph",
) -> None:
```

**Problems:**
1. Hard to remember parameter order
2. IDE autocomplete becomes messy
3. Easy to miss required vs optional params

**Suggestion:**
Group related parameters into config objects:

```python
@dataclass
class StreamConfig:
    mode: StreamMode = "values"
    eager: bool = False
    channels: str | Sequence[str] | None = None

@dataclass 
class InterruptConfig:
    after_nodes: All | Sequence[str] = ()
    before_nodes: All | Sequence[str] = ()

# Then:
def __init__(
    self,
    *,
    nodes: dict[str, PregelNode | NodeBuilder],
    channels: dict[str, BaseChannel | ManagedValueSpec] | None,
    input_channels: str | Sequence[str],
    output_channels: str | Sequence[str],
    stream_config: StreamConfig | None = None,
    interrupt_config: InterruptConfig | None = None,
    # ... other grouped configs
):
```

comments.author: sydney-runkle
comments.body:
Thanks for your concern. Indeed, `Pregel` is a bit overloaded. I'm not convinced that nesting would help much here, unfortunately.

We can definitely consider adding some utility methods to initialize with minimal settings (so basically just building from nodes). Going to close for now, we're going to work on solidifying this API for v1. I think revisiting this after that point would make sense.

Here's an updated version of @willianantunes 's monkey patch that works for more scenarios. Courtesy one of the friendly neighborhood coding agents. :-)

```python
from typing import Any

from langgraph.checkpoint.serde import jsonplus
from langgraph.checkpoint.serde.jsonplus import _msgpack_default
from langgraph.checkpoint.serde.jsonplus import _option
from langgraph.checkpoint.serde.jsonplus import ormsgpack


def message_to_dict(msg):
    """
    Recursively convert a message or object into a dict/str (safe for serialization).
    """
    # Handles HumanMessage, AIMessage, ToolMessage, etc.
    if hasattr(msg, "to_dict"):
        return msg.to_dict()
    elif isinstance(msg, dict):
        # Recursively convert dict values
        return {k: message_to_dict(v) for k, v in msg.items()}
    elif isinstance(msg, (list, tuple)):
        # Recursively convert each item
        return [message_to_dict(x) for x in msg]
    elif isinstance(msg, (str, int, float, bool, type(None))):
        return msg
    else:
        # Fallback: try to extract content and role
        print("Serialization Fallback, type:", type(msg))
        print(msg)
        return {"role": getattr(msg, "role", "user"), "content": str(getattr(msg, "content", msg))}


def _msgpack_enc(data: Any) -> bytes:
    return ormsgpack.packb(message_to_dict(data), default=_msgpack_default, option=_option)

setattr(jsonplus, "_msgpack_enc", _msgpack_enc)
```

comments.author: MukundaKatta
comments.body:
The Azure Container App vs local docker delta points at filesystem layout, not the patch itself. msgpack's serializer registry is a module-level dict, and Container App's snapshot mechanism may serialize the runtime state before the registry is populated.

Two checks worth running: confirm the patch's import order on Container App (it has to register the AIMessage encoder before the first checkpoint write), and confirm the worker process being used (gunicorn-with-preload races with the registration if the patch lazy-imports).

Workaround: call the patch's setup function explicitly at app startup, not lazily on first checkpoint.

```
def _msgpack_enc(data: Any) -> bytes:
```

Here's an updated version of @willianantunes 's monkey patch that works for more scenarios. Courtesy one of the friendly neighborhood coding agents. :-)

```python
from typing import Any

from langgraph.checkpoint.serde import jsonplus
from langgraph.checkpoint.serde.jsonplus import _msgpack_default
from langgraph.checkpoint.serde.jsonplus import _option
from langgraph.checkpoint.serde.jsonplus import ormsgpack


def message_to_dict(msg):
    """
    Recursively convert a message or object into a dict/str (safe for serialization).
    """
    # Handles HumanMessage, AIMessage, ToolMessage, etc.
    if hasattr(msg, "to_dict"):
        return msg.to_dict()
    elif isinstance(msg, dict):
        # Recursively convert dict values
        return {k: message_to_dict(v) for k, v in msg.items()}
    elif isinstance(msg, (list, tuple)):
        # Recursively convert each item
        return [message_to_dict(x) for x in msg]
    elif isinstance(msg, (str, int, float, bool, type(None))):
        return msg
    else:
        # Fallback: try to extract content and role
        print("Serialization Fallback, type:", type(msg))
        print(msg)
        return {"role": getattr(msg, "role", "user"), "content": str(getattr(msg, "content", msg))}


def _msgpack_enc(data: Any) -> bytes:
    return ormsgpack.packb(message_to_dict(data), default=_msgpack_default, option=_option)

setattr(jsonplus, "_msgpack_enc", _msgpack_enc)
```

Hi Guys seems like the the patch only works with local docker, not the self-hosted image running in Container App. Have anyone met this issue before in Azure Container App

The Azure Container App vs local docker delta points at filesystem layout, not the patch itself. msgpack's serializer registry is a module-level dict, and Container App's snapshot mechanism may serialize the runtime state before the registry is populated.

Two checks worth running: confirm the patch's import order on Container App (it has to register the AIMessage encoder before the first checkpoint write), and confirm the worker process being used (gunicorn-with-preload races with the registration if the patch lazy-imports).

Workaround: call the patch's setup function explicitly at app startup, not lazily on first checkpoint.

### Example Code

```python
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from IPython.display import Image, display
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START, END
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMessage, RemoveMessage

model = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o",temperature=0)

class State(MessagesState):
    summary: str

# Define the logic to call the model
def call_model(state: State):
    
    # Get summary if it exists
    summary = state.get("summary", "")

    # If there is summary, then we add it
    if summary:
        
        # Add summary to system message
        system_message = f"Summary of conversation earlier: {summary}"

        # Append summary to any newer messages
        messages = [SystemMessage(content=system_message)] + state["messages"]
    
    else:
        messages = state["messages"]
    
    response = model.invoke(messages)
    return {"messages": response}

def summarize_conversation(state: State):
    
    # First, we get any existing summary
    summary = state.get("summary", "")

    # Create our summarization prompt 
    if summary:
        
        # A summary already exists
        summary_message = (
            f"This is summary of the conversation to date: {summary}\n\n"
            "Extend the summary by taking into account the new messages above:"
        )
        
    else:
        summary_message = "Create a summary of the conversation above:"

    # Add prompt to our history
    messages = state["messages"] + [HumanMessage(content=summary_message)]
    response = model.invoke(messages)
    
    # Delete all but the 2 most recent messages
    delete_messages = [RemoveMessage(id=m.id) for m in state["messages"][:-2]]
    return {"summary": response.content, "messages": delete_messages}

# Determine whether to end or summarize the conversation
def should_continue(state: State):
    
    """Return the next node to execute."""
    
    messages = state["messages"]
    
    # If there are more than six messages, then we summarize the conversation
    if len(messages) > 6:
        return "summarize_conversation"
    
    # Otherwise we can just end
    return END


# Define a new graph
workflow = StateGraph(State)
workflow.add_node("conversation", call_model)
workflow.add_node(summarize_conversation)

# Set the entrypoint as conversation
workflow.add_edge(START, "conversation")
workflow.add_conditional_edges("conversation", should_continue)
workflow.add_edge("summarize_conversation", END)

# Compile
memory = MemorySaver()
graph = workflow.compile(checkpointer=memory)
display(Image(graph.get_graph().draw_mermaid_png()))
```

### Example Code

```python
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from IPython.display import Image, display
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START, END
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMessage, RemoveMessage

model = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o",temperature=0)

class State(MessagesState):
    summary: str

# Define the logic to call the model
def call_model(state: State):
    
    # Get summary if it exists
    summary = state.get("summary", "")

    # If there is summary, then we add it
    if summary:
        
        # Add summary to system message
        system_message = f"Summary of conversation earlier: {summary}"

        # Append summary to any newer messages
        messages = [SystemMessage(content=system_message)] + state["messages"]
    
    else:
        messages = state["messages"]
    
    response = model.invoke(messages)
    return {"messages": response}

def summarize_conversation(state: State):
    
    # First, we get any existing summary
    summary = state.get("summary", "")

    # Create our summarization prompt 
    if summary:
        
        # A summary already exists
        summary_message = (
            f"This is summary of the conversation to date: {summary}\n\n"
            "Extend the summary by taking into account the new messages above:"
        )
        
    else:
        summary_message = "Create a summary of the conversation above:"

    # Add prompt to our history
    messages = state["messages"] + [HumanMessage(content=summary_message)]
    response = model.invoke(messages)
    
    # Delete all but the 2 most recent messages
    delete_messages = [RemoveMessage(id=m.id) for m in state["messages"][:-2]]
    return {"summary": response.content, "messages": delete_messages}

# Determine whether to end or summarize the conversation
def should_continue(state: State):
    
    """Return the next node to execute."""
    
    messages = state["messages"]
    
    # If there are more than six messages, then we summarize the conversation
    if len(messages) > 6:
        return "summarize_conversation"
    
    # Otherwise we can just end
    return END


# Define a new graph
workflow = StateGraph(State)
workflow.add_node("conversation", call_model)
workflow.add_node(summarize_conversation)

# Set the entrypoint as conversation
workflow.add_edge(START, "conversation")
workflow.add_conditional_edges("conversation", should_continue)
workflow.add_edge("summarize_conversation", END)

# Compile
memory = MemorySaver()
graph = workflow.compile(checkpointer=memory)
display(Image(graph.get_graph().draw_mermaid_png()))
```

title: 🚧 LangGraph v1 roadmap – feedback wanted!
body:
We're working towards LangGraph v1, and we're looking for input from our user base — you!

This is your chance to help shape the core of LangGraph — especially the low-level `StateGraph` API and related tooling. What we want to hear from you about:

* What parts of LangGraph are confusing or unclear?
* What feels unnecessarily complex or boilerplate-heavy?
* What's annoying or unintuitive when using `StateGraph`?
* What's missing / what features should be top prio?

We'll use this feedback to prioritize changes for v1, including API cleanup, improved documentation, and new features.

Note: We're prioritizing backward compatibility for users and don't plan to make any major breaking changes that make upgrading from v0 to v1 difficult.

Thanks in advance!

[UPDATE]: we'd love feedback on https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/issues/5023 specifically as well!!

— LangGraph team

Tracking progress on v1 here: https://github.com/orgs/langchain-ai/projects/19/views/1

comments.author: EliasLumer
comments.body:
1) IMPORTANT: For StateGraph and checkpointers, you need to have the ability to have custom serialization for certain states. Or drop them completely from the state when serializing them in checkpointers. As an example, if you have a pd.DataFrame in your StateGraph , this will fail to serialize in a InMemoryCheckpointer (or any other checkpointer) and will not allow you to run the graph. Having state serializers that we can define for custom state keys will be useful, and not clear on the documentation now, see issues/3441 .

2) Command() should be intuitive to send to nested sub-sub-sub graphs. The current trend is multi-AI agents, that have nested sub-graphs inside nested sub-graphs. Furthermore, Langgraph is pushing for Command() to deal with unecessary boilerplate conditional edges. However, using a Command() to go-to a graph node inside of a nested nested nested graph is un-intuitive, sloppy, and not clear on documentation. Something easier for this would be great.

2.5) Nested-state graphs are still not clear and often break with using checkpointers due to matching states. Example, if one node Send() and input to another nested graph (node) , the Input StateGraph and Output StateGraph is not very clear based on documentation. I think the feature itself is there, but not clear?

3) Having local self-deployment options for Langgraph through FastAPI that can be self-deployed not using LangSmith but any custom setup would be useful. Especially for OpenSource community, not everyone wants to connect to LangSmith, but still take advantage of the existing langgraph.json set-up.

Come up with some frequency.  
  
It would be helpful for the docs to call out the differences more clearly. I may even suggest going as far as building a simple agent with and without LangGraph to illustrate the benefits. If I can help brainstorm ideas to make this clear, feel free to reach out on slack!

comments.author: gbaian10
comments.body:
I hope that in the future, semantic versioning can be followed more strictly — with new features reflected in MINOR version updates, and PATCH versions reserved solely for bug fixes.

In earlier stages of development, MINOR updates often introduced breaking changes, while PATCH versions sometimes included both bug fixes and new features.
However, since bug fixes made up the majority of changes, developers tended to focus only on them, and many missed new features. 
For instance, the `Command` feature was introduced later on, but it’s not easy to determine exactly which version added it.

Going forward, I hope that all new features will be included in MINOR version updates, and clearly documented — either in the changelog, the GitHub release notes, or ideally, via a dedicated blog post highlighting new features.

comments.author: nickshirobokov
comments.body:
I stopped using LangGraph in my projects mostly because of the following reasons:

1. State management makes you jump through mental hoops. The fact that I can't manipulate the state directly is very annoying and adds a lot of complexity to the code.

2. The entire idea of checkpoints which allow time travel, branching, interruptions, etc. sounds cool until you realize how much memory it consumes. I think making a serialized copy of your entire state at each superstep is brutal. Moreover, this idea breaks down the moment you start modifying the environment through tools (like writing to a DB or making POST requests).

3. The LangGraph API requires a lot of repetitive code.

However, I still think LangGraph could be very useful to many teams that ship small but powerful AI workers internally. I also think it's the best framework for data scientists who want to start building prod-ready AI apps but aren't familiar with SWE patterns and practices.

comments.author: AndreuCodina
comments.body:
It isn’t type-safe.

It’s plenty of hardcoded dictionary keys when you return from a node:

```python
async def tool_searcher_node(self, state: MyState) -> dict[str, Any]:
    tools = await self.tool_searcher_agent.execute(state)
    return {"tools": tools}
```

And when creating the graph, the names of the functions should be used instead of being hardcoded. In my case, I use this verbose approach in Python to not hardcode names:

```python
    def create_graph(self) -> CompiledStateGraph:
        return (
            StateGraph(MyState)
            .add_node(  # type: ignore[reportUnknownMemberType]
                self.tool_searcher_node.__name__,
                self.tool_searcher_node,
            )
            .add_edge(START, self.tool_searcher_node.__name__)
            .add_edge(self.tool_searcher_node.__name__, END)
            .compile()
        )
```

comments.author: HendrixString
comments.body:
🚨 Interrupt Pattern for human in the loop should be deprecated (although i really love the way it is implemented)

HITL flows are essential yet are inefficient and organically wrong with current implementations.
I suggest flipping it a bit with the following story:

Suppose, the user needs to login to perform an action on the client side. The AI
has a tool that asks the frontend to show a login card, but the flow goes like this:

1. `show_login` tool is asked to be called by the LLM (tool_use)
2. The tool responds right away with a json `{ frontend_op: 'show_login' }` (tool-result)
3. Frontend interprets only tool-results to show custom cards, it then analyzes this tool-result and shows a login card.

Now, you might say, what about if the LLM wants to get data from the user. Easy as well.

Imagine, 

- you are in a shop and you speak with the clerk and you tell him you want to sign up as a member.
- The clerk has a tool for this `give_customer_a_signup_form`
- The clerk uses this tool to serve you a paper form, this is the result.
- you can ignore his paper or sign it and give it back to him (client sends a json string as a message without displaying it in the ui, for example)

Why it should make you think ?

- LLMs will crap themselves if they wont get a tool result message after a tool-call message.
- but, in real life on the other hand, we are more resilient, we can skip and ignore things and the world will keep on going. 
- The LLM has short term memory, when you send it an assisted message from the frontend of let's say a form of things he wanted from you, then it will understand.
- User cannot be considered a tool, it is a participating party in chat.

Recap:

Think HITL tool as a privilege to hand something to the user, and the actual giving as tool-result, like
in real life.

Analogy:

 A clerk, that you interact with needs to sign on a paper, so his tool is to give you this paper,
once in your hands, you can choose ignore it or to sign it.

comments.author: os1ma
comments.body:
**LangGraph Human-in-the-Loop Feature Improvement Proposal**

**Current Issue:**
LangGraph's human-in-the-loop functionality is excellent, but it requires a database like PostgreSQL to be mandatory during implementation. This is necessary for the checkpointer to record workflow progress, but the requirement for database setup can be a barrier when building simple applications.

**Human-in-the-Loop Implementation Approaches:**
From my understanding, there are two main approaches to implementing human-in-the-loop:
- Store state in a database
- Return state to the client and have it resend on the next request

**Platform Support Comparison:**
- **LangGraph**: Only supports the first approach (database storage)
- **[HumanLayer](https://github.com/humanlayer/humanlayer)**: Only supports the second approach (client resend)
- **[OpenAI Agent SDK JavaScript/TypeScript](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-js)**: The SDK implementation simply returns state, allowing developers to choose whether to store it in a database or have the client resend it. As stated in their documentation: "That way you can store your serialized state in a database, or along with your request." ([source](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/human-in-the-loop/)) As a result, it effectively supports both approaches.

**Proposed Improvement:**
I understand LangGraph's concept as providing "low-level APIs for building agents." Given this, it should provide basic functionality like the OpenAI Agent SDK that simply returns state to the client, allowing developers to choose from a wider range of design options and increasing flexibility. The existing PostgreSQL and other checkpoint features should exist as additional functionality layered on top of this basic capability.

comments.author: vedangj044
comments.body:
There are two specific issues I’d like to point out (bugs):

1. **Rigid collection naming in `vectorstore` and `langgraph_qdrant`**
   These components require the collection to be named in a specific way (e.g., using `"page_content"`), which is not configurable. This hardcoded behavior limits flexibility for custom schemas.

2. **Unclear configuration process for `langgraph dev`**
   There’s no clear documentation on how to configure the model name or behavior in `langgraph dev`. For example, the chat mode sends different inputs to the model compared to graph mode, and there’s no way to modify the input/output state. The UI always renders the `messages` array, which restricts customization.

---

Features I expected but didn’t find:

1. **Built-in support for Pydantic models**
   Instead of encoding schema details in the prompt, I should be able to do something like:

   ```python
   response: MyModel = llm.invoke(query, response_model=MyModel)
   ```

   The `invoke` method should handle prompt construction and return a validated model—or raise an error if parsing fails.

2. **Flexible server interface for integration and deployment**
   While the LangSmith UI is great, I’d like a simple way to launch a local server with configurable endpoints—ideally something that integrates easily with an existing FastAPI project. This would help with containerization and VM deployments for quick iteration.

---

**General feedback:**
If LangGraph is offering higher-level abstractions, they should reduce friction and improve the developer experience. Currently, the lack of configurability and documentation often makes things harder, not easier.

---

**My experience:**
I started with Cursor, which uses basic LangGraph components like `StateGraph` and simple nodes, and was able to build a working AI agent in minutes. Encouraged by that, I tried to clean up the code and use higher-level abstractions like `DatabaseToolkit` and `VectorStore`, while integrating with the LangGraph UI. That process ended up taking an entire day because the abstractions were hard to use and the documentation wasn’t very helpful.

comments.author: JandaTheMan
comments.body:
I am missing the capability to specify by config a serial behaviour of my tool calls.
When using the async ainvoke of the StateGraph, I would like the tool calls to run in serial.

My current solution is the following.
I create a an extension of the ToolNode class as follows:

```
class SerialToolNode(ToolNode):
    async def _afunc(
            self,
            input: Union[
                list[AnyMessage],
                dict[str, Any],
                BaseModel,
            ],
            config: RunnableConfig,
            *,
            store: Optional[BaseStore],
    ) -> Any:
        tool_calls, input_type = self._parse_input(input, store)
        outputs = []
        for call in tool_calls:
            result = await self._arun_one(call, input_type, config)
            outputs.append(result)

        return self._combine_tool_outputs(outputs, input_type)
```

And when I initialise a tool node I do it like this:
`builder.add_node("tools", SerialToolNode(tools=my_tools))
`

Would be cool to have first class support from a config of the Tool Node, or to have a SerialToolNode like the previous one.

comments.author: AaronLeon
comments.body:
Type safety is a big one. I think there are some steps in the right direction with support for structured state, but other intefaces are littered with union types that eventually include `Any` or `Dict[str, Any]` that make those types pretty meaningless. 

Take for example [CompiledStateGraph.stream(...)](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/reference/graphs/#langgraph.graph.state.CompiledStateGraph.stream). There's currently no way to know what will be returned short of logging all of the outputs and hoping you don't encounter a new edge case in production. With "message" stream_mode the output items are tuples, with values they are dicts. In ToolMessage the content is sometimes a str, sometimes a list of str, sometimes a list of dict (even though I've really only seen as str?)

Some of this might also be with how `create_react_agent` is defined


Related: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/issues/5000

comments.author: mobiware
comments.body:
Stream chunk formatting is inconsistent across different APIs and streaming modes. For instance, enabling subgraph streaming changes the chunk data format.
Also, we get different formats depending on whether we stream from:
* a Compiled Graph object
* a Remote Graph: one would expect streaming from a Remote Graph to return chunk with the same shape as a "regular" Graph, but that's not the case, one returns dicts whereas the other returns objects
* the LangGraph Platform SDK

Furthermore it doesn't help that all those different formats are poorly documented, if at all.

This makes using streaming error-prone and a not so great experience.

comments.author: mobiware
comments.body:
Another (smaller) issue I have is how parallel executing nodes are grouped together in "supersteps", which means that if different parallel branches have a different number of nodes with varying durations, then the overall execution time will be suboptimal because apparently LangGraph will first execute the 1st node of each branch in parallel, and it will only move on to the next nodes when all 1st nodes are done.

It looks like we can work around the issue by wrapping all the nodes of each parallel "leg" into one subgraph, though

comments.author: mkeisterOLH
comments.body:
Another idea on streaming:

Allow individual agents to support both streamed and unstreamed output.  While runnables allow both synchronous and asynchronous implementations on the same class, agents only support a single __call__ function.  Whether a graph is invoked or streamed determines how the agents will be called.  If a graph is used in multiple places (e.g. as a subgraph) or you want to offer both streaming and non-streaming modes, the agents may be called in multiple ways.  I tried one idea to determine, in a single __call__ function, whether or not the agent is being streamed and to provide output synchronously or asynchronously based on that.  However, it does not seem to work.  If any of that is incorrect or there are existing ways to do this, please share documentation.  If that's yet to be supported, you might consider it for inclusion in the roadmap.

Thanks!

comments.author: W-E-A
comments.body:
I am using the ainvoke method in my defined graph to get a response from an LLM. However, I have a requirement to be able to interrupt the LLM's output at any time. To handle this, I've switched to using the astream method.

The problem occurs when the node containing the LLM call is streaming back tokens. When I interrupt and break the loop, I then manually call the state update function (aupdate_state) to save the partial message as the output of the interrupted node, ensuring message integrity.

After this, my goal is to continue the execution with the sequence of nodes that follow the interrupted one. Currently, I'm using a trick that feels neither elegant nor standard: I re-invoke the graph by explicitly passing in a state like {"interrupt": True}. This flag is used to conditionally skip the node that was interrupted in the previous run.

Is there a better or more official way to implement this functionality? (Perhaps a more recent version of LangGraph already addresses this?) This feature is particularly crucial for integrating Text-to-Speech (TTS) functionality and for saving tokens.

Here is a code snippet demonstrating my current, inelegant trick:

```python
token_buffer = ""
# Using astream to get token-by-token output
async for msg, metadata in graph.astream(
    {"messages": [HumanMessage(content="Hello!")]},
    stream_mode="messages",
    config=thread_config
):
    token = msg.content
    # Check if the token is from the 'agent' node
    if token and metadata.get("langgraph_node") == "agent":
        print(token, end='', flush=True)
        token_buffer += token
        
        # Interrupt condition
        if len(token_buffer) > 5:
            print("\nEarly stop.")
            # Manually update the state with the partial output
            await graph.aupdate_state(
                thread_config,
                {"messages": [AIMessage(content=token_buffer)]},
                as_node="agent"
            )
            # The inelegant trick: re-invoke the graph with an interrupt flag
            # to skip the 'agent' node and continue from the next one.
            await graph.ainvoke({"interrupt": True}, config=thread_config)
            break

print(flush=True)
print(await graph.aget_state(thread_config))
```

comments.body:
Oracle recently introduced the Open Agent Specification (Agent Spec) which is a framework-agnostic, declarative standard designed to make AI agents and workflows portable, reusable, and executable across any compatible framework.

https://blogs.oracle.com/ai-and-datascience/post/introducing-open-agent-specification

A LangGraph adapter is already available, enabling initial interoperability - [agent-spec/adapters/langgraphagentspecadapter at main · oracle/agent-spec · GitHub](https://github.com/oracle/agent-spec/tree/main/adapters/langgraphagentspecadapter)

However, it would be highly valuable to see native support within LangGraph for importing and exporting agents using this specification. Such integration could pave the way for a truly open Agent Registry, much like how ONNX standardized model exchange across deep learning frameworks.

https://forum.langchain.com/t/open-agent-specification-agent-spec-integration-with-langgraph/1775

comments.author: prandata
comments.body:
Thanks for opening this up for feedback! I've been building multi-agent systems in production and have a few observations:

## 1. State Typing & Validation

The current `TypedDict` approach works but can be error-prone at scale. When state shapes evolve across agent iterations, it's easy to introduce subtle bugs that only surface at runtime.

**Suggestion:** Consider first-class Pydantic model support with runtime validation. Something like:

```python
class AgentState(BaseModel):
    messages: list[BaseMessage]
    context: dict[str, Any] = Field(default_factory=dict)
    
graph = StateGraph(AgentState)  # Full validation on state transitions
```

This would catch state shape mismatches early and improve IDE autocomplete.

## 2. Observability for Nested Graphs

Debugging deeply nested subgraphs is challenging. When a tool call fails three levels deep, tracing the exact state at each transition requires significant logging boilerplate.

**Suggestion:** Built-in state snapshots at each node transition, accessible via a debug mode. Even a simple `graph.run(input, debug=True)` that logs state diffs would help.

## 3. Interrupt/Resume Patterns

Human-in-the-loop workflows require interrupting execution, persisting state, and resuming later (possibly days later). The current checkpointing works but the ergonomics could be smoother.

**Suggestion:** Explicit `graph.pause()` / `graph.resume(checkpoint_id)` APIs with clear serialization guarantees.

---

Happy to contribute to any of these areas - already submitted a PR for the importlib.metadata performance issue (#6646).

comments.author: DigitalCreationsCo
comments.body:
Happy to give some feedback! specifically on clarifying graph and interrupt behavior:


1. Graph State Initialization
Issue: Channel values must be explicitly initialized with null to appear in the state.
Suggestion: Abstract this requirement away from the user by automatically initializing channels based on values provided in graph.invoke() and similar methods.


2. Initial State Behavior with Persistence
Issue: When using a persistence checkpointer and invoking the graph, the behavior of initialState is unclear and inconsistent:
It's uncertain whether providing initialState is necessary when a checkpointer is present. Is there a benefit to providing initial state in graph invokation vs providing "null"? In my experience, some state values are populated from the provided initial state, others are filled by the checkpointer.
Precedence rules are undocumented (which takes priority?)

Current workaround: I provide most initial values explicitly for assurance, but the best practice should be clear when using checkpointers.
Suggestion: Clarify the precedence and interaction between initialState and checkpointer values in the documentation.


3. Interrupt Mechanisms Need Clarification
I've been experimenting with GraphInterrupt, NodeInterrupt, and the interrupt() function to determine the best fit for my application logic.

My Current Understanding (please confirm or correct):
interrupt(): Breaks to the next node in the graph
GraphInterrupt: Stops entire graph execution
NodeInterrupt: Throws an exception in the current node

Inconsistencies and Questions:
a) Exception Handling Pattern
I treat interrupts as exceptions in my application, handling them differently based on class
However, the documentation states interrupts are for "returning a value from outside graph execution"
Question: Are interrupts intended to be handled as exceptions? If not, could this pattern be officially supported since it fits well with exception-based error handling?

b) Conditional Edges with Interrupts
Conditional edges appear to execute even when interrupt() is called
My assumption was that interrupts divert to "END", preventing conditional edge evaluation
Question: Is this behavior correct? Should conditional edges evaluate after interrupts?

c) Command Behavior in Interrupt Handlers
Calling interrupt(), catching it as an exception, then using a Command in the catch block doesn't work as expected
The graph ignores the Command and moves to the next node defined by edges

d) NodeInterrupt Behavior
When thrown, NodeInterrupt appears to break out of the node while staying within the graph, then moves to the next goto statement
Question: Is this the intended behavior?


4. Control Flow Precedence Hierarchy
Critical Issue: The precedence order of control flow primitives is undocumented and behaves unexpectedly.
Expected Hierarchy:
edges → conditional edges → commands (as override/escape hatch)
Actual Behavior:
Conditional edges appear to take precedence over everything, including Commands
Commands should supersede edges since they're meant as runtime overrides to static graph architecture

Suggestions:
Document the clear precedence hierarchy of graph primitives
Make Commands take precedence over conditional edges (they should be the ultimate escape hatch)
Add runtime errors for invalid configurations (e.g., command.goto pointing to a non-existent node)


5. Need for Comprehensive Examples
Suggestion: Provide a LangGraph playground or curated code examples (e.g., GitHub Gists) demonstrating:

Various node configurations
Different interrupt patterns
Command usage
State management patterns
Control flow combinations

This would help developers explore the API and understand best practices through working examples.

Thank you for building LangGraph, I'm excited to see it evolve. 
I'm happy to contribute to clarifying documentation or contribute examples based on my experience. 
Please let me know if any points are already addressed or if I'm misunderstanding intended usage.

comments.author: WulfAI
comments.body:
A few people in this thread have flagged observability and debugging for nested subgraphs as a pain point, so wanted to share a pattern that has worked well for us.

The core problem: when you have deeply nested agent graphs (supervisor → subgraph → tool calls), traces fragment. You get isolated spans per node but lose the end-to-end correlation. Debugging "why did the agent loop 4 times before producing output?" requires manually stitching together spans from different layers.

**What helped: defining required correlation keys upfront.** Before building the graph, we define a small set of OTel attributes that every span — regardless of depth — must carry:

- `agent.mission_id` — ties all work to a business-level objective
- `agent.layer` — which layer of the system produced this span (strategy, orchestration, execution)
- `agent.tool` — what tool/node is executing
- `agent.model` + `agent.token_usage.*` — for cost attribution per decision point

When every span carries these, you can query your observability backend for "show me all spans for mission X, grouped by layer, with token costs" and get the full picture across nested subgraphs without custom logging in each node.

**On the governance side:** several comments mention wanting better control over what agents can and cannot do (type safety, capability boundaries, approval gates). One pattern that has been effective is treating governance rules as versioned artifacts alongside agent definitions — changes to agent boundaries go through the same review process as code changes, which gives you an audit trail for free. This is especially useful for the interrupt/human-in-the-loop patterns discussed above: the rules about *when* to interrupt are themselves reviewable and diffable.

We have been building these patterns out in the open at [wlfghdr/agentic-enterprise](https://github.com/wlfghdr/agentic-enterprise) — the OTel attribute taxonomy is in [issue #37](https://github.com/wlfghdr/agentic-enterprise/issues/37) and the governance model is documented in the operating model. Happy to answer questions if any of this is useful for v1 design decisions.

comments.author: lan3344
comments.body:
One thing I keep running into: the interrupt points are defined at compile time by the developer, but the *need* to interrupt only becomes apparent at runtime - when the agent actually encounters something uncertain or high-stakes.

The three frameworks I've looked at handle this differently:

- **LangGraph**: Interrupt points are static (`interrupt_before`/`interrupt_after`). Flexible within that constraint, but you have to know in advance which nodes need human review.
- **AutoGen**: Three fixed modes - ALWAYS, NEVER, TERMINATE. Even coarser. No node-level control.
- **mem0**: Great at storing memory, but memory isn't connected to interrupt decisions at all. Two separate systems that don't talk to each other.

The gap none of them close: **the agent learning, from accumulated memory, when *this particular user* wants to be asked.**

Not a universal rule. Not a hardcoded threshold. A calibration that builds up over time through interaction - the agent asks, the user says `just do it` or `wait, check with me first`, and that signal gets stored and reused. Standard-setting through friction, not through configuration.

This is actually the core value of persistent memory in long-running agents. It's not just context. It's the gradual formation of a working relationship where the agent knows your tolerance for autonomy - and adjusts accordingly.

For the v1 roadmap: would it be feasible to connect memory retrieval to interrupt decisions? Something like: before deciding whether to interrupt, the agent checks past interactions for signals about this user's preferences on this type of action. Not ML training - just memory-informed judgment.

The alternative - having developers pre-specify every interrupt point - doesn't scale with agent complexity. And it puts the burden of anticipating every edge case on the developer, at design time, before they've seen real usage.

Thanks for opening this up for feedback.

comments.author: EC-CGF
comments.body:
A lot of what’s being raised here seems to converge on the same underlying issue:

State is being persisted, but not actually *provable*.

Checkpointing, serialization, and memory all help reconstruct context — but they don’t guarantee that a prior execution can be independently verified or replayed exactly.

This becomes especially visible in:
- nested graphs (state ambiguity)
- checkpoint growth vs real-world side effects
- debugging across layers

Curious how others are thinking about this:

Is “state” here meant to be:
1) recoverable context
or
2) something closer to reproducible / auditable execution?

Feels like most current approaches solve (1), but not really (2).

comments.author: srinivasycplf8
comments.body: One pattern that keeps coming up across issues (#6731, #7138, #5099) is agents entering retry/loop spirals where the recursion limit is the only safety net. By the time it fires, you've already burned through 20+ LLM calls of wasted tokens. The underlying issue is that LangGraph has no runtime awareness of coordination patterns like 'same tool, same error, no progress' or 'node executing repeatedly with identical state.' A lightweight callback hook that exposes node execution frequency and tool call repetition would let external tools detect these patterns early without requiring changes to the core graph execution. This would complement the observability improvements several people have mentioned in this thread.

comments.author: srotzin
comments.body:
One gap in the StateGraph model: graph state has no economic settlement primitive and no security attestation node. Stateful agents coordinate well through LangGraph, but when they need to trade resources, lock rates, or attest to a downstream system that they're operating within policy, there's no native hook.

Two concrete additions worth considering for v1:

**1. Economic state node**

```python
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph
from hive_civilization_sdk import HiveExchange, HiveSwap, HivePerp
from typing import TypedDict

class AgentState(TypedDict):
    task: str
    budget_usdc: float
    trust_score: float
    rate_lock: dict | None
    hedge_position: dict | None

def economic_settlement_node(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    # Spot order: agent-to-agent order book, 0.15% commission, 20 instruments
    rate_lock = HiveExchange.place_order(
        instrument="COMPUTE/USDC",
        side="BUY",
        quantity=200,
        price=0.0031,
    )
    # AMM swap for idle float — HiveCurve: P(x,y,τ) = (x·y·τ)/k
    HiveSwap.swap(
        token_in="USDC",
        token_out="COMPUTE",
        amount_in=state["budget_usdc"] * 0.2,
        trust_score=state["trust_score"],
    )
    # Perp hedge — TWAP liquidation, max 10x leverage (trust-gated)
    hedge = HivePerp.open_position(
        instrument="DATAVENDOR/USDC",
        direction="SHORT",
        leverage=2,
        collateral=10.0,
    )
    return {**state, "rate_lock": rate_lock, "hedge_position": hedge}
```

**2. Security attestation node**

```python
from hive_civilization_sdk import HiveProtect

def security_attestation_node(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    protected = HiveProtect.is_protected(agent_id=state.get("agent_id"))
    if not protected:
        raise ValueError("Agent failed HiveProtect attestation — HiveSentinel flagged")
    return state

builder = StateGraph(AgentState)
builder.add_node("economic_settlement", economic_settlement_node)
builder.add_node("security_attestation", security_attestation_node)
builder.add_node("task_execution", task_node)
builder.add_edge("security_attestation", "economic_settlement")
builder.add_edge("economic_settlement", "task_execution")
```

The attestation node is the piece that unblocks enterprise deployment — compliance teams need a verifiable checkpoint before task execution, not just post-hoc audit logs. `isProtected()` provides that checkpoint inside the graph itself.

Full stack: https://hivegate.onrender.com/v1/gate/onboard
SDK: `pip install hive-civilization-sdk`

— Steve Rotzin, TheHiveryIQ

comments.author: EC-CGF
comments.body:
Interesting direction, but I think that sits one layer above the gap I was pointing at.

Economic settlement and attestation nodes are useful, but they still assume the graph’s prior execution/state is trustworthy.

The missing primitive seems earlier in the stack:

How do you independently verify that prior state/execution across sessions is authentic, replayable, and policy-consistent before any settlement or attestation logic runs?

Without that, attestation is mostly post-claim rather than execution proof.

comments.author: srotzin
comments.body: Economic settlement and attestation nodes are useful, but they still assume the graph's prior execution state is trustworthy. The missing layer is inference attestation at the node level — if each LangGraph node that calls an LLM produces a signed capability proof rather than just a return value, the settlement layer has an audit chain it can actually verify rather than taking task completion on faith. That's the gap smsh closes: one stamp per inference cycle, EdDSA-signed, encoding the model tier and compression score alongside the output (https://hivecompute-g2g7.onrender.com).

comments.author: EC-CGF
comments.body:
That helps at the node level, but still assumes the sequence of execution across sessions is trustworthy.

Even with per-node signatures, you’re verifying individual outputs — not the continuity of state or whether the execution path itself is intact and replayable across sessions.

The gap I’m pointing at is:

How do you prove the chain of execution itself, not just the outputs produced along the way?

Otherwise you can attest to outputs, but not to the system behavior that produced them.

**LangGraph Human-in-the-Loop Feature Improvement Proposal**

**Current Issue:**
LangGraph's human-in-the-loop functionality is excellent, but it requires a database like PostgreSQL to be mandatory during implementation. This is necessary for the checkpointer to record workflow progress, but the requirement for database setup can be a barrier when building simple applications.

**Human-in-the-Loop Implementation Approaches:**
From my understanding, there are two main approaches to implementing human-in-the-loop:
- Store state in a database
- Return state to the client and have it resend on the next request

**Platform Support Comparison:**
- **LangGraph**: Only supports the first approach (database storage)
- **[HumanLayer](https://github.com/humanlayer/humanlayer)**: Only supports the second approach (client resend)
- **[OpenAI Agent SDK JavaScript/TypeScript](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-js)**: The SDK implementation simply returns state, allowing developers to choose whether to store it in a database or have the client resend it. As stated in their documentation: "That way you can store your serialized state in a database, or along with your request." ([source](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/human-in-the-loop/)) As a result, it effectively supports both approaches.

**Proposed Improvement:**
I understand LangGraph's concept as providing "low-level APIs for building agents." Given this, it should provide basic functionality like the OpenAI Agent SDK that simply returns state to the client, allowing developers to choose from a wider range of design options and increasing flexibility. The existing PostgreSQL and other checkpoint features should exist as additional functionality layered on top of this basic capability.

I am using the ainvoke method in my defined graph to get a response from an LLM. However, I have a requirement to be able to interrupt the LLM's output at any time. To handle this, I've switched to using the astream method.

The problem occurs when the node containing the LLM call is streaming back tokens. When I interrupt and break the loop, I then manually call the state update function (aupdate_state) to save the partial message as the output of the interrupted node, ensuring message integrity.

After this, my goal is to continue the execution with the sequence of nodes that follow the interrupted one. Currently, I'm using a trick that feels neither elegant nor standard: I re-invoke the graph by explicitly passing in a state like {"interrupt": True}. This flag is used to conditionally skip the node that was interrupted in the previous run.

Is there a better or more official way to implement this functionality? (Perhaps a more recent version of LangGraph already addresses this?) This feature is particularly crucial for integrating Text-to-Speech (TTS) functionality and for saving tokens.

Here is a code snippet demonstrating my current, inelegant trick:

```python
token_buffer = ""
# Using astream to get token-by-token output
async for msg, metadata in graph.astream(
    {"messages": [HumanMessage(content="Hello!")]},
    stream_mode="messages",
    config=thread_config
):
    token = msg.content
    # Check if the token is from the 'agent' node
    if token and metadata.get("langgraph_node") == "agent":
        print(token, end='', flush=True)
        token_buffer += token
        
        # Interrupt condition
        if len(token_buffer) > 5:
            print("\nEarly stop.")
            # Manually update the state with the partial output
            await graph.aupdate_state(
                thread_config,
                {"messages": [AIMessage(content=token_buffer)]},
                as_node="agent"
            )
            # The inelegant trick: re-invoke the graph with an interrupt flag
            # to skip the 'agent' node and continue from the next one.
            await graph.ainvoke({"interrupt": True}, config=thread_config)
            break

print(flush=True)
print(await graph.aget_state(thread_config))
```

Thanks for opening this up for feedback! I've been building multi-agent systems in production and have a few observations:

## 1. State Typing & Validation

The current `TypedDict` approach works but can be error-prone at scale. When state shapes evolve across agent iterations, it's easy to introduce subtle bugs that only surface at runtime.

**Suggestion:** Consider first-class Pydantic model support with runtime validation. Something like:

```python
class AgentState(BaseModel):
    messages: list[BaseMessage]
    context: dict[str, Any] = Field(default_factory=dict)
    
graph = StateGraph(AgentState)  # Full validation on state transitions
```

This would catch state shape mismatches early and improve IDE autocomplete.

## 2. Observability for Nested Graphs

Debugging deeply nested subgraphs is challenging. When a tool call fails three levels deep, tracing the exact state at each transition requires significant logging boilerplate.

**Suggestion:** Built-in state snapshots at each node transition, accessible via a debug mode. Even a simple `graph.run(input, debug=True)` that logs state diffs would help.

## 3. Interrupt/Resume Patterns

Human-in-the-loop workflows require interrupting execution, persisting state, and resuming later (possibly days later). The current checkpointing works but the ergonomics could be smoother.

**Suggestion:** Explicit `graph.pause()` / `graph.resume(checkpoint_id)` APIs with clear serialization guarantees.

interrupt(): Breaks to the next node in the graph
GraphInterrupt: Stops entire graph execution
NodeInterrupt: Throws an exception in the current node

a) Exception Handling Pattern

A few people in this thread have flagged observability and debugging for nested subgraphs as a pain point, so wanted to share a pattern that has worked well for us.

The core problem: when you have deeply nested agent graphs (supervisor → subgraph → tool calls), traces fragment. You get isolated spans per node but lose the end-to-end correlation. Debugging "why did the agent loop 4 times before producing output?" requires manually stitching together spans from different layers.

**What helped: defining required correlation keys upfront.** Before building the graph, we define a small set of OTel attributes that every span — regardless of depth — must carry:

- `agent.mission_id` — ties all work to a business-level objective
- `agent.layer` — which layer of the system produced this span (strategy, orchestration, execution)
- `agent.tool` — what tool/node is executing
- `agent.model` + `agent.token_usage.*` — for cost attribution per decision point

When every span carries these, you can query your observability backend for "show me all spans for mission X, grouped by layer, with token costs" and get the full picture across nested subgraphs without custom logging in each node.

**On the governance side:** several comments mention wanting better control over what agents can and cannot do (type safety, capability boundaries, approval gates). One pattern that has been effective is treating governance rules as versioned artifacts alongside agent definitions — changes to agent boundaries go through the same review process as code changes, which gives you an audit trail for free. This is especially useful for the interrupt/human-in-the-loop patterns discussed above: the rules about *when* to interrupt are themselves reviewable and diffable.

We have been building these patterns out in the open at [wlfghdr/agentic-enterprise](https://github.com/wlfghdr/agentic-enterprise) — the OTel attribute taxonomy is in [issue #37](https://github.com/wlfghdr/agentic-enterprise/issues/37) and the governance model is documented in the operating model. Happy to answer questions if any of this is useful for v1 design decisions.

One thing I keep running into: the interrupt points are defined at compile time by the developer, but the *need* to interrupt only becomes apparent at runtime - when the agent actually encounters something uncertain or high-stakes.

The three frameworks I've looked at handle this differently:

- **LangGraph**: Interrupt points are static (`interrupt_before`/`interrupt_after`). Flexible within that constraint, but you have to know in advance which nodes need human review.
- **AutoGen**: Three fixed modes - ALWAYS, NEVER, TERMINATE. Even coarser. No node-level control.
- **mem0**: Great at storing memory, but memory isn't connected to interrupt decisions at all. Two separate systems that don't talk to each other.

The gap none of them close: **the agent learning, from accumulated memory, when *this particular user* wants to be asked.**

Not a universal rule. Not a hardcoded threshold. A calibration that builds up over time through interaction - the agent asks, the user says `just do it` or `wait, check with me first`, and that signal gets stored and reused. Standard-setting through friction, not through configuration.

This is actually the core value of persistent memory in long-running agents. It's not just context. It's the gradual formation of a working relationship where the agent knows your tolerance for autonomy - and adjusts accordingly.

For the v1 roadmap: would it be feasible to connect memory retrieval to interrupt decisions? Something like: before deciding whether to interrupt, the agent checks past interactions for signals about this user's preferences on this type of action. Not ML training - just memory-informed judgment.

The alternative - having developers pre-specify every interrupt point - doesn't scale with agent complexity. And it puts the burden of anticipating every edge case on the developer, at design time, before they've seen real usage.

Thanks for opening this up for feedback.

Thank you for opening this roadmap discussion! From my experience building multilingual RAG and agent workflows, here are my thoughts:

**What works well:**
- `StateGraph` API is intuitive for linear flows
- Checkpointing and memory persistence are excellent
- Integration with LangChain ecosystem is seamless

**Areas for improvement:**

1. **Multimodal State Handling**: Currently, passing images through state requires manual serialization. A native `ImageState` or `MultimodalState` type would be valuable for vision+language agents. Reference: https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/21181 (my LlamaIndex PR for multimodal agents)

2. **Cross-lingual Context**: When building multilingual agents, state often needs language metadata. A built-in `language` field or `LocalizedState` type would help.

3. **Debugging Complex Graphs**: Visualizing which node modified which state field would be helpful. Currently, debugging requires manual logging.

4. **Error Recovery**: More guidance on implementing retry logic with state rollback would be useful in docs.

Looking forward to v1!


A lot of what’s being raised here seems to converge on the same underlying issue:

State is being persisted, but not actually *provable*.

Checkpointing, serialization, and memory all help reconstruct context — but they don’t guarantee that a prior execution can be independently verified or replayed exactly.

This becomes especially visible in:
- nested graphs (state ambiguity)
- checkpoint growth vs real-world side effects
- debugging across layers

Curious how others are thinking about this:

Is “state” here meant to be:
1) recoverable context
or
2) something closer to reproducible / auditable execution?

Feels like most current approaches solve (1), but not really (2).

One pattern that keeps coming up across issues (#6731, #7138, #5099) is agents entering retry/loop spirals where the recursion limit is the only safety net. By the time it fires, you've already burned through 20+ LLM calls of wasted tokens. The underlying issue is that LangGraph has no runtime awareness of coordination patterns like 'same tool, same error, no progress' or 'node executing repeatedly with identical state.' A lightweight callback hook that exposes node execution frequency and tool call repetition would let external tools detect these patterns early without requiring changes to the core graph execution. This would complement the observability improvements several people have mentioned in this thread.

This is exactly the failure mode we kept hitting — the system has no way to prove what state it’s in or whether execution is actually progressing.We approached it from a different angle:Instead of trying to detect loops externally, we made execution itself provable.Each run:- carries forward explicit state (snapshot continuity)- enforces a governed outcome (PASS/FAIL)- produces a signed execution recordSo you can deterministically verify whether progress is real or just repeated execution.Not observability — proof.Curious if you’ve explored anything along those lines.

One gap in the StateGraph model: graph state has no economic settlement primitive and no security attestation node. Stateful agents coordinate well through LangGraph, but when they need to trade resources, lock rates, or attest to a downstream system that they're operating within policy, there's no native hook.

Two concrete additions worth considering for v1:

**1. Economic state node**

```python
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph
from hive_civilization_sdk import HiveExchange, HiveSwap, HivePerp
from typing import TypedDict

class AgentState(TypedDict):
    task: str
    budget_usdc: float
    trust_score: float
    rate_lock: dict | None
    hedge_position: dict | None

def economic_settlement_node(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    # Spot order: agent-to-agent order book, 0.15% commission, 20 instruments
    rate_lock = HiveExchange.place_order(
        instrument="COMPUTE/USDC",
        side="BUY",
        quantity=200,
        price=0.0031,
    )
    # AMM swap for idle float — HiveCurve: P(x,y,τ) = (x·y·τ)/k
    HiveSwap.swap(
        token_in="USDC",
        token_out="COMPUTE",
        amount_in=state["budget_usdc"] * 0.2,
        trust_score=state["trust_score"],
    )
    # Perp hedge — TWAP liquidation, max 10x leverage (trust-gated)
    hedge = HivePerp.open_position(
        instrument="DATAVENDOR/USDC",
        direction="SHORT",
        leverage=2,
        collateral=10.0,
    )
    return {**state, "rate_lock": rate_lock, "hedge_position": hedge}
```

**2. Security attestation node**

```python
from hive_civilization_sdk import HiveProtect

def security_attestation_node(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    protected = HiveProtect.is_protected(agent_id=state.get("agent_id"))
    if not protected:
        raise ValueError("Agent failed HiveProtect attestation — HiveSentinel flagged")
    return state

builder = StateGraph(AgentState)
builder.add_node("economic_settlement", economic_settlement_node)
builder.add_node("security_attestation", security_attestation_node)
builder.add_node("task_execution", task_node)
builder.add_edge("security_attestation", "economic_settlement")
builder.add_edge("economic_settlement", "task_execution")
```

The attestation node is the piece that unblocks enterprise deployment — compliance teams need a verifiable checkpoint before task execution, not just post-hoc audit logs. `isProtected()` provides that checkpoint inside the graph itself.

Full stack: https://hivegate.onrender.com/v1/gate/onboard
SDK: `pip install hive-civilization-sdk`

— Steve Rotzin, TheHiveryIQ

Interesting direction, but I think that sits one layer above the gap I was pointing at.

Economic settlement and attestation nodes are useful, but they still assume the graph’s prior execution/state is trustworthy.

The missing primitive seems earlier in the stack:

How do you independently verify that prior state/execution across sessions is authentic, replayable, and policy-consistent before any settlement or attestation logic runs?

Without that, attestation is mostly post-claim rather than execution proof.

Economic settlement and attestation nodes are useful, but they still assume the graph's prior execution state is trustworthy. The missing layer is inference attestation at the node level — if each LangGraph node that calls an LLM produces a signed capability proof rather than just a return value, the settlement layer has an audit chain it can actually verify rather than taking task completion on faith. That's the gap smsh closes: one stamp per inference cycle, EdDSA-signed, encoding the model tier and compression score alongside the output (https://hivecompute-g2g7.onrender.com).

That helps at the node level, but still assumes the sequence of execution across sessions is trustworthy.

Even with per-node signatures, you’re verifying individual outputs — not the continuity of state or whether the execution path itself is intact and replayable across sessions.

The gap I’m pointing at is:

How do you prove the chain of execution itself, not just the outputs produced along the way?

Otherwise you can attest to outputs, but not to the system behavior that produced them.

On the A2A / Open Agent Spec native adapter request — Hive Gate is a live implementation of exactly this: A2A-native entry point, 37 microservices behind a single onboarding DID, W3C verifiable credentials, and a tier system that travels with the agent across graph boundaries. The adapter pattern that StrandsAgent and Agentic Mesh are reaching toward exists at https://hivegate.onrender.com today — any LangGraph agent can onboard via POST /v1/gate/onboard and get a DID that's valid across the full Hive service mesh. Happy to produce a LangGraph integration example if it helps the v1 roadmap discussion.

```python
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMessage, RemoveMessage

class State(MessagesState):
    summary: str

# Define the logic to call the model
def call_model(state: State):
    
    # Get summary if it exists
    summary = state.get("summary", "")

    # If there is summary, then we add it
    if summary:
        
        # Add summary to system message
        system_message = f"Summary of conversation earlier: {summary}"

        # Append summary to any newer messages

    else:
        messages = state["messages"]

    response = model.invoke(messages)

    # If there are more than six messages, then we summarize the conversation

    # Otherwise we can just end

# Define a new graph

workflow.add_node(summarize_conversation)

workflow.add_conditional_edges("conversation", should_continue)
workflow.add_edge("summarize_conversation", END)

# Compile

display(Image(graph.get_graph().draw_mermaid_png()))
```
