title: LangGraph API 0.7.60: Redis TLS cluster PubSub fails with port 0 (go-redis v9.18.0 regression)
body:
## Description

LangGraph API **v0.7.60** fails to stream run results when using a **TLS-only Redis cluster** (`--port 0 --tls-port 6379`). The Go runtime's PubSub component connects to port 0 instead of the correct TLS port 6379. Version **0.7.56** works correctly.

## Error

```
HTTPException(500: failed to get Redis client for thread)
```

Go runtime logs:
```
dial tcp 172.30.0.12:0: connect: connection refused
component=pubsub node_address=172.30.0.12:0
```

## Root cause

The upgrade of `github.com/redis/go-redis/v9` from **v9.17.3** (in 0.7.56) to **v9.18.0** (in 0.7.60). Filed upstream: https://github.com/redis/go-redis/issues/3726

Standard Redis operations work fine — only PubSub connections get the wrong port. This means thread creation succeeds, but streaming (which uses PubSub) fails.

## Reproduction

Full reproduction environment with docker-compose:

### docker-compose.yml
```yaml
networks:
  redis-net:
    driver: bridge
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.30.0.0/24

services:
  redis-1: &redis-node
    image: redis:7
    command: >
      redis-server
      --port 0
      --tls-port 6379
      --tls-cert-file /tls/redis-cert.pem
      --tls-key-file /tls/redis-key.pem
      --tls-ca-cert-file /tls/ca-cert.pem
      --tls-replication yes
      --tls-cluster yes
      --cluster-enabled yes
      --cluster-config-file nodes.conf
      --cluster-node-timeout 5000
      --tls-auth-clients no
      --appendonly yes
    volumes:
      - ./tls:/tls:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: redis-cli --tls --cert /tls/redis-cert.pem --key /tls/redis-key.pem --cacert /tls/ca-cert.pem ping
      interval: 3s
      timeout: 2s
      retries: 5
    networks:
      redis-net:
        ipv4_address: 172.30.0.11

  redis-2:
    <<: *redis-node
    networks: { redis-net: { ipv4_address: 172.30.0.12 } }
  redis-3:
    <<: *redis-node
    networks: { redis-net: { ipv4_address: 172.30.0.13 } }
  redis-4:
    <<: *redis-node
    networks: { redis-net: { ipv4_address: 172.30.0.14 } }
  redis-5:
    <<: *redis-node
    networks: { redis-net: { ipv4_address: 172.30.0.15 } }
  redis-6:
    <<: *redis-node
    networks: { redis-net: { ipv4_address: 172.30.0.16 } }

  redis-init:
    image: redis:7
    volumes:
      - ./tls:/tls:ro
    depends_on:
      redis-1: { condition: service_healthy }
      redis-2: { condition: service_healthy }
      redis-3: { condition: service_healthy }
      redis-4: { condition: service_healthy }
      redis-5: { condition: service_healthy }
      redis-6: { condition: service_healthy }
    entrypoint: >
      bash -c "redis-cli --tls --cert /tls/redis-cert.pem --key /tls/redis-key.pem
      --cacert /tls/ca-cert.pem --cluster create
      redis-1:6379 redis-2:6379 redis-3:6379 redis-4:6379 redis-5:6379 redis-6:6379
      --cluster-replicas 1 --cluster-yes && tail -f /dev/null"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "bash", "-c", "redis-cli --tls --cert /tls/redis-cert.pem --key /tls/redis-key.pem --cacert /tls/ca-cert.pem -h redis-1 -c cluster info | grep cluster_state:ok"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20
    networks: { redis-net: { ipv4_address: 172.30.0.10 } }

  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: postgres
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
    healthcheck:
      test: pg_isready -U postgres
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 1s
      retries: 5
    networks: { redis-net: { ipv4_address: 172.30.0.20 } }

  langgraph-api:
    build:
      context: .
      args:
        LANGGRAPH_VERSION: "${LANGGRAPH_VERSION:-0.7.60}"
    ports:
      - "2025:8000"
    volumes:
      - ./tls:/tls:ro
    depends_on:
      redis-init: { condition: service_healthy }
```

## Description

LangGraph API **v0.7.60** fails to stream run results when using a **TLS-only Redis cluster** (`--port 0 --tls-port 6379`). The Go runtime's PubSub component connects to port 0 instead of the correct TLS port 6379. Version **0.7.56** works correctly.

## Error

```
HTTPException(500: failed to get Redis client for thread)
```

Go runtime logs:

```
dial tcp 172.30.0.12:0: connect: connection refused
component=pubsub node_address=172.30.0.12:0
```

title: Type-Safe Streaming and Invoke for LangGraph
body:
# Type-Safe Streaming and Invoke for LangGraph

## The Problem

LangGraph's `.stream()`, `.astream()`, `.invoke()`, and `.ainvoke()` methods have **no meaningful type information** today. Regardless of which `stream_mode` you use, the return type is `Iterator[Any]` — you get no autocomplete, no type checking, and no way for your editor to tell you what shape the data is in.

This is especially painful when:

- **Using Pydantic or dataclass state schemas** — you define a typed schema but get plain `dict` objects back from streaming and invoke.
- **Switching between stream modes** — each mode returns a completely different shape (`dict`, `tuple[AnyMessage, dict]`, `Any`, etc.), but the type system can't help you remember which is which.
- **Handling interrupts** — the `__interrupt__` key is mixed into the state dictionary, which pollutes your state, breaks Pydantic/dataclass coercion, and forces manual filtering.

### Why not just use `@overload`?

Python's only mechanism for "parameter X controls return type Y" is `@overload`. The matrix is 8 stream modes x 2 subgraph values = **16+ overloads per method**, across `stream`/`astream` on `Pregel`, `PregelProtocol`, `RemoteGraph`, and the SDK. A proof-of-concept required hundreds of signatures and was still incomplete. Every new stream mode multiplies the combinatorics — this approach is unsustainable.

## Proposal: `stream_version="v2"` with typed stream parts

We're adding a `stream_version: Literal["v1", "v2"]` parameter (defaulting to `"v1"`) to `.stream()`, `.astream()`, `.invoke()`, and `.ainvoke()`. When `stream_version="v2"`, every chunk is a self-describing `StreamPart` TypedDict with a `type` discriminator:

```python
from langgraph.types import StreamPart, ValuesStreamPart, UpdatesStreamPart

async for part in graph.astream(inputs, stream_version="v2"):
    if part["type"] == "values":
        # part is narrowed to ValuesStreamPart
        # part["data"] is your output type (Pydantic model, dataclass, or dict)
        # part["interrupts"] is tuple[Interrupt, ...]
        print(part["data"])
    elif part["type"] == "updates":
        # part is narrowed to UpdatesStreamPart
        # part["data"] is dict[str, Any] mapping node names to outputs
        print(part["data"])
    elif part["type"] == "messages":
        # part is narrowed to MessagesStreamPart
        # part["data"] is tuple[AnyMessage, dict[str, Any]]
        print(part["data"])
```

### Stream part types

Every v2 stream part is a TypedDict with three common keys: `type`, `ns`, and `data`. The `type` field is a `Literal` that enables type narrowing:

| `type` | TypedDict | `data` type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `"values"` | `ValuesStreamPart` | `OutputT` (Pydantic model, dataclass, or dict) | Also has `interrupts: tuple[Interrupt, ...]` |
| `"updates"` | `UpdatesStreamPart` | `dict[str, Any]` | Node name -> output mapping |
| `"messages"` | `MessagesStreamPart` | `tuple[AnyMessage, dict[str, Any]]` | (message, metadata) pair |
| `"custom"` | `CustomStreamPart` | `Any` | Whatever was passed to `StreamWriter` |
| `"checkpoints"` | `CheckpointStreamPart` | `CheckpointPayload` | Checkpoint metadata with typed values |
| `"tasks"` | `TasksStreamPart` | `TaskPayload \| TaskResultPayload` | Task start/result events |
| `"debug"` | `DebugStreamPart` | `DebugPayload` | Debug events (checkpoint, task, task_result) |

The full union type:

```python
StreamPart = (
    ValuesStreamPart[OutputT]
    | UpdatesStreamPart
    | MessagesStreamPart
    | CustomStreamPart
    | CheckpointStreamPart[StateT]
    | TasksStreamPart
    | DebugStreamPart[StateT]
)
```

### Why TypedDict?

- **Zero-cost JSON round-trip.** TypedDict is a dict at runtime — `orjson.loads()` produces the right type directly. No per-chunk construction cost.
- **SDK consistency.** All API types in `langgraph_sdk/schema.py` are already TypedDicts.
- **Type narrowing via `part["type"]`.** Standard Python pattern for discriminated unions.

## Additional improvements (all gated behind `stream_version="v2"`)

### 1. Pydantic/dataclass state coercion

When your graph uses a Pydantic model or dataclass as its state schema, v2 stream parts return your **actual typed objects** instead of plain dicts:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class MyState(BaseModel):
    messages: list[str]
    count: int

graph = StateGraph(MyState)
# ... build graph ...
compiled = graph.compile()

async for part in compiled.astream(inputs, stream_mode="values", stream_version="v2"):
    # part["data"] is MyState, not dict!
    print(part["data"].count)       # autocomplete works
    print(part["data"].messages)    # type-checked
```

This also applies to `"checkpoints"` and `"debug"` stream parts — nested `values` dicts are coerced to the state schema type.

### 2. Clean interrupt handling

In v1, interrupts are injected as a `__interrupt__` key inside the state dictionary. This pollutes the state with metadata and breaks Pydantic/dataclass coercion (which chokes on the extra key).

In v2, `__interrupt__` is **extracted** from the payload and placed in a dedicated `interrupts` field on `ValuesStreamPart`:

```python
# v1 (today)
for chunk in graph.stream(inputs, stream_mode="values"):
    if "__interrupt__" in chunk:
        interrupts = chunk["__interrupt__"]
        del chunk["__interrupt__"]  # manual cleanup
    state = chunk

# v2
for part in graph.stream(inputs, stream_mode="values", stream_version="v2"):
    state = part["data"]           # clean — no __interrupt__ key
    interrupts = part["interrupts"]  # typed tuple[Interrupt, ...]
```

### 3. Typed `invoke()` return with `GraphOutput`

`invoke()` with `stream_version="v2"` returns a `GraphOutput[OutputT]` dataclass instead of a plain dict:

```python
from langgraph.types import GraphOutput

result = graph.invoke(inputs, stream_version="v2")
# result is GraphOutput[MyState]
result.value        # MyState (your Pydantic model / dataclass / dict)
result.interrupts   # tuple[Interrupt, ...]
```

`GraphOutput` implements `__getitem__` and `__contains__` for backward compatibility, so existing dict-access patterns still work during migration:

```python
result["messages"]       # delegates to result.value["messages"]
result["__interrupt__"]  # delegates to result.interrupts
```

## SDK support

The Python SDK (`langgraph-sdk`) also gets `stream_version` support. When `stream_version="v2"`, the SDK wraps raw SSE events into typed `StreamPartV2` dicts with the same `type`/`ns`/`data` structure — giving you the same type-safe experience whether you're running locally or against a deployed LangGraph server.

## Migration path

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Breaking changes** | None — `stream_version` defaults to `"v1"` |
| **Overloads needed** | 1 per method (v1 vs v2), not 16+ |
| **New methods** | 0 |
| **API server changes** | None |
| **Future plan** | Default to `"v2"` in next major version |

## Timeline

- **v1.1** (current): `stream_version="v2"` available as opt-in across `Pregel`, `RemoteGraph`, and SDK
- **Next major**: `stream_version="v2"` becomes the default
- **Major+1**: `stream_version="v1"` removeds

## Open questions
* Should we use `stream_version` or `version` (`stream_version` is a little funky in `invoke` and `ainvoke`)
* Right now, haven't added support in sdk for changes to `wait`, could do that in the future

WIP on the 1.1 branch: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/6961

comments.author: KartikPawade
comments.body:
@sydney-runkle ,

Great RFC! 
A few gaps I noticed while reviewing the implementation on the 1.1 branch:
1. SDK ValuesStreamPart is missing the interrupts field
The core ValuesStreamPart has interrupts: tuple[Interrupt, ...], but the SDK version in langgraph_sdk/schema.py doesn't have this field at all. SDK users consuming version="v2" have no typed way to access interrupts on values parts, which defeats one of the key improvements listed in this RFC.

2. RemoteGraph emits ns as tuple but SDK schema declares list[str]
In remote.py, ns is a tuple when yielded in v2 chunks, but StreamPartV2 in schema.py declares ns: list[str]. A simple list(ns) wrap before yielding would fix it.

3. SyncRunsClient.stream — stream_resumable missing from thread_id: str overloads
The async client and the thread_id: None sync overloads include stream_resumable, but the sync thread_id: str overloads don't. Runtime works fine but mypy will reject it.

text:
# Type-Safe Streaming and Invoke for LangGraph

# Type-Safe Streaming and Invoke for LangGraph

## The Problem

LangGraph's `.stream()`, `.astream()`, `.invoke()`, and `.ainvoke()` methods have **no meaningful type information** today. Regardless of which `stream_mode` you use, the return type is `Iterator[Any]` — you get no autocomplete, no type checking, and no way for your editor to tell you what shape the data is in.

This is especially painful when:

- **Using Pydantic or dataclass state schemas** — you define a typed schema but get plain `dict` objects back from streaming and invoke.
- **Switching between stream modes** — each mode returns a completely different shape (`dict`, `tuple[AnyMessage, dict]`, `Any`, etc.), but the type system can't help you remember which is which.
- **Handling interrupts** — the `__interrupt__` key is mixed into the state dictionary, which pollutes your state, breaks Pydantic/dataclass coercion, and forces manual filtering.

### Why not just use `@overload`?

Python's only mechanism for "parameter X controls return type Y" is `@overload`. The matrix is 8 stream modes x 2 subgraph values = **16+ overloads per method**, across `stream`/`astream` on `Pregel`, `PregelProtocol`, `RemoteGraph`, and the SDK. A proof-of-concept required hundreds of signatures and was still incomplete. Every new stream mode multiplies the combinatorics — this approach is unsustainable.

## Proposal: `stream_version="v2"` with typed stream parts

We're adding a `stream_version: Literal["v1", "v2"]` parameter (defaulting to `"v1"`) to `.stream()`, `.astream()`, `.invoke()`, and `.ainvoke()`. When `stream_version="v2"`, every chunk is a self-describing `StreamPart` TypedDict with a `type` discriminator:

```python
from langgraph.types import StreamPart, ValuesStreamPart, UpdatesStreamPart

async for part in graph.astream(inputs, stream_version="v2"):
    if part["type"] == "values":
        # part is narrowed to ValuesStreamPart
        # part["data"] is your output type (Pydantic model, dataclass, or dict)
        # part["interrupts"] is tuple[Interrupt, ...]
        print(part["data"])
    elif part["type"] == "updates":
        # part is narrowed to UpdatesStreamPart
        # part["data"] is dict[str, Any] mapping node names to outputs
        print(part["data"])
    elif part["type"] == "messages":
        # part is narrowed to MessagesStreamPart
        # part["data"] is tuple[AnyMessage, dict[str, Any]]
        print(part["data"])
```

### Stream part types

Every v2 stream part is a TypedDict with three common keys: `type`, `ns`, and `data`. The `type` field is a `Literal` that enables type narrowing:

| `type` | TypedDict | `data` type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `"values"` | `ValuesStreamPart` | `OutputT` (Pydantic model, dataclass, or dict) | Also has `interrupts: tuple[Interrupt, ...]` |
| `"updates"` | `UpdatesStreamPart` | `dict[str, Any]` | Node name -> output mapping |
| `"messages"` | `MessagesStreamPart` | `tuple[AnyMessage, dict[str, Any]]` | (message, metadata) pair |
| `"custom"` | `CustomStreamPart` | `Any` | Whatever was passed to `StreamWriter` |
| `"checkpoints"` | `CheckpointStreamPart` | `CheckpointPayload` | Checkpoint metadata with typed values |
| `"tasks"` | `TasksStreamPart` | `TaskPayload \| TaskResultPayload` | Task start/result events |
| `"debug"` | `DebugStreamPart` | `DebugPayload` | Debug events (checkpoint, task, task_result) |

The full union type:

```python
StreamPart = (
    ValuesStreamPart[OutputT]
    | UpdatesStreamPart
    | MessagesStreamPart
    | CustomStreamPart
    | CheckpointStreamPart[StateT]
    | TasksStreamPart
    | DebugStreamPart[StateT]
)
```

### Why TypedDict?

- **Zero-cost JSON round-trip.** TypedDict is a dict at runtime — `orjson.loads()` produces the right type directly. No per-chunk construction cost.
- **SDK consistency.** All API types in `langgraph_sdk/schema.py` are already TypedDicts.
- **Type narrowing via `part["type"]`.** Standard Python pattern for discriminated unions.

## Additional improvements (all gated behind `stream_version="v2"`)

### 1. Pydantic/dataclass state coercion

When your graph uses a Pydantic model or dataclass as its state schema, v2 stream parts return your **actual typed objects** instead of plain dicts:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class MyState(BaseModel):
    messages: list[str]
    count: int

graph = StateGraph(MyState)
# ... build graph ...
compiled = graph.compile()

async for part in compiled.astream(inputs, stream_mode="values", stream_version="v2"):
    # part["data"] is MyState, not dict!
    print(part["data"].count)       # autocomplete works
    print(part["data"].messages)    # type-checked
```

This also applies to `"checkpoints"` and `"debug"` stream parts — nested `values` dicts are coerced to the state schema type.

### 2. Clean interrupt handling

In v1, interrupts are injected as a `__interrupt__` key inside the state dictionary. This pollutes the state with metadata and breaks Pydantic/dataclass coercion (which chokes on the extra key).

In v2, `__interrupt__` is **extracted** from the payload and placed in a dedicated `interrupts` field on `ValuesStreamPart`:

```python
# v1 (today)
for chunk in graph.stream(inputs, stream_mode="values"):
    if "__interrupt__" in chunk:
        interrupts = chunk["__interrupt__"]
        del chunk["__interrupt__"]  # manual cleanup
    state = chunk

# v2
for part in graph.stream(inputs, stream_mode="values", stream_version="v2"):
    state = part["data"]           # clean — no __interrupt__ key
    interrupts = part["interrupts"]  # typed tuple[Interrupt, ...]
```

### 3. Typed `invoke()` return with `GraphOutput`

`invoke()` with `stream_version="v2"` returns a `GraphOutput[OutputT]` dataclass instead of a plain dict:

```python
from langgraph.types import GraphOutput

result = graph.invoke(inputs, stream_version="v2")
# result is GraphOutput[MyState]
result.value        # MyState (your Pydantic model / dataclass / dict)
result.interrupts   # tuple[Interrupt, ...]
```

`GraphOutput` implements `__getitem__` and `__contains__` for backward compatibility, so existing dict-access patterns still work during migration:

```python
result["messages"]       # delegates to result.value["messages"]
result["__interrupt__"]  # delegates to result.interrupts
```

## SDK support

The Python SDK (`langgraph-sdk`) also gets `stream_version` support. When `stream_version="v2"`, the SDK wraps raw SSE events into typed `StreamPartV2` dicts with the same `type`/`ns`/`data` structure — giving you the same type-safe experience whether you're running locally or against a deployed LangGraph server.

## Migration path

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Breaking changes** | None — `stream_version` defaults to `"v1"` |
| **Overloads needed** | 1 per method (v1 vs v2), not 16+ |
| **New methods** | 0 |
| **API server changes** | None |
| **Future plan** | Default to `"v2"` in next major version |

## Timeline

- **v1.1** (current): `stream_version="v2"` available as opt-in across `Pregel`, `RemoteGraph`, and SDK
- **Next major**: `stream_version="v2"` becomes the default
- **Major+1**: `stream_version="v1"` removeds

## Open questions
* Should we use `stream_version` or `version` (`stream_version` is a little funky in `invoke` and `ainvoke`)
* Right now, haven't added support in sdk for changes to `wait`, could do that in the future

title: Does `CompiledSubAgent` support state parameter passing?
body:
I've got a LangGraph runnable that expects specific state keys (like location, industry, etc.) to function properly.
Currently, when I use CompiledSubAgent to integrate this runnable with my deep agent, the subagent gets invoked but the required state parameters aren't being passed through - leading to KeyErrors when the runnable tries to access them.
I found a workaround by wrapping my runnable as a tool with an explicit args_schema, which lets the main agent extract and pass parameters correctly. 
But this feels heavyweight for what should be a simple subagent invocation.
What I'm looking for:
A way to tell CompiledSubAgent: "Hey, this runnable needs these specific state keys populated before you invoke it" - similar to how tools have args_schema to define their required parameters.

Where the middleware extracts the needed parameters from the task description and populates the state before invoking the runnable.
Is there currently a way to do this with CompiledSubAgent that I'm missing? Or would this be a worthwhile addition?

Thanks

comments.author: Shahar19
Beehive324
comments.body:
> I’m having the same issue. any insights regarding how to pass from deep agent, custom state keys to compiled sub agents? Any docs or examples that I’ve missed? [@Beehive324](https://github.com/Beehive324) can you share additional high level details or example of your workaround? Thanks!
@Shahar19 https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents#using-compiledsubagent, found a work around using the docs, messages state key is required for the compiledSubAgent so I just added a messages state key and a parsing node to populate custom state keys given the message

title: Bug: SyncPregelLoop.put_writes caches ERROR/INTERRUPT writes (async has guard, sync does not)
body:
## Checked other resources

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.
- [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code.
- [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package).
- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

## Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

This is a code-level inconsistency between `SyncPregelLoop` and `AsyncPregelLoop` found via source analysis.

`SyncPregelLoop.put_writes` (line 1063 of `pregel/_loop.py`) is missing the ERROR/INTERRUPT guard that exists in `AsyncPregelLoop.put_writes` (line 1247).

**Sync version (missing guard):**

```python
# SyncPregelLoop.put_writes — line 1063
def put_writes(self, task_id: str, writes: WritesT) -> None:
    super().put_writes(task_id, writes)
    if not writes or self.cache is None or not hasattr(self, "tasks"):
        return
    task = self.tasks.get(task_id)
    if task is None or task.cache_key is None:
        return
    # No check for ERROR/INTERRUPT — goes straight to cache.set
    self.submit(
        self.cache.set,
        {(task.cache_key.ns, task.cache_key.key): (task.writes, task.cache_key.ttl)},
    )
```

**Async version (correct):**

```python
# AsyncPregelLoop.put_writes — line 1239
def put_writes(self, task_id: str, writes: WritesT) -> None:
    super().put_writes(task_id, writes)
    if not writes or self.cache is None or not hasattr(self, "tasks"):
        return
    task = self.tasks.get(task_id)
    if task is None or task.cache_key is None:
        return
    if writes[0][0] in (INTERRUPT, ERROR):
        # only cache successful tasks
        return
    self.submit(
        self.cache.aset,
        {(task.cache_key.ns, task.cache_key.key): (task.writes, task.cache_key.ttl)},
    )
```

To reproduce at runtime: run a graph synchronously with caching enabled where a node raises an exception or calls `interrupt()`. The failed result gets cached. On the next invocation with the same inputs, the cached error/interrupt is replayed instead of re-executing the task.

## Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

No stack trace (silent bug). The error manifests as incorrect cached results: failed tasks are persisted to the cache and replayed on subsequent runs.

## Description

`SyncPregelLoop.put_writes()` caches all task writes (including ERROR and INTERRUPT writes) because it is missing the guard present in the async counterpart. The async version correctly checks `if writes[0][0] in (INTERRUPT, ERROR): return` before writing to cache, ensuring only successful task results are cached.

This causes silent data corruption in sync mode with caching: a task that fails or is interrupted has its failure persisted to the cache. Any subsequent invocation with the same cache key replays the cached failure instead of re-executing the task, even if the underlying issue has been resolved.

**Fix direction:** Add the same guard to `SyncPregelLoop.put_writes`:

```python
if writes[0][0] in (INTERRUPT, ERROR):
    # only cache successful tasks
    return
```

## System Info

Not system-dependent. This is a code-level inconsistency between `SyncPregelLoop` and `AsyncPregelLoop` in `libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_loop.py`. Affects any version with caching support.

comments.body: I reproduced this locally on the current codebase. In the sync path, a cached `interrupt()` result is replayed on the next invocation and currently blows up in `accept_push -> output_writes` with `IndexError: deque index out of range`, which confirms that `SyncPregelLoop.put_writes` is persisting `INTERRUPT` writes that the async path already filters out. I'm working on a fix to align the sync cache guard with the async implementation and add regression coverage for both `INTERRUPT` and `ERROR` writes.

title: Bug: _infer_handled_types raises AttributeError on non-class type annotations
body:
## Checked other resources

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.
- [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code.
- [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package).
- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

## Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
from typing import TypeVar
from langgraph.prebuilt.tool_node import _infer_handled_types

T = TypeVar("T", bound=Exception)

def my_handler(e: T) -> str:
    return str(e)

# Crashes with AttributeError: 'TypeVar' object has no attribute '__mro__'
result = _infer_handled_types(my_handler)
```

## Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```
AttributeError: 'TypeVar' object has no attribute '__mro__'
```

Traceback points to `tool_node.py` line 489:
```python
if Exception in exception_type.__mro__:
```

## Description

`_infer_handled_types` (in `libs/prebuilt/langgraph/prebuilt/tool_node.py`, line 488-489) accesses `exception_type.__mro__` without verifying that `exception_type` is actually a class. The function handles `Union`/`UnionType` origins (line 476) but does not guard against other non-class type hints before accessing `.__mro__`.

Any non-class type annotation on the handler's first parameter triggers the crash: `TypeVar`, generic aliases like `list[Exception]`, or unresolved forward references.

**Relevant code:**

```python
# tool_node.py, lines 488-489
exception_type = type_hints[first_param.name]
if Exception in exception_type.__mro__:  # crashes if not a class
    return (exception_type,)
```

**Fix direction:** Add an `isinstance` guard:

```python
exception_type = type_hints[first_param.name]
if isinstance(exception_type, type) and issubclass(exception_type, Exception):
    return (exception_type,)
```

## System Info

Not system-dependent. Affects `libs/prebuilt/langgraph/prebuilt/tool_node.py` line 489 in any version containing `_infer_handled_types`.

title: Bug: aupdate_state missing | None in values type annotation (sync has it)
body:
## Checked other resources

## Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
from langgraph.pregel.main import Pregel

# Type checking reveals the inconsistency:
# Sync version accepts None:
#   def update_state(self, config, values: dict[str, Any] | Any | None, ...) 
#
# Async version rejects None:
#   async def aupdate_state(self, config, values: dict[str, Any] | Any, ...)
#
# Protocol definition includes None for both:
#   values: dict[str, Any] | Any | None

# This type-checks fine:
# graph.update_state(config, None)

# This causes a type error in mypy/pyright:
# await graph.aupdate_state(config, None)
```

## Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

No runtime error. This is a type annotation inconsistency that causes false positives in static type checkers (mypy, pyright) when calling `aupdate_state` with `None`.

## Description

The sync `update_state` (line 2333 of `libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/main.py`) accepts `values: dict[str, Any] | Any | None`, but the async `aupdate_state` (line 2346) accepts `values: dict[str, Any] | Any` (missing `| None`).

The `PregelProtocol` definition in `protocol.py` line 87 specifies `| None` for both methods.

**Sync (correct):**
```python
# main.py, line 2333
values: dict[str, Any] | Any | None,
```

**Async (missing `| None`):**
```python
# main.py, line 2346
values: dict[str, Any] | Any,
```

**Fix:** Change line 2346 to:
```python
values: dict[str, Any] | Any | None,
```

## System Info

Not system-dependent. Affects `libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/main.py` line 2346.

comments.author: passionworkeer
comments.body: Type annotation inconsistencies between sync and async versions can be confusing. Consider using a type alias or protocol to share the type definition. This would make it easier to maintain consistency across versions.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python

from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

class State(TypedDict):
    result: str

    interrupt(None)
    return {}

def work_node(state: State):
    return {"result": "done"}

builder = StateGraph(State)
builder.add_node("checkpoint", checkpoint_node)
builder.add_node("work", work_node)
builder.add_edge(START, "checkpoint")
builder.add_edge("checkpoint", "work")
builder.add_edge("work", END)

graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}}

# Run until interrupt
graph.invoke({"result": ""}, config)

# Resume with None — crashes
graph.invoke(Command(resume=None), config)
```

```shell
    with SyncPregelLoop(

    self.updated_channels = self._first(
                            ~~~~~~~~~~~^
        input_keys=self.input_keys,
        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
    ...<2 lines>...
        else None,
        ^^^^^^^^^^
    )
    ^
  File "/Users/tsalacinski/Projects/2026-03-05-langgraph-bugfixes/resume_is_map_bug/sample/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/langgraph/pregel/_loop.py", line 663, in _first

                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'resume_is_map' where it is not associated with a value
```

### Description

In `PregelLoop._first()` (`langgraph/pregel/_loop.py`), the variable `resume_is_map` is defined only inside the `if (resume := self.input.resume) is not None:` block (line 646), but is referenced unconditionally on lines 661 and 663:

```python
# resume_is_map defined ONLY here (when resume is not None)
if (resume := self.input.resume) is not None:
    if resume_is_map := (isinstance(resume, dict) and ...):
        ...

# referenced UNCONDITIONALLY — UnboundLocalError when resume is None
for tid, c, v in map_command(cmd=self.input):
    if not (c == RESUME and resume_is_map):   # <-- crash
        writes[tid].append((c, v))
if not writes and not resume_is_map:          # <-- crash
    raise EmptyInputError(...)
```

When `Command(resume=None)` is used, the guard `is not None` skips the block, leaving `resume_is_map` uninitialized.

While `None` is not a valid resume value (it's the default/sentinel for "no resume provided" on `Command`), the error handling path should not crash with an unrelated `UnboundLocalError`. Instead, it should fall through to the existing `EmptyInputError("Received empty Command input")`.

**Fix:** Initialize `resume_is_map = False` before the conditional block.

title: Feature: Cryptographic action receipts for agent step verification (AAR)
body:
## Problem

LangGraph enables building stateful multi-step agent workflows. Each step in a graph executes actions (tool calls, LLM invocations, API requests) but there's no standard cryptographic proof of what each step did.

For enterprise deployments, agent commerce (x402, Stripe agent checkout), and compliance, verifiable action provenance is increasingly required. Mastercard announced their [Verifiable Intent](https://www.mastercard.com/us/en/news-and-trends/stories/2026/verifiable-intent.html) standard on March 5, 2026 — confirming this gap matters at the payment-network level.

## Agent Action Receipts (AAR)

[AAR v1.0](https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec) — Ed25519-signed JSON receipts per agent action:

- Each graph node execution → signed receipt with input/output SHA-256 hashes
- Receipt chain across the graph = verifiable execution trace
- Privacy-preserving: hashes prove integrity without exposing content
- Compatible with Mastercard Verifiable Intent (bidirectional mapping)
- Compatible with x402 (Coinbase) for payment-gated actions

### Integration idea

```python
# Conceptual: receipt-aware node wrapper
@node
def tool_call_node(state):
    result = call_tool(state)
    receipt = create_receipt(
        agent_id='my-agent/v1',
        action={'type': 'tool_call', 'target': tool.name},
        input_hash=hash(state),
        output_hash=hash(result),
    )
    state['receipts'].append(receipt)
    return state
```

### SDK

TypeScript: `npm install botindex-aar` (live). Python SDK in development.

- Spec: https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec
- Landing: https://aar.botindex.dev

MIT licensed. Happy to discuss or contribute.

## Problem

LangGraph enables building stateful multi-step agent workflows. Each step in a graph executes actions (tool calls, LLM invocations, API requests) but there's no standard cryptographic proof of what each step did.

For enterprise deployments, agent commerce (x402, Stripe agent checkout), and compliance, verifiable action provenance is increasingly required. Mastercard announced their [Verifiable Intent](https://www.mastercard.com/us/en/news-and-trends/stories/2026/verifiable-intent.html) standard on March 5, 2026 — confirming this gap matters at the payment-network level.

## Agent Action Receipts (AAR)

[AAR v1.0](https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec) — Ed25519-signed JSON receipts per agent action:

- Each graph node execution → signed receipt with input/output SHA-256 hashes
- Receipt chain across the graph = verifiable execution trace
- Privacy-preserving: hashes prove integrity without exposing content
- Compatible with Mastercard Verifiable Intent (bidirectional mapping)
- Compatible with x402 (Coinbase) for payment-gated actions

```python
# Conceptual: receipt-aware node wrapper

    receipt = create_receipt(

        input_hash=hash(state),
        output_hash=hash(result),
    )
    state['receipts'].append(receipt)
    return state
```

title: Feature: Cryptographic action receipts (AAR) for provable agent execution
body:
## Problem

When LangGraph agents execute multi-step workflows, there's no standardized way to cryptographically prove what happened at each node. Audit logs exist, but they're mutable and unsigned — a compromised system can rewrite history without detection.

For regulated domains (finance, healthcare, legal), this is a blocker. Compliance teams need tamper-proof evidence that Agent X performed Action Y with Input Z at Time T.

## Proposal: Agent Action Receipt (AAR) Integration

AAR is a lightweight spec for Ed25519-signed receipts that capture agent actions with cryptographic integrity:

```json
{
  "receiptId": "uuid",
  "agent": "langgraph-node-analyzer",
  "action": "analyze_document",
  "inputHash": "sha256-of-input",
  "outputHash": "sha256-of-output",
  "timestamp": "2026-03-08T15:00:00Z",
  "signature": "ed25519-detached-signature"
}
```

Key properties:
- **Offline verifiable** — deterministic canonical JSON, single `nacl.sign.detached.verify()` call
- **PII-free** — SHA-256 hashes of inputs/outputs, never raw data
- **Composable** — receipts chain via Session Continuity Certificates (SCC) for cross-session provenance

## Integration surface for LangGraph

Each graph node execution could emit an AAR receipt. The natural hook is the `RunnableConfig` callbacks — a `AARCallbackHandler` that signs receipts at node boundaries.

## Resources

- Spec: https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec
- SDK: https://www.npmjs.com/package/botindex-aar (115+ daily downloads)
- Hosted signing: https://botindex.dev (for teams that don't want to manage keys)
- Active discussion: crewAI #4754, FINOS AI Governance #266, AWS Agent Squad #429

comments.author: aeoess
comments.body:
This is exactly what we ship in the Agent Passport System.

Our `ActionReceipt` is an Ed25519-signed record containing: agent identity, declared intent, policy decision, execution result, timestamp, and beneficiary attribution. Every receipt is part of a 3-signature chain:

1. **Intent Declaration** (signed by agent) — what am I about to do?
2. **PolicyDecision** (signed by policy engine) — is this within delegation scope + values floor?
3. **ActionReceipt** (signed by agent) — what happened, with cryptographic proof

Receipts are immutable — a compromised system cannot rewrite them without invalidating the Ed25519 signatures. For regulated domains, this is exactly the tamper-proof audit trail you describe.

Additionally, our **cascade revocation** means if an agent's authority is revoked after the fact, all receipts remain valid as historical evidence but future actions are instantly blocked.

The protocol is framework-agnostic (npm package, MCP server). Integration with LangGraph would mean wrapping node execution in our intent-policy-receipt chain.

481 tests, Apache 2.0.

comments.author: pshkv
kinthaiofficial
comments.body:
Excellent proposal. AARs for LangGraph are especially important because graph-based workflows have clear node boundaries that map naturally to receipt points.

From implementing signed receipts across 31 agents in production:

**Per-node receipt generation in graph workflows**

Each LangGraph node should emit a receipt on completion:

```python
@dataclass
class NodeReceipt:
    node_id: str              # graph node identifier
    agent_did: str            # Ed25519 did:key of the executing agent
    input_hash: str           # SHA-256 of node input state
    output_hash: str          # SHA-256 of node output state
    state_diff_hash: str      # SHA-256 of the state delta (what changed)
    parent_receipt: str       # hash of the upstream node's receipt
    delegation_chain: list[str]
    timestamp: int
    signature: bytes          # Ed25519 over canonical form
```

The `state_diff_hash` is LangGraph-specific and powerful — instead of hashing the full state (which can be large), hash only the delta. This lets you verify that each node only modified what it claimed to modify.

**Hash chain integrity across the graph**

In a LangGraph workflow, the receipt chain follows the graph edges:

```
Node A receipt → hash → Node B.parent_receipt
Node B receipt → hash → Node C.parent_receipt
```

For parallel branches (common in LangGraph), each branch maintains its own receipt chain. At a merge node, the receipt references all parent receipt hashes.

**Deterministic replay for compliance**

For the strongest guarantee: record all external inputs (LLM responses, tool outputs) alongside the receipt chain. An auditor can:
1. Load the graph definition
2. Replay with recorded external inputs
3. Verify that the computed receipts match the recorded ones

If they match: provably correct execution. If not: tampering detected.

**Cost attribution per node**

Each receipt includes the millicent cost of that node's execution. The delegation chain lets you attribute costs to the root delegator:

```python
def total_workflow_cost(receipts: list[NodeReceipt]) -> int:
    return sum(r.cost_millicents for r in receipts)
# Attributable to receipts[0].delegation_chain[0]
```

**Related:**
- [Your AI Agent Needs a Wallet: Economic Models for Autonomous Agents](https://blog.kinthai.ai/agent-wallet-economic-models-autonomous-agents) — per-task cost attribution via delegation chains
- [221 Agents: Multi-Agent Coordination Lessons](https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons) — audit trails at scale

Running signed receipts at [agents.kinthai.ai](https://agents.kinthai.ai) on OpenClaw.

comments.author: vaaraio
comments.body:
The proposal is right that mutable audit logs are the blocker. One thing the receipt-emitting approaches in this thread underweight: emitting the receipt is the easy half. For regulated domains the property you actually need is that an independent party can verify a receipt without trusting the process that wrote it, and that the trail survives the signing key being compromised later.

Two design points follow from that:

- Specify the verifier, not just the receipt fields. Given a receipt, the verifier recomputes the canonical form, checks the signature against the declared issuer key, and checks the link to the previous receipt. Specs that fix only the emitter shape tend to be unverifiable across implementations.
- Anchor the chain head to an external timestamp (RFC 3161). Ed25519 proves who, not when. If the key leaks, an attacker can backdate a rewritten chain; an external time anchor makes the chain's existence provable against a clock you do not control.

LangGraph's node boundaries map onto this cleanly: one decision record per node before the side effect, one outcome record after, paired by a back-link. We ship this in Vaara (Apache-2.0, https://github.com/vaaraio/vaara), and the record shape is being standardized at the MCP layer in https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/pull/2828 . Offered as a reference, not a dependency.

comments.author: aeoess
comments.body:
The verifier point is the right one to lead with, and it's the same line we hold: a receipt spec that fixes only the emitter shape is unverifiable across implementations. Given a receipt, the verifier recomputes the canonical form, checks the signature against the declared issuer key, and checks the prior-record link. If the spec doesn't pin those three steps, two conformant emitters can produce receipts neither can check.

On the RFC 3161 anchor, agreed on the threat, and I'd keep it a separate property rather than fold it into the signature. Ed25519 proves who, not when, so signature validity stays an offline check against a pinned key and the time anchor rides as a composable inclusion proof on the chain head. A verifier with no clock authority can still check who and what offline, and reaches for the external anchor only to settle when. The key-leak backdating case is exactly why the two shouldn't be the same field: if the time guarantee depends on the same key that signed, a leaked key breaks both at once.

What APS doesn't do today is mandate the anchor. We record a staleness window on the freshness side and leave the external timestamp as an optional inclusion proof, which composes with what you're describing rather than competing. The node-boundary mapping you gave (one decision record before the side effect, one outcome record after, paired by back-link) is the same split we run. APS uses a similar split in draft-pidlisnyi-aps-01 if a concrete reference helps.

comments.author: sunfishloop
comments.body:
We've been running a production multi-agent system (SunfishLoop, github.com/sunfishloop/sunfishloop) with 20+ agents cross CrewAI/AutoGen/LangGraph, and cryptographic receipts are something we had to solve for the same reasons you mention — compliance traceability across framework boundaries.

Our approach was slightly different: since agents have wallet-based identity (Ed25519 keypairs registered via /llms.txt), every inter-agent action can be accompanied by a signature. We didn't build a separate receipt spec — we used the wallet signature itself as the proof, with the interaction payload (action, input_hash, output_hash, timestamp) as the signed message. This makes receipts offline-verifiable with a single nacl.sign.detached.verify() call, same as AAR.

One thing we found important in practice: the receipt should also include a reference to the task/market context, not just the action hash. Otherwise when you're auditing a chain of 20 micro-interactions, you can't reconstruct what happened without cross-referencing external logs. A task_id or conversation_id field in the receipt payload makes offline audit practical.

Composable receipts via your Session Continuity Certificates concept would be a neat addition — we've been manually linking chains of interactions in a local SQLite per agent, but a standard chain format would be cleaner.

comments.author: chopmob-cloud
comments.body:
The verifier point raised above is correct and it is the one to lead with for regulated domains: a receipt spec that fixes only the emitter shape is unverifiable across implementations.

`draft-hopley-x402-compliance-receipt-02` ([datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-hopley-x402-compliance-receipt/)) specifies both emitter and verifier: given a receipt, the verifier recomputes the JCS-canonical form, checks the Falcon-1024 / Ed25519 signature against the published issuer key, and checks the content-hash back-link to the prior record. Three steps pinned. Two conformant implementations can cross-check without trusting each other's runtime.

On the RFC 3161 anchor: agreed that Ed25519 proves who, not when. For payment-bearing receipts, `draft-hopley-x402-settlement-attestation-01` ([datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-hopley-x402-settlement-attestation/)) carries `settlement_timestamp_ms` as a chain-verified external clock anchor -- settlement finality on a public ledger is the independently verifiable timestamp that makes the when provable without a TSA call. For non-payment receipts, the compliance receipt format leaves a hook for `tsp_token` (RFC 3161 inclusion proof) as a composable optional field, keeping the time anchor separate from the signature exactly as described above.

For LangGraph node boundaries: compliance receipt (pre-execution gate node, `ALLOW` / `REFER` / `DENY`, JCS-canonical, signed) + settlement attestation (post-execution outcome node, `SETTLED` / `PENDING_FINALITY` / `REVERSED`) is the concrete receipt pair for regulated workloads. One decision record per node before the side effect, one outcome record after, paired by content-hash back-link.

Reference implementation: `algovoi-substrate` (PyPI / npm, Apache 2.0). Deployed in production across 8 chain families.

*AlgoVoi (chopmob-cloud) -- [docs.algovoi.co.uk/settlement-attestation](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/settlement-attestation)*

This is exactly the problem SINT Protocol's Evidence Ledger was designed to solve. We've been building [SINT Protocol](https://github.com/pshkv/sint-protocol) — a formal security and governance layer for AI agents — and the cryptographic audit receipt is a core component.

**How SINT's Evidence Ledger works:**

Every action produces an `EvidenceLedgerEvent` that is:
1. **Hash-chained**: `event_k.previousHash = SHA256(canonical(event_{k-1}))` — a gap or modification anywhere in the chain is immediately detectable
2. **Ed25519-signed**: Each event carries the agent's identity (`agentId: Ed25519PublicKey`) bound to the token that authorized the action
3. **Sequence-numbered**: Monotonically increasing `sequenceNumber: bigint` — no silent deletions possible
4. **TEE-attestable** (for T3/irreversible actions): Optional TEE ProofReceipt with `intel-sgx | arm-trustzone | amd-sev` backend — the event is attested to have been written inside a secure enclave at the stated timestamp

```typescript
interface SintLedgerEvent {
  eventId: UUIDv7;
  sequenceNumber: bigint;    // monotonic, no gaps
  timestamp: ISO8601;        // microsecond precision
  eventType: SintEventType;  // e.g., "action.completed"
  agentId: Ed25519PublicKey;
  tokenId?: UUIDv7;          // capability token that authorized this
  payload: Record<string, unknown>;
  previousHash: SHA256;      // hash chain link
  hash: SHA256;              // over all fields above
}
```

**For LangGraph specifically:** A `SintLedgerEvent` per node execution gives you: the agent identity (which agent invoked this node), the token that authorized it, the input/output hashes in `payload`, and the chain link to the previous event. Chain verification is `O(n)` and can be done by any third party who has only the events themselves — no trusted audit server required.

**The compliance query pattern:**
```typescript
// "Prove that agent X performed action Y on date D"
const events = await ledger.query({
  agentId: agentPublicKey,
  eventType: "action.completed",
  fromTimestamp: "2026-04-01T00:00:00.000000Z"
});
const intact = await ledger.verifyChain(events[0].sequenceNumber, events.at(-1)!.sequenceNumber);
// intact === true: cryptographic proof the chain wasn't modified
```

The ledger supports selective disclosure — you can prove a specific action happened without revealing the entire audit log.

Reference implementation: https://github.com/pshkv/sint-protocol — `packages/gate-evidence-ledger` with 29 tests. Open to discussing how this could be adapted as the AAR backend for LangGraph.

Composable receipts via your Session Continuity Certificates concept would be a neat addition — we've been manually linking chains of interactions in a local SQLite per agent, but a standard chain format would be cleaner.

The verifier point raised above is correct and it is the one to lead with for regulated domains: a receipt spec that fixes only the emitter shape is unverifiable across implementations.

`draft-hopley-x402-compliance-receipt-02` ([datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-hopley-x402-compliance-receipt/)) specifies both emitter and verifier: given a receipt, the verifier recomputes the JCS-canonical form, checks the Falcon-1024 / Ed25519 signature against the published issuer key, and checks the content-hash back-link to the prior record. Three steps pinned. Two conformant implementations can cross-check without trusting each other's runtime.

On the RFC 3161 anchor: agreed that Ed25519 proves who, not when. For payment-bearing receipts, `draft-hopley-x402-settlement-attestation-01` ([datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-hopley-x402-settlement-attestation/)) carries `settlement_timestamp_ms` as a chain-verified external clock anchor -- settlement finality on a public ledger is the independently verifiable timestamp that makes the when provable without a TSA call. For non-payment receipts, the compliance receipt format leaves a hook for `tsp_token` (RFC 3161 inclusion proof) as a composable optional field, keeping the time anchor separate from the signature exactly as described above.

For LangGraph node boundaries: compliance receipt (pre-execution gate node, `ALLOW` / `REFER` / `DENY`, JCS-canonical, signed) + settlement attestation (post-execution outcome node, `SETTLED` / `PENDING_FINALITY` / `REVERSED`) is the concrete receipt pair for regulated workloads. One decision record per node before the side effect, one outcome record after, paired by content-hash back-link.

Reference implementation: `algovoi-substrate` (PyPI / npm, Apache 2.0). Deployed in production across 8 chain families.

*AlgoVoi (chopmob-cloud) -- [docs.algovoi.co.uk/settlement-attestation](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/settlement-attestation)*

### Checked other resources

- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.

- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
"""
  Minimal reproducer: LangGraph memory leak with durability="async" (default).

  The default async durability causes _checkpointer_put_after_previous coroutine
  chains to accumulate across supersteps when checkpoint writes have any latency.
  Each pending coroutine is a bound method on AsyncPregelLoop, keeping the loop,
  its channels, and checkpoint data alive.

  Usage:
      python repro_leak.py

  Expected output:
      durability="async" accumulates checkpoint dicts proportional to superstep
      count; durability="sync" stays constant.

  Tested with langgraph==1.0.10, Python 3.14.
  """

  import asyncio
  import gc
  import tracemalloc
  from typing import Annotated, Any, TypedDict
  from operator import add

  from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
  from langgraph.checkpoint.base import Checkpoint, CheckpointMetadata
  from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
  from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableConfig

  STEPS = 200
  CHECKPOINT_LATENCY_MS = 10  # Simulate realistic DB write latency


  # -- Slow checkpointer that simulates DB latency ----------------------------

  class SlowMemorySaver(MemorySaver):
      """MemorySaver with artificial write latency to simulate a real DB."""

      async def aput(
          self,
          config: RunnableConfig,
          checkpoint: Checkpoint,
          metadata: CheckpointMetadata,
          new_versions: Any,
      ) -> RunnableConfig:
          await asyncio.sleep(CHECKPOINT_LATENCY_MS / 1000)
          return await super().aput(config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions)


  # -- Counters sampled from inside the graph ---------------------------------

  samples: list[tuple[int, int, int]] = []


  def count_checkpoint_dicts() -> int:
      return sum(
          1 for obj in gc.get_objects()
          if type(obj) is dict and "channel_values" in obj and "channel_versions" in obj
      )


  def count_config_dicts() -> int:
      return sum(
          1 for obj in gc.get_objects()
          if type(obj) is dict and "configurable" in obj
          and isinstance(obj.get("configurable"), dict)
          and "thread_id" in obj["configurable"]
      )


  # -- Graph -------------------------------------------------------------------

  class CounterState(TypedDict):
      counter: int
      items: Annotated[list[str], add]


  def increment(state: CounterState) -> CounterState:
      step = state["counter"]

      # Sample every 50 steps
      if step % 50 == 0 and step > 0:
          cp = count_checkpoint_dicts()
          cfg = count_config_dicts()
          samples.append((step, cp, cfg))

      return {
          "counter": step + 1,
          "items": [f"step-{step}"],
      }


  def should_continue(state: CounterState) -> str:
      return "loop" if state["counter"] < STEPS else "done"


  def build_graph() -> StateGraph:
      g = StateGraph(CounterState)
      g.add_node("increment", increment)
      g.add_edge(START, "increment")
      g.add_conditional_edges(
          "increment", should_continue, {"loop": "increment", "done": END}
      )
      return g


  async def run_test(durability: str, thread_id: str) -> dict:
      global samples
      samples = []

      checkpointer = SlowMemorySaver()
      graph = build_graph().compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)
      config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}}

      tracemalloc.start()
      tracemalloc.reset_peak()

      async for event in graph.astream(
          {"counter": 0, "items": []},
          config,
          durability=durability,
      ):
          pass

      _, peak_mem = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
      tracemalloc.stop()

      peak_cp = max((cp for _, cp, _ in samples), default=0)
      peak_cfg = max((cfg for _, _, cfg in samples), default=0)

      return {
          "durability": durability,
          "peak_checkpoint_dicts": peak_cp,
          "peak_config_dicts": peak_cfg,
          "peak_traced_mb": round(peak_mem / 1024 / 1024, 1),
          "samples": list(samples),
      }


  async def main() -> None:
      print(
          f"Running {STEPS}-superstep graph with "
          f"{CHECKPOINT_LATENCY_MS}ms checkpoint latency...\n"
      )

      print("1) durability='async' (default):")
      r1 = await run_test("async", "t-async")
      for step, cp, cfg in r1["samples"]:
          print(f"   step {step:3d}: checkpoint_dicts={cp}, config_dicts={cfg}")
      print(
          f"   peak: {r1['peak_checkpoint_dicts']} checkpoint_dicts, "
          f"{r1['peak_config_dicts']} config_dicts, "
          f"{r1['peak_traced_mb']} MB traced"
      )

      gc.collect()

      print("\n2) durability='sync':")
      r2 = await run_test("sync", "t-sync")
      for step, cp, cfg in r2["samples"]:
          print(f"   step {step:3d}: checkpoint_dicts={cp}, config_dicts={cfg}")
      print(
          f"   peak: {r2['peak_checkpoint_dicts']} checkpoint_dicts, "
          f"{r2['peak_config_dicts']} config_dicts, "
          f"{r2['peak_traced_mb']} MB traced"
      )

      print("\n--- Result ---")
      if r1["peak_checkpoint_dicts"] > r2["peak_checkpoint_dicts"] + 5:
          print(
              f"✗ async accumulated {r1['peak_checkpoint_dicts']} checkpoint dicts "
              f"vs {r2['peak_checkpoint_dicts']} for sync"
          )
          print(
              f"  Peak memory: {r1['peak_traced_mb']} MB (async) "
              f"vs {r2['peak_traced_mb']} MB (sync)"
          )
      else:
          print("✓ No significant difference detected")


  if __name__ == "__main__":
      asyncio.run(main())
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell

```

### Description

With durability="async" (default), each superstep submits a checkpoint write via self.submit(self._checkpointer_put_after_previous, prev_future, ...). Since the bound method captures self (the loop), and each coroutine holds prev (the prior future), this builds a chain: Task[N] → coroutine → self + prev=Task[N-1] → ... that grows with every superstep. Nothing resolves until AsyncBackgroundExecutor.__aexit__ at the end of astream(). With any checkpointer that has write latency, the coroutines can't complete before new ones are submitted, so checkpoint dicts, config dicts, and channel data accumulate proportionally to superstep count. durability="sync" awaits each future immediately, breaking the chain.

comments.author: pawel-twardziak
comments.body:
In the source code I see this flow:

**1. checkpoint writes are submitted without backpressure (`durability="async"`)**

each superstep submits a checkpoint write as a background asyncio task
https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_loop.py#L837-L847
ech call to `self.submit()` creates a new `asyncio.Task` via `AsyncBackgroundExecutor.submit()`
https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_executor.py#L142-L169
this is non-blocking - the main loop continues immediately

**2. tasks form a sequential chain via `await prev`**

the `_checkpointer_put_after_previous` coroutine 
https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_loop.py#L1260-L1274
awaits the previous task before writing

This means tasks complete sequentially: task N must wait for task N-1 to finish before starting its own `aput()`

**3. `durability="sync"` has backpressure; `durability="async"` does not**

the critical difference is in
https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/main.py#L3129-L3130
when `durability="sync"` after each tick the stream loop explicitly awaits the checkpoint future

This provides backpressure - the next superstep cannot begin until the previous checkpoint write completes. At most 1 checkpoint task is pending at any time

when `durability="async"` no such wait exists and the loop immediately proceeds to the next superstep, allowing tasks to pile up

**accumulation**

With checkpoint write latency `L` and superstep time `S`
- tasks submitted after `T` time: `T / S`
- tasks completed after `T` time: `max(0, (T - L) / L)` (sequential chain)

For the reproducer (200 supersteps, S~0.1ms, L=10ms)
- fter 200 supersteps (~20ms elapsed): ~200 tasks submitted, ~2 completed
- ~198 pending tasks, each holding a full `copy_checkpoint()` in their coroutine frame

Each pending coroutine retains
- `self` (the `AsyncPregelLoop` instance, including channels and all state)
- `checkpoint` (a full deep copy via `copy_checkpoint()`)
- `config`, `metadata`, `new_versions`
- `prev` (a reference to the previous `asyncio.Task`)

With growing state each checkpoint copy becomes larger, leading to memory growth proportional to `O(N^2)` in the worst case

The workaround is to use `durability="sync"` explicitly
and there are some potential fix directions imho

comments.author: passionworkeer
comments.body: Memory leaks in async durability mode are tricky. Have you considered using weakrefs for the coroutine chains, or implementing a bounded cache for the put operations? A potential workaround could be explicitly calling cleanup in the finally block.

comments.author: pawel-twardziak
comments.body:
> Memory leaks in async durability mode are tricky. Have you considered using weakrefs for the coroutine chains, or implementing a bounded cache for the put operations? A potential workaround could be explicitly calling cleanup in the finally block.

"weakrefs for the coroutine chains" - imho this won't work. The prev parameter in _checkpointer_put_after_previous is an asyncio.Task that the coroutine must await. You can't await a weakref.ref - you need a strong reference to the task to await it. If you used a weakref and the task got GC'd before being awaited, you'd lose checkpoint writes silently (data corruption). The whole point of the chain is to guarantee ordering.

"bounded cache for put operations" - this isn't a caching problem. The accumulation is of pending coroutines each holding a full copy_checkpoint() in their frame. A "bounded cache" dosn't address why the coroutines pile up - that's a backpressur problem, not a cache eviction problem.

"cleanup in the finally block" - partally right direction, but insufficient. Adding del prev in the finally block of _checkpointer_put_after_previous would break the reference chain between completed tasks, but it does NOT reduce the number of concurrently  pending coroutines. With 200 supersteps and 10ms checkpoint latency, you'd still have ~198 pending coroutines, each holding its own checkpoint copy. The del only helps GC completed tasks marginally faster - the real memory cost is in the pending ones.

From my understanding, the problem is fundamentally about backpressure - the loop submits checkpoint writes faster than they complete, with no mechanism to slow down. The fix   belongs in main.py where the stream loop runs, not inside the coroutine itslf. Awaiting the previous checkpoint future when it hasn't completed is the correct, minimal fix imho.

comments.author: celyrt2-alt
comments.body:
Thank you for your work and your prompt reply.
The fix is working but I think it's not really solving the issue because it's basically collapsing the async behaviour into the sync one where it matters most.

Before I open the issue I looked into it a bit and I didn't find an obvious fix.

If we have to lose async benefit may I suggest a different approach ? Replace _checkpointer_put_after_previous with a bounded queue and a single writer task.

```
CHECKPOINT_WRITE_BUFFER_SIZE = X

self._checkpoint_queue: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=CHECKPOINT_WRITE_BUFFER_SIZE)
self._checkpoint_writer_task = asyncio.create_task(self._checkpoint_writer())

async def _checkpoint_writer(self):
"""Single consumer — ordering guaranteed by queue FIFO."""
    while True:
        config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions = await self._checkpoint_queue.get()
        try:
            await self.checkpointer.aput(config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions)
        finally:
            self._checkpoint_queue.task_done()
```

```
# in the superstep, instead of submit(_checkpointer_put_after_previous, prev, ...)
    await self._checkpoint_queue.put((config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions))
```
finally

await queue.join() in __aexit__ waits for all pending writes to finish

about CHECKPOINT_WRITE_BUFFER_SIZE that's a whole different discussion, numbers higher than 2 would help to absorb burst, and I think it should be. In this way small contained graphs get the old async behaviour, big graphs gets slowed down for cleanup operations. I think it's a good behaviour and it might be eventually configurable as well.

comments.author: pawel-twardziak
comments.body:
thanks for your feedback @celyrt2-alt 

this backpressure fix efficiently collapses `durability="async"` - true, whenever checkpoint writes are slower than supersteps - which is a common case with real databases. `.done()` check only preserves async benefit when writes are faster then supersteps (rare with real db). You are right that the distinction between `async with backpressure` and `sync` disappears when it matters.

The bounded queue genuinely provides a middle ground - with `maxsize=4` you can run 4 supersteps before blocking, absorbing bursts while bounding memory to O(4) checkpoint copies. That would be correct.

But the sketch has a silent error propagation problem. In the current chain approach, if `aput()` raises, the exception propagates via `asyncio.Future` and gets re-raised in `AsyncBackgroudExecutor.__aexit__`. With the queue approach if `aput()` raises in the writer task:

- the main loop has no idea - `queue.put()` succeeds fine
- the writer task dies silently
- all subsequent checkpoint writes are lost
- `queue.join()` in `__aexit__` hangs forever (items never marked done)

A correct implementation needs explicit error forwarding. Like storing the exeption and re-raising on the next `put()` or checking a sentinel before each superstep . That's doable but adds complexity.

My aim is to fix it with as little effort and additional complexity as possible.

So the queue would be the better long term architecture but the wrong choice for a bug fix for now.

What I would do:
- ship the minimal backpressure fix now - it's safe, correct and solves the memory issue
- follow-up: refactor to a bounded queue with a proper error propagation, making `CHECKPOINT_WRITE_BUFFER_SIZE` configuralbe - which would be a feature enhancement, not a bugfix 

I can propose a PR with the follow-up enhancement.

comments.author: pawel-twardziak
comments.body: @celyrt2-alt  the second PR (bounded checkpoint writer feature) is ther #7111 - if you tested it, would be great.

comments.author: celyrt2-alt
comments.body:
> [celyrt2-alt](https://github.com/celyrt2-alt) the second PR (bounded checkpoint writer feature) is ther [#7111](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/7111) - if you tested it, would be great.

In my scenario I would run it with something like 100-150, so relatively small graphs can be bursted through and cleaned up a the end, long running big graphs get backpressure.

  > langgraph_sdk: 0.3.9
  > langgraph: 1.0.10
  > langgraph-checkpoint-postgres: 3.0.4

I’d like to take this on.

This looks like a real runtime / lifecycle issue in the async durability path rather than a usage problem. I’m reproducing it locally now and will trace where `_checkpointer_put_after_previous` keeps chaining instead of releasing completed awaitables.

If the repro matches the report, I’ll open a fix with a regression test.

It should wait at the next superstep, right (put_after_previous)? 

In the source code I see this flow:

**1. checkpoint writes are submitted without backpressure (`durability="async"`)**

each superstep submits a checkpoint write as a background asyncio task
https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_loop.py#L837-L847
ech call to `self.submit()` creates a new `asyncio.Task` via `AsyncBackgroundExecutor.submit()`
https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_executor.py#L142-L169
this is non-blocking - the main loop continues immediately

**2. tasks form a sequential chain via `await prev`**

the `_checkpointer_put_after_previous` coroutine 
https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_loop.py#L1260-L1274
awaits the previous task before writing

This means tasks complete sequentially: task N must wait for task N-1 to finish before starting its own `aput()`

**3. `durability="sync"` has backpressure; `durability="async"` does not**

the critical difference is in
https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/main.py#L3129-L3130
when `durability="sync"` after each tick the stream loop explicitly awaits the checkpoint future

This provides backpressure - the next superstep cannot begin until the previous checkpoint write completes. At most 1 checkpoint task is pending at any time

when `durability="async"` no such wait exists and the loop immediately proceeds to the next superstep, allowing tasks to pile up

**accumulation**

With checkpoint write latency `L` and superstep time `S`
- tasks submitted after `T` time: `T / S`
- tasks completed after `T` time: `max(0, (T - L) / L)` (sequential chain)

For the reproducer (200 supersteps, S~0.1ms, L=10ms)
- fter 200 supersteps (~20ms elapsed): ~200 tasks submitted, ~2 completed
- ~198 pending tasks, each holding a full `copy_checkpoint()` in their coroutine frame

Each pending coroutine retains
- `self` (the `AsyncPregelLoop` instance, including channels and all state)
- `checkpoint` (a full deep copy via `copy_checkpoint()`)
- `config`, `metadata`, `new_versions`
- `prev` (a reference to the previous `asyncio.Task`)

With growing state each checkpoint copy becomes larger, leading to memory growth proportional to `O(N^2)` in the worst case

The workaround is to use `durability="sync"` explicitly
and there are some potential fix directions imho


> With growing state each checkpoint copy becomes larger, leading to memory growth proportional to `O(N^2)` in the worst case
> 
> The workaround is to use `durability="sync"` explicitly and there are some potential fix directions imho

I confirm that this workaround works, it's actually what I implemented before opening this issue, sorry for not mentioning clearly that.

@celyrt2-alt I've proposed a fix - could you check it out and test it in action?

Memory leaks in async durability mode are tricky. Have you considered using weakrefs for the coroutine chains, or implementing a bounded cache for the put operations? A potential workaround could be explicitly calling cleanup in the finally block.

> Memory leaks in async durability mode are tricky. Have you considered using weakrefs for the coroutine chains, or implementing a bounded cache for the put operations? A potential workaround could be explicitly calling cleanup in the finally block.

"weakrefs for the coroutine chains" - imho this won't work. The prev parameter in _checkpointer_put_after_previous is an asyncio.Task that the coroutine must await. You can't await a weakref.ref - you need a strong reference to the task to await it. If you used a weakref and the task got GC'd before being awaited, you'd lose checkpoint writes silently (data corruption). The whole point of the chain is to guarantee ordering.

"bounded cache for put operations" - this isn't a caching problem. The accumulation is of pending coroutines each holding a full copy_checkpoint() in their frame. A "bounded cache" dosn't address why the coroutines pile up - that's a backpressur problem, not a cache eviction problem.

"cleanup in the finally block" - partally right direction, but insufficient. Adding del prev in the finally block of _checkpointer_put_after_previous would break the reference chain between completed tasks, but it does NOT reduce the number of concurrently  pending coroutines. With 200 supersteps and 10ms checkpoint latency, you'd still have ~198 pending coroutines, each holding its own checkpoint copy. The del only helps GC completed tasks marginally faster - the real memory cost is in the pending ones.

From my understanding, the problem is fundamentally about backpressure - the loop submits checkpoint writes faster than they complete, with no mechanism to slow down. The fix   belongs in main.py where the stream loop runs, not inside the coroutine itslf. Awaiting the previous checkpoint future when it hasn't completed is the correct, minimal fix imho.

Thank you for your work and your prompt reply.
The fix is working but I think it's not really solving the issue because it's basically collapsing the async behaviour into the sync one where it matters most.

Before I open the issue I looked into it a bit and I didn't find an obvious fix.

If we have to lose async benefit may I suggest a different approach ? Replace _checkpointer_put_after_previous with a bounded queue and a single writer task.

```
CHECKPOINT_WRITE_BUFFER_SIZE = X

self._checkpoint_queue: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=CHECKPOINT_WRITE_BUFFER_SIZE)
self._checkpoint_writer_task = asyncio.create_task(self._checkpoint_writer())

async def _checkpoint_writer(self):
"""Single consumer — ordering guaranteed by queue FIFO."""
    while True:
        config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions = await self._checkpoint_queue.get()
        try:
            await self.checkpointer.aput(config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions)
        finally:
            self._checkpoint_queue.task_done()
```

```
# in the superstep, instead of submit(_checkpointer_put_after_previous, prev, ...)
    await self._checkpoint_queue.put((config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions))
```
finally

await queue.join() in __aexit__ waits for all pending writes to finish

about CHECKPOINT_WRITE_BUFFER_SIZE that's a whole different discussion, numbers higher than 2 would help to absorb burst, and I think it should be. In this way small contained graphs get the old async behaviour, big graphs gets slowed down for cleanup operations. I think it's a good behaviour and it might be eventually configurable as well.



thanks for your feedback @celyrt2-alt 

this backpressure fix efficiently collapses `durability="async"` - true, whenever checkpoint writes are slower than supersteps - which is a common case with real databases. `.done()` check only preserves async benefit when writes are faster then supersteps (rare with real db). You are right that the distinction between `async with backpressure` and `sync` disappears when it matters.

The bounded queue genuinely provides a middle ground - with `maxsize=4` you can run 4 supersteps before blocking, absorbing bursts while bounding memory to O(4) checkpoint copies. That would be correct.

But the sketch has a silent error propagation problem. In the current chain approach, if `aput()` raises, the exception propagates via `asyncio.Future` and gets re-raised in `AsyncBackgroudExecutor.__aexit__`. With the queue approach if `aput()` raises in the writer task:

- the main loop has no idea - `queue.put()` succeeds fine
- the writer task dies silently
- all subsequent checkpoint writes are lost
- `queue.join()` in `__aexit__` hangs forever (items never marked done)

A correct implementation needs explicit error forwarding. Like storing the exeption and re-raising on the next `put()` or checking a sentinel before each superstep . That's doable but adds complexity.

My aim is to fix it with as little effort and additional complexity as possible.

So the queue would be the better long term architecture but the wrong choice for a bug fix for now.

What I would do:
- ship the minimal backpressure fix now - it's safe, correct and solves the memory issue
- follow-up: refactor to a bounded queue with a proper error propagation, making `CHECKPOINT_WRITE_BUFFER_SIZE` configuralbe - which would be a feature enhancement, not a bugfix 

I can propose a PR with the follow-up enhancement.

@celyrt2-alt  the second PR (bounded checkpoint writer feature) is ther #7111 - if you tested it, would be great.

> [celyrt2-alt](https://github.com/celyrt2-alt) the second PR (bounded checkpoint writer feature) is ther [#7111](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/7111) - if you tested it, would be great.

So this seems to work, the only thing I think can be improved is to have CHECKPOINT_WRITE_BUFFER_SIZE  as an option like the durability setting.
In my scenario I would run it with something like 100-150, so relatively small graphs can be bursted through and cleaned up a the end, long running big graphs get backpressure.



good call @celyrt2-alt  - added:

```py
await graph.ainvoke(
    "input",                                                                       
    {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1", "__pregel_checkpoint_write_buffer_size": 150}},                                                                             
    durability="async",                                                            
)  
```

the defaut is still 4

At the end of the day, I released two PRs, a fix and a feature.
The feature is obviously open for discussion.
I personally believe this optimization is worth undertaking. I can justify it if needed, unless the concept becomes outdated in the meantime.
