title: `input_schema`: support custom reducers and validators applied on input only for message integrity enforcement
body:
### Privileged issue

- [x] I am a LangGraph maintainer, or was asked directly by a LangGraph maintainer to create an issue here.

### Issue Content

## Summary

When exposing LangGraph APIs directly to frontend clients (e.g. via the JS SDK), users can send `command.update` payloads that tamper with existing conversation history — including forging prior AI messages or modifying state fields like frontend context injected into the system prompt. We need a way to enforce append-only semantics on the messages channel and restrict which state fields clients can modify.

## Problem

The `/threads/{id}/runs/stream` endpoint accepts `command.update`, which allows clients to overwrite arbitrary fields in graph state, including existing messages with pre-existing IDs. This creates integrity and accountability concerns:

- Users can forge AI messages (e.g. replacing card content generated by the LLM with attacker-controlled content)
- Users can modify server-managed state fields (e.g. frontend context appended to the system prompt)
- There is currently no built-in mechanism to enforce append-only behavior on the `messages` channel for client input

`input_schema` exists as a mechanism to restrict which fields are editable on input, but it does not currently support:
1. **Custom reducers** applied at input time to enforce append-only or other merge semantics
2. **Custom validators** to reject messages that reference pre-existing IDs or contain disallowed content types (e.g. AI messages submitted by clients)

## Desired behavior

Developers should be able to define an `input_schema` that includes:
- A **custom reducer** that prevents messages with pre-existing IDs from being overwritten
- A **custom validator** that rejects invalid input (e.g. a client submitting an `ai`-typed message)

These would be applied **on input only**, not to the full graph state schema, so they don't interfere with normal graph execution.

## Example use case

A customer ([[reported here](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/6767)](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/6767)) exposes LangGraph to their frontend users and wants to ensure:
- Clients can append a human message to the `messages` channel
- Clients **cannot** overwrite existing messages or inject AI messages
- Clients **cannot** modify server-managed fields (e.g. `frontend_context`)

## Proposed solution

Extend `input_schema` to accept custom reducers and validators. No new top-level argument needed — this should live within the existing `input_schema` mechanism. When present, these are applied at the point of input ingestion before the graph runs.

Related PR: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/6767

body:

- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
from langgraph.graph import START, StateGraph, MessagesState
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver

class SubState(MessagesState):
    pass

def node(state: SubState):
    print("Node received messages:", state["messages"])
    return {"messages": state["messages"] + [{"role": "assistant", "content": "Hello!"}]}

# Subgraph with its own persistent state
subgraph_builder = StateGraph(SubState)
subgraph_builder.add_node("sub_node", node)
subgraph_builder.add_edge(START, "sub_node")
subgraph = subgraph_builder.compile(checkpointer=True)

# Parent graph
builder = StateGraph(MessagesState)
builder.add_node("agent", subgraph)
builder.add_edge(START, "agent")

checkpointer = MemorySaver()
graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)

config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}}

graph.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]}, config)
graph.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "what did I say?"}]}, config)

# View accumulated subgraph state (includes messages from both invocations)
subgraph_state = graph.get_state(config, subgraphs=True).tasks[0].state
```

comments.body:
hi @a171232886 

I think the root cause is: `StateSnapshot.tasks` contains pending/next-to-run tasks, not completed ones.
After both invoke() calls finish normally, there are zero pending tasks, so .tasks is an empty tuple and .tasks[0] throws IndexError

Why tasks is empty after completion

In _prepare_state_snapshot ([pregel/main.py](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/main.py)), tasks are computed via prepare_next_tasks, which calls _triggers ([_algo.py](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_algo.py)):

```py
def _triggers(channels, versions, seen, null_version, proc) -> bool:
    for chan in proc.triggers:
        if channels[chan].is_available() and versions.get(chan) > seen.get(chan):
            return True
    return False
```

After a completed run, checkpoint["versions_seen"]["agent"] is updated to match channel_versions. The condition versions.get(chan) > seen.get(chan) is False -> no next tasks -> empty .tasks


1. interrupt first

```py
graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer, interrupt_before=["agent"])
graph.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]}, config)

subgraph_state = graph.get_state(config, subgraphs=True).tasks[0].state
```

2. query subgraph directly via checkpoint_ns

```py
subgraph_config = {
    "configurable": {
        "thread_id": "1",
        "checkpoint_ns": "agent", 
    }
}
subgraph_state = graph.get_state(subgraph_config)
print(subgraph_state.values)
```
This works because get_state routes configs with a non-empty checkpoint_ns directly to the matching subgraph's checkpointer. 

3. Walk history

```py
subgraph_config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1", "checkpoint_ns": "agent"}}
for snap in graph.get_state_history(subgraph_config):
    print(snap.values)
```

But I got an error:

    subgraph_state = graph.get_state(config, subgraphs=True).tasks[0].state

hi @a171232886 

I think the root cause is: `StateSnapshot.tasks` contains pending/next-to-run tasks, not completed ones.
After both invoke() calls finish normally, there are zero pending tasks, so .tasks is an empty tuple and .tasks[0] throws IndexError

Why tasks is empty after completion

In _prepare_state_snapshot ([pregel/main.py](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/main.py)), tasks are computed via prepare_next_tasks, which calls _triggers ([_algo.py](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_algo.py)):

```py
def _triggers(channels, versions, seen, null_version, proc) -> bool:
    for chan in proc.triggers:
        if channels[chan].is_available() and versions.get(chan) > seen.get(chan):
            return True
    return False
```

After a completed run, checkpoint["versions_seen"]["agent"] is updated to match channel_versions. The condition versions.get(chan) > seen.get(chan) is False -> no next tasks -> empty .tasks


1. interrupt first

```py
graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer, interrupt_before=["agent"])
graph.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]}, config)

subgraph_state = graph.get_state(config, subgraphs=True).tasks[0].state
```

2. query subgraph directly via checkpoint_ns

```py
subgraph_config = {
    "configurable": {
        "thread_id": "1",
        "checkpoint_ns": "agent", 
    }
}
subgraph_state = graph.get_state(subgraph_config)
print(subgraph_state.values)
```
This works because get_state routes configs with a non-empty checkpoint_ns directly to the matching subgraph's checkpointer. 

3. Walk history

```py
subgraph_config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1", "checkpoint_ns": "agent"}}
for snap in graph.get_state_history(subgraph_config):
    print(snap.values)
```

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import Annotated

from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain_core.messages import BaseMessage
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langchain_google_genai import ChatGoogleGenerativeAI
from langgraph.graph import END, StateGraph
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages
from langgraph.graph.state import CompiledStateGraph
from langgraph.types import Command
from typing_extensions import TypedDict


class ParentState(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[Sequence[BaseMessage], add_messages]
    a: bool
    b: bool
    c: bool


tools_called: set[str] = set()


@tool
def fetch_file_info(sha256: str) -> Command:
    """Fetch basic file metadata"""
    tools_called.add("a")
    return Command(
        graph=Command.PARENT,
        goto="result_node",
        update={"a": True},
    )


@tool
def fetch_file_sources(sha256: str) -> Command:
    """Fetch file source/origin information"""
    tools_called.add("b")
    return Command(
        graph=Command.PARENT,
        goto="result_node",
        update={"b": True},
    )


@tool
def fetch_file_relations(sha256: str) -> Command:
    """Fetch file relationship"""
    tools_called.add("c")
    return Command(
        graph=Command.PARENT,
        goto="result_node",
        update={"c": True},
    )


TOOLS = [fetch_file_info, fetch_file_sources, fetch_file_relations]

PROMPT = (
    "You are a file analysis assistant. "
    "Given a SHA256 hash, call ALL THREE tools (fetch_file_info, "
    "fetch_file_sources, fetch_file_relations) IN PARALLEL to gather "
    "complete information about the file. Always call all three at once."
)


def build_graph() -> CompiledStateGraph[ParentState, None, ParentState, ParentState]:
    model = ChatGoogleGenerativeAI(
        model="gemini-3-flash-preview",
        vertexai=True,
        location="global",
    )

    agent = create_agent(model, TOOLS, system_prompt=PROMPT)  # type: ignore

    def result_node(state: ParentState) -> ParentState:
        return state

    parent = StateGraph(ParentState)
    parent.add_node("agent", agent)
    parent.add_node("result_node", result_node)
    parent.set_entry_point("agent")
    parent.add_edge("result_node", END)
    return parent.compile()  # type: ignore


if __name__ == "__main__":
    graph = build_graph()
    import langchain_core.globals

    langchain_core.globals.set_debug(True)
    langchain_core.globals.set_verbose(True)

    result = graph.invoke(
        {"messages": [("user", "Analyze file abc123def456")]},  # type: ignore
    )
    print("Tools called:", tools_called)
    print("Tools in state:", {k for k in result if k != "messages"})

```

Newer models, like `gemini-3-flash-preview`, can call several tools in one turn. If the tool returns a goto `Command` with `Command.PARENT` set, all the later tool results are discarded and ignored.

In the reporduction script, you'd expect A, B and C in `Tools in state` output, but there will only be one:

comments.author: tluma
comments.body: Hey Tasssadar! 👋 Based on the LangGraph code, `Command.PARENT` can only be used when a **single** tool returns a navigation command. When several tools are called in parallel, the runtime checks for multiple `graph=Command.PARENT` returns and raises an error (see the raise at [state.py L1550](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/graph/state.py#L1550)). This is why only the first tool’s update makes it into the state – the other tool results are discarded to avoid ambiguous parent‑graph navigation. The behavior is intentional, not a bug. 🛠️ To achieve what you want, let the tools just return state updates (no `graph` field) and add a separate node that, after all tools have finished, decides to go to `result_node` (or returns a single `Command.PARENT` from that node). In short, you can’t have each parallel tool navigate to the parent graph; you need to consolidate the navigation in one place. For more details on `Command` see the [Command docs](https://github.com/langchain-ai/docs/blob/main/src/oss/langgraph/graph-api.mdx#command).

Hey Tasssadar! 👋 Based on the LangGraph code, `Command.PARENT` can only be used when a **single** tool returns a navigation command. When several tools are called in parallel, the runtime checks for multiple `graph=Command.PARENT` returns and raises an error (see the raise at [state.py L1550](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/langgraph/langgraph/graph/state.py#L1550)). This is why only the first tool’s update makes it into the state – the other tool results are discarded to avoid ambiguous parent‑graph navigation. The behavior is intentional, not a bug. 🛠️ To achieve what you want, let the tools just return state updates (no `graph` field) and add a separate node that, after all tools have finished, decides to go to `result_node` (or returns a single `Command.PARENT` from that node). In short, you can’t have each parallel tool navigate to the parent graph; you need to consolidate the navigation in one place. For more details on `Command` see the [Command docs](https://github.com/langchain-ai/docs/blob/main/src/oss/langgraph/graph-api.mdx#command).

title: ToolNode: surface model output metadata in tool error messages to enable self-correction
body:
## Problem

When a tool call fails, the `ToolNode` creates a `ToolMessage(status="error")` containing only the exception text. The model receives this error but has **no access to its own output metadata** — information like why it stopped generating, how many tokens it used, or whether its output was complete.

This metadata *is* available on the originating `AIMessage.response_metadata` (every provider populates `stop_reason`/`finish_reason`, token counts, etc.), but it's never included in the error the model sees. Without this context, the model cannot diagnose root causes and may retry the same failing approach indefinitely.

### What we hit

In an autonomous agent workflow, a model called `write_file` with large content. The output hit `max_tokens=16384`, truncating the tool call JSON mid-argument. Pydantic raised `content: Field required` — a confusing error that gave no hint about truncation. The model retried 249 times, never learning *why* its arguments were malformed.

This affects any user whose model hits output limits while generating tool calls — large file writes, complex structured outputs, multi-tool parallel calls, etc.

## Reproduction

1. Use any model with a `max_tokens` setting (e.g., 16384)
2. Have the model call a tool with arguments large enough to exceed that limit
3. The tool call JSON gets truncated → validation fails → model gets a cryptic error → retries indefinitely

## Proposed Solution

Surface relevant `AIMessage.response_metadata` in tool error messages so the model can self-correct.

**General approach:** In `ToolNode._func` / `_afunc`, after tool execution, inspect the originating `AIMessage.response_metadata`. When metadata contains signals that explain the error (e.g., output truncation), append that context to the error `ToolMessage`.

**Specific first implementation:** Detect output truncation via `stop_reason == "max_tokens"` (Anthropic) / `finish_reason == "length"` (OpenAI). When detected and a tool call errors, append:

> Note: The model's previous response was cut off because it hit the max output token limit, which may have resulted in malformed tool call arguments. Consider reducing the size of the input to this tool or breaking it into smaller calls.

This is:
- **Zero-config** — works automatically for all users
- **Provider-agnostic** — checks both Anthropic and OpenAI conventions
- **Non-breaking** — only appends to existing error messages, no API changes
- **Extensible** — the same pattern can surface other metadata signals in the future (rate limits, content filtering, etc.)

Models like Claude and GPT-4 understand what token limits mean and can adapt (e.g., chunking writes) when given this context.

## Affected Component

`libs/prebuilt/langgraph/prebuilt/tool_node.py`

comments.author: pawel-twardziak
comments.body: Very useful feature!

comments.author: karsharma10
comments.body: +1 this is sweet

comments.author: mykolademyanov
comments.body:
This looks like a classic infinite-loop failure mode.

If `max_tokens` cuts off the tool call JSON, the model receives a validation error without any signal that the output was truncated — so retries often produce the same broken call again and again.

In practice this usually needs more than better error messages. Runtimes tend to add retry budgets or divergence checks to stop loops when no progress is made.

Short breakdown of this failure pattern:
https://agentpatterns.tech/en/failures/infinite-loop

comments.author: vinayakSharm
comments.body:
@mykolademyanov 

  Thanks for the link. That's a great breakdown of the failure pattern. You're absolutely right that retry budgets and divergence checks are important safeguards at the runtime level.

  This PR is intentionally focused on a narrower gap: the model has no access to its own output metadata when a tool call fails. Right now, response_metadata (stop reason, token counts, etc.) is available on the AIMessage but never surfaced in the error. So the model is making decisions with incomplete information.

  The way I see it, these are complementary layers:
  1. Give the model the information it needs to self-correct (this PR) — a model that sees stop_reason: max_tokens can adapt on its own (e.g., chunk a large write into smaller calls)
  2. Add runtime-level safeguards (retry budgets, loop detection) — for when self-correction isn't enough

  Neither replaces the other. But surfacing metadata is the lower cost fix that helps the model avoid the loop in the first place, rather than just catching it after the fact.

comments.author: mykolademyanov
comments.body:
@vinayakSharm 
Fair distinction. Surfacing metadata is the cheaper fix and helps the model avoid the loop earlier — runtime safeguards are the fallback. Good to have both layers.

title: langgraph dev: .langgraph_api runtime files cause continuous watchfiles log spam
body:
## Summary

`langgraph dev` writes runtime checkpoint files to `.langgraph_api/` inside the project directory. Since this directory is within uvicorn's watched tree, watchfiles detects these writes every ~10 seconds and logs noisy `"N changes detected"` lines continuously, even though no actual reload occurs.

## Reproduction

```bash
pip install langgraph-cli[inmem]
langgraph dev
```

Output (repeating every ~10 seconds):
```
2026-03-14T02:09:38Z [info] 12 changes detected [watchfiles.main]
2026-03-14T02:09:48Z [info] 12 changes detected [watchfiles.main]
2026-03-14T02:09:58Z [info] 12 changes detected [watchfiles.main]
```

The files being detected are the runtime pickles in `.langgraph_api/`:
```
.langgraph_api/.langgraph_checkpoint.1.pckl
.langgraph_api/.langgraph_checkpoint.2.pckl
.langgraph_api/.langgraph_checkpoint.3.pckl
.langgraph_api/.langgraph_ops.pckl
.langgraph_api/.langgraph_retry_counter.pckl
.langgraph_api/store.pckl
.langgraph_api/store.vectors.pckl
```

No spurious reloads occur (uvicorn's `FileFilter` discards non-`.py` files), but the log noise drowns out useful output.

## Root cause

Two things combine to cause this:

1. **`langgraph_api/cli.py:run_server()`** calls `uvicorn.run()` with `reload_excludes=None`, so `.langgraph_api` is not excluded from the watcher
2. **uvicorn passes `watch_filter=None`** to `watchfiles.watch()`, disabling all directory-level filtering — so even if `reload_excludes` were passed, watchfiles would still scan and log everything (the excludes only affect uvicorn's secondary `FileFilter`, not the watchfiles scanner itself). This is filed upstream as encode/uvicorn#2842.

## Suggested fixes

**Option A — Pass `reload_excludes`** (partial fix, helps when uvicorn fixes their side):
```python
# in langgraph_api/cli.py run_server()
uvicorn.run(
    ...
    reload_excludes=[".langgraph_api"],
    ...
)
```
This alone won't silence the logs today (due to the uvicorn issue above), but it's good hygiene and will work once uvicorn fixes `watch_filter=None`.

**Option B — Write runtime state outside the project tree** (full fix, independent of uvicorn):
Write `.langgraph_api/` to a location outside the watched directory, e.g. `~/.cache/langgraph/<project-hash>/` or a temp directory. This completely avoids the watcher regardless of how uvicorn is configured.

**Option C — Patch the watcher in `run_server()`** (full fix, local to langgraph):
```python
from watchfiles import DefaultFilter
from uvicorn.supervisors.watchfilesreload import WatchFilesReload

_orig_init = WatchFilesReload.__init__
_filter = DefaultFilter(
    ignore_dirs=[*DefaultFilter.ignore_dirs, ".langgraph_api"],
)

def _patched_init(self, config, target, sockets):
    _orig_init(self, config, target, sockets)
    self.watcher = watch(
        *self.reload_dirs,
        watch_filter=_filter,
        stop_event=self.should_exit,
        yield_on_timeout=True,
        ignore_permission_denied=True,
    )

WatchFilesReload.__init__ = _patched_init
```

## User workaround

Create a `dev.py` wrapper that patches the watcher before starting the CLI:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Wrapper around langgraph dev that fixes the watchfiles filter."""

import sys
from watchfiles import DefaultFilter, watch
from uvicorn.supervisors.watchfilesreload import WatchFilesReload

_orig_init = WatchFilesReload.__init__
_filter = DefaultFilter(
    ignore_dirs=[*DefaultFilter.ignore_dirs, ".langgraph_api", ".ipynb_checkpoints"],
)

def _patched_init(self, config, target, sockets):
    _orig_init(self, config, target, sockets)
    self.watcher = watch(
        *self.reload_dirs,
        watch_filter=_filter,
        stop_event=self.should_exit,
        yield_on_timeout=True,
        ignore_permission_denied=True,
    )

WatchFilesReload.__init__ = _patched_init

from langgraph_cli.cli import cli

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) == 1:
        sys.argv.append("dev")
    cli()
```

Then run `python dev.py` instead of `langgraph dev`.

## Related

- encode/uvicorn#2842 — uvicorn passes `watch_filter=None` to `watchfiles.watch()`, making `reload_excludes` ineffective for suppressing log noise

## Environment

- langgraph-api 0.7.70
- langgraph-cli 0.2.14
- uvicorn 0.34.0
- watchfiles 1.0.5
- Python 3.13.7
- Linux (Fedora 42)

comments.author: ori-cofounder
comments.body:
The cleanest fix is to exclude `.langgraph_api/` from watchfiles explicitly when starting the dev server.

**Option 1: watchfiles `ignore` pattern (preferred)**

```python
# In the langgraph-cli dev server startup:
from watchfiles import watch

for changes in watch(
    ".",
    ignore_paths=[".langgraph_api", ".git", "__pycache__"],
    # or via regex:
    watch_filter=lambda change, path: not path.startswith(".langgraph_api")
):
    handle_reload(changes)
```

**Option 2: write runtime files outside the project tree**

Move checkpoint files to a temp directory:
```python
import tempfile
RUNTIME_DIR = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="langgraph_"))
```

**Option 3: `.gitignore`-style config**

Add `.langgraph_api` to a default `.watchfiles_ignore` or respect `.gitignore` patterns (watchfiles supports this via `GitWatcher`).

Option 1 is the least invasive — just add the path to the ignore list in the CLI's dev server initialization. The checkpoint files are runtime artifacts, not source code, so they should never trigger a reload.

comments.body:
as the uvicorn maintainer explained in encode/uvicorn#2842, uvicorn passes watch_filter=None to watchfiles.watch(). This means:

1. Option 1 (ignore paths via watch config): I tried this - reload_excludes=[".langgraph_api"]. It gets passed to uvicorn's FileFilter, but that filter runs after watchfiles has already detected and logged the changes. The INFO messages are emitted by watchfiles before uvicorn's filter ever sees them.
2. Option 2 (move files to temp dir): Would work but requires changes to langgraph-api (the server package), not the CLI. Much bigger scope.
3. Option 3 (GitWatcher/.gitignore): We don't control how uvicorn initializes watchfiles, so we can't switch to GitWatcher.

title: checkpoint: add stable tie-breaks for equal timestamp ordering
body:
## Problem
Checkpoint readers currently fall back to raw `checkpoint_id` ordering. When two checkpoints share the same timestamp bucket, repeated reads can drift by backend or rerun because there is no explicit secondary ordering contract.

## Why now
Higher-throughput graphs and async persistence make timestamp collisions normal rather than rare, and replay/debug receipts need deterministic ordering across memory, SQLite, and Postgres implementations.

## Expected behavior
Latest-checkpoint selection and checkpoint listing should order by checkpoint timestamp first, with a deterministic secondary tie-break that is preserved across backends.

## Claim-to-codepath map
- `libs/checkpoint/langgraph/checkpoint/memory/__init__.py`
- `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/__init__.py`
- `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/utils.py`
- `libs/checkpoint-postgres/langgraph/checkpoint/postgres/__init__.py`
- `libs/checkpoint-postgres/langgraph/checkpoint/postgres/base.py`
- `libs/checkpoint-conformance/langgraph/checkpoint/conformance/spec/test_put.py`

## Evidence packet
- Commit under test: `744a7c7fa583bb86c2adc88cb5f77e2bcaf5285d`
- Runtime: Python checkpointer test harness on macOS
- Repro concept: save multiple checkpoints with identical `ts` values but distinct IDs, then compare repeated `get_tuple` / `list` reads across backends.

## Validation requirements
- Add regression coverage for equal-timestamp checkpoints.
- Verify stable latest and list ordering for repeated reads.
- Run format, lint, and targeted tests in touched checkpoint libraries.

title: Free OWASP security scanner for AI agents: mcps-audit
body:
## Summary

Sharing a free tool: **mcps-audit** scans AI agent code against the OWASP Agentic AI Top 10 + OWASP MCP Top 10.

```bash
npx mcps-audit ./my-agent
```

We ran it against LangGraph's codebase (public repo, static analysis):

- **322 files** scanned, 132,759 lines
- **1,018 findings**: 12 CRITICAL, 56 HIGH, 941 MEDIUM, 9 LOW
- Key findings: injection patterns in redirect generation, missing logging across most modules, excessive permission patterns in store operations

Pattern-based static analysis only — no code execution, no data leaves the machine.

- **GitHub**: https://github.com/razashariff/mcps-audit

MIT licensed. Node.js 18+.

title: Add restart-safety coverage for put_writes idempotency
body:
Problem
The shared conformance suite verifies duplicate `put_writes` calls within one saver instance, but it does not currently protect the retry-safe contract across saver restarts, which is the operational case users hit after process or network failure.

Why now
`put_writes` is the pending-write boundary for resumed graphs. A restart-specific regression would not be caught by the existing `test_put_writes_idempotent` coverage even though the runtime contract is supposed to survive retries.

Evidence packet
- Commit under test: `0f2478cecbd55de8beeb22f87dce5dbafd9ace78`
- Runtime: macOS 15.3 / Darwin 25.3.0 arm64, Python `3.14.0`
- Relevant codepaths:
  - `libs/checkpoint-conformance/langgraph/checkpoint/conformance/spec/test_put_writes.py`
  - `libs/checkpoint-postgres/langgraph/checkpoint/postgres/base.py`
  - `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/__init__.py`
- Minimal repro:
  1. Persist a checkpoint.
  2. Call `put_writes` / `aput_writes` for a task.
  3. Re-open the saver and replay the exact same payload.
  4. Read `pending_writes` back from `get_tuple` / `list`.
- Expected: one stable pending-write set after replay, unchanged by the second write.
- Actual: current conformance coverage exercises only same-process duplicates, so restart regressions can slip through unnoticed.

Scope
This is a contract-validation gap around runtime behavior, not a broad framework redesign.

Validation target
Add restart-aware coverage that fails if replaying the same pending writes after re-opening the saver duplicates or mutates checkpoint state.

title: RFC: AMP (Agent Message Protocol) — standard for LangGraph agents to be discoverable across frameworks
body:
## The gap

LangGraph is excellent for building stateful, graph-based agents. Once deployed, there's no standard way for a LangGraph agent to advertise its capabilities to other agents — or to receive structured task requests from agents built on other frameworks.

## AMP — Agent Message Protocol

[AMP](https://github.com/laufferw/amp-protocol) is a minimal open protocol addressing exactly this. It's intentionally simple:

**Step 1 — be discoverable:** publish `/.well-known/agent.json`
```json
{
  "amp": "1.0",
  "id": "your-agent.example.com",
  "capabilities": ["document analysis", "summarization", "question answering"],
  "protocol": "amp/1.0",
  "endpoints": {
    "message": "https://your-agent.example.com/api/amp/message"
  }
}
```

**Step 2 — receive tasks:** accept `POST /api/amp/message` with an intent envelope

```json
{
  "amp": "1.0",
  "from": {"id": "orchestrator.example.com"},
  "to": "your-agent.example.com",
  "intent": "Summarize the following research paper and extract key claims",
  "context": {"background": "For a literature review pipeline"}
}
```

A LangGraph agent could treat the `intent` field as the initial human message, injecting it into the graph's entry node. The response maps naturally to an AMP response envelope.

## Why now

The agent ecosystem is fragmenting across frameworks. Without a common discovery/communication layer, every cross-framework integration requires bespoke glue. AMP is a proposal for that common layer — intentionally minimal, fully open, no lock-in.

- Spec (fits in one page): https://github.com/laufferw/amp-protocol  
- Live reference hub: https://agentboard.fyi  
- Zero-dep Python + JS libs included

Opening as RFC — interested in the team's perspective on cross-framework agent communication.

comments.author: kinthaiofficial
comments.body:
AMP fills a real gap. We implemented a similar discovery mechanism for inter-agent communication and `.well-known/agent.json` is the right starting point. Some additions from production experience:

**Agent Cards need cost metadata**

The `.well-known/agent.json` should include cost estimates. Without them, a delegating agent can't do budget planning:

```json
{
  "agent_id": "did:key:z6Mk...",
  "capabilities": [
    {
      "name": "code_review",
      "input_schema": { ... },
      "cost_estimate": {
        "min_millicents": 50,
        "max_millicents": 500,
        "avg_latency_ms": 3200
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

In a multi-agent system, the caller needs to reserve budget before delegating. Without cost metadata in the Agent Card, every delegation is a blind spend commitment.

**Session-scoped auth for repeated interactions**

AMP's per-request auth (Bearer tokens, API keys) works for one-off interactions. For agents that communicate frequently, session-scoped HMAC tokens reduce overhead:

```
# At session start: Ed25519 signed handshake → derive session key
session_key = derive(agent_a.private_key, agent_b.public_key)

# Per-message: HMAC instead of full asymmetric verification
mac = hmac_sha256(session_key, canonical(message))
```

~10x faster per-message auth while maintaining cryptographic guarantees at the session level.

**Delegation chain context**

AMP should include a delegation chain field in task requests. This enables:
1. **Cycle detection**: if the same agent_id appears twice → delegation loop
2. **Cost attribution**: charge the root delegator
3. **Capability narrowing**: child capabilities ≤ parent capabilities

```json
{
  "task": { ... },
  "delegation_chain": ["did:key:root", "did:key:parent", "did:key:current"],
  "budget_remaining_millicents": 5000
}
```

**Related:**
- [221 Agents: Multi-Agent Coordination Lessons](https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons) — agent discovery and coordination at scale
- [Your AI Agent Needs a Wallet: Economic Models for Autonomous Agents](https://blog.kinthai.ai/agent-wallet-economic-models-autonomous-agents) — why Agent Cards need economic metadata

Running this at [agents.kinthai.ai](https://agents.kinthai.ai) on OpenClaw.

comments.author: Jairooh
comments.body: Great RFC — the discovery layer is clean. Once agents call each other across frameworks, governance becomes critical: pre-execution safety checks, cost limits, approval workflows, and compliance tracking. AgentShield handles this governance layer specifically for agent-to-agent orchestration.

comments.author: sunfishloop
comments.body:
We faced this exact problem with our open-source project SunfishLoop (github.com/sunfishloop/sunfishloop) — a production agent social network with 20+ agents across CrewAI, AutoGen, and LangGraph.

What we found is that a custom protocol isn't strictly necessary for cross-framework discovery if you layer on existing standards. Our approach:

1. **/llms.txt** for discovery — each agent exposes a standard AI-crawlable endpoint at /llms.txt. No custom registry needed, discovery is just crawling.
2. **Agent Protocol** (/agent-protocol.json) for capability introspection — describes what tasks/functions the agent can perform. This is an existing standard, not a new one.
3. **JSON/slots payloads** for the wire format — instead of defining a new binary/message format, agents post structured JSON. LangGraph agents, CrewAI agents, and AutoGen agents all produce and consume the same slot schema.

The key insight: you don't need a new protocol to make agents discoverable. Existing web standards + Agent Protocol + a well-defined slot schema handle 90% of interop. The remaining 10% (which protocol to use for what) is better solved by letting agents declare their supported protocols in their Agent Card than by mandating one.

Would be happy to share more about what worked and what broke in production.

comments.author: NicolasPrimeau
comments.body:
The `.well-known/agent.json` + intent-envelope split is a clean minimal core, and treating `intent` as the graph's entry message is the right instinct. Two gaps from building a cross-agent message layer:

The envelope is synchronous point-to-point: it assumes `to` is reachable at send time, one sender to one endpoint. Real fleets also need durable delivery (a receiver that runs later drains an inbox, so a handoff isn't lost if the target is offline) and fan-out (one agent emits "done", several react, without N directed calls). Worth leaving room for store-and-forward and a subscribe channel, not just live POST.

On discovery: routing through AgentBoard as a hub reintroduces a central coordinator, which cuts against the no-lock-in goal. I went peer-to-peer in [Artel](https://github.com/NicolasPrimeau/artel) (agents mesh over feeds, no central registry) so discovery survives any one node going down. The `.well-known` self-description fits that fine; it's the mandatory hub routing I'd make optional.

AMP fills a real gap. We implemented a similar discovery mechanism for inter-agent communication and `.well-known/agent.json` is the right starting point. Some additions from production experience:

**Agent Cards need cost metadata**

The `.well-known/agent.json` should include cost estimates. Without them, a delegating agent can't do budget planning:

```json
{
  "agent_id": "did:key:z6Mk...",
  "capabilities": [
    {
      "name": "code_review",
      "input_schema": { ... },
      "cost_estimate": {
        "min_millicents": 50,
        "max_millicents": 500,
        "avg_latency_ms": 3200
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

In a multi-agent system, the caller needs to reserve budget before delegating. Without cost metadata in the Agent Card, every delegation is a blind spend commitment.

**Session-scoped auth for repeated interactions**

AMP's per-request auth (Bearer tokens, API keys) works for one-off interactions. For agents that communicate frequently, session-scoped HMAC tokens reduce overhead:

```
# At session start: Ed25519 signed handshake → derive session key
session_key = derive(agent_a.private_key, agent_b.public_key)

# Per-message: HMAC instead of full asymmetric verification
mac = hmac_sha256(session_key, canonical(message))
```

~10x faster per-message auth while maintaining cryptographic guarantees at the session level.

**Delegation chain context**

AMP should include a delegation chain field in task requests. This enables:
1. **Cycle detection**: if the same agent_id appears twice → delegation loop
2. **Cost attribution**: charge the root delegator
3. **Capability narrowing**: child capabilities ≤ parent capabilities

```json
{
  "task": { ... },
  "delegation_chain": ["did:key:root", "did:key:parent", "did:key:current"],
  "budget_remaining_millicents": 5000
}
```

**Related:**
- [221 Agents: Multi-Agent Coordination Lessons](https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons) — agent discovery and coordination at scale
- [Your AI Agent Needs a Wallet: Economic Models for Autonomous Agents](https://blog.kinthai.ai/agent-wallet-economic-models-autonomous-agents) — why Agent Cards need economic metadata

Running this at [agents.kinthai.ai](https://agents.kinthai.ai) on OpenClaw.

Great RFC — the discovery layer is clean. Once agents call each other across frameworks, governance becomes critical: pre-execution safety checks, cost limits, approval workflows, and compliance tracking. AgentShield handles this governance layer specifically for agent-to-agent orchestration.

We faced this exact problem with our open-source project SunfishLoop (github.com/sunfishloop/sunfishloop) — a production agent social network with 20+ agents across CrewAI, AutoGen, and LangGraph.

What we found is that a custom protocol isn't strictly necessary for cross-framework discovery if you layer on existing standards. Our approach:

1. **/llms.txt** for discovery — each agent exposes a standard AI-crawlable endpoint at /llms.txt. No custom registry needed, discovery is just crawling.
2. **Agent Protocol** (/agent-protocol.json) for capability introspection — describes what tasks/functions the agent can perform. This is an existing standard, not a new one.
3. **JSON/slots payloads** for the wire format — instead of defining a new binary/message format, agents post structured JSON. LangGraph agents, CrewAI agents, and AutoGen agents all produce and consume the same slot schema.

The key insight: you don't need a new protocol to make agents discoverable. Existing web standards + Agent Protocol + a well-defined slot schema handle 90% of interop. The remaining 10% (which protocol to use for what) is better solved by letting agents declare their supported protocols in their Agent Card than by mandating one.

Would be happy to share more about what worked and what broke in production.

The `.well-known/agent.json` + intent-envelope split is a clean minimal core, and treating `intent` as the graph's entry message is the right instinct. Two gaps from building a cross-agent message layer:

The envelope is synchronous point-to-point: it assumes `to` is reachable at send time, one sender to one endpoint. Real fleets also need durable delivery (a receiver that runs later drains an inbox, so a handoff isn't lost if the target is offline) and fan-out (one agent emits "done", several react, without N directed calls). Worth leaving room for store-and-forward and a subscribe channel, not just live POST.

On discovery: routing through AgentBoard as a hub reintroduces a central coordinator, which cuts against the no-lock-in goal. I went peer-to-peer in [Artel](https://github.com/NicolasPrimeau/artel) (agents mesh over feeds, no central registry) so discovery survives any one node going down. The `.well-known` self-description fits that fine; it's the mandatory hub routing I'd make optional.

title: How to add CLI orchestration layer on top of LangGraph agents?
body:
## Context

I've been building workflows where LangGraph handles the agent logic (state machines, routing, memory) but I needed a way to **orchestrate multiple LangGraph-based agents from a single CLI** — queue tasks, track state, retry failures, and coordinate agents via messaging.

## The Problem

When running 3+ LangGraph agents in parallel:
- Which agent is handling which task?
- What happens when one crashes?
- How do agents hand off context to each other?
- How do you enforce a review step before marking a task complete?

I ended up building **ORCH** to solve this — a CLI runtime that wraps any agent (including LangGraph apps) in a typed task queue with a validated state machine:

```
todo → in_progress → review → done
         ↓
      retrying (auto-retry on failure)
```

## What it looks like

```bash
npm install -g @oxgeneral/orch

# Add your LangGraph agent as a shell adapter
orch agent add "Researcher" --adapter shell --cmd "python langgraph_researcher.py"
orch agent add "Writer" --adapter shell --cmd "python langgraph_writer.py"

# Create and assign tasks
orch task add "Research AI trends 2026" --assignee researcher
orch task add "Write summary report" --depends-on <task-id>

# Launch + monitor in TUI
orch run --all
orch tui
```

Each agent runs in an isolated workspace. Output flows through the queue. If an agent fails, it retries automatically. There's a mandatory review gate before done.

**GitHub**: https://github.com/oxgeneral/ORCH
**npm**: `npm install -g @oxgeneral/orch`

## Questions for the community

- Has anyone built a similar CLI orchestration layer on top of LangGraph?
- How are you handling agent failure recovery in production LangGraph workflows?
- Is there interest in a more formal LangGraph adapter for ORCH?

Interested in how others are solving the multi-agent coordination problem at the infrastructure level.

comments.author: m13v
comments.body: I run parallel Claude agents on the same codebase and hit every problem here. the state machine is right but found the review gate carries more weight than expected: having an LLM validate output before handoff catches hallucinated assumptions before they compound. without it, agent B writes code based on agent A's wrong conclusion and you're debugging two layers deep. for failure recovery, the harder problem isn't retry logic - it's detecting when an agent is genuinely stuck vs stuck-looking-productive. task heartbeat plus output token velocity catches this better than timeouts alone. an agent can timeout fine but spend 10 minutes confidently hallucinating with perfect token throughput.

comments.author: pandego
comments.body:
Nice write-up. This is a real gap once you move past single-agent demos.

If you want a LangGraph-native adapter path, the highest-leverage pieces are usually:

1. **Checkpoint boundary per task transition**
   - persist graph state on each `todo -> in_progress -> review -> done` edge
   - recovery becomes resume-from-checkpoint, not full rerun

2. **Leased task ownership**
   - assign task with lease TTL + heartbeat
   - if agent dies, lease expires and scheduler requeues safely

3. **Idempotency key on tool side effects**
   - retries should replay compute, not duplicate writes/tickets/commits
   - key = `(task_id, transition_version, tool_call_id)` works well

4. **Review as a first-class graph node**
   - model reviewer/human reviewer as explicit node, not external flag
   - makes audit/replay much cleaner

If you publish an adapter contract (`start`, `heartbeat`, `checkpoint`, `finalize`, `abort`) I'd expect other LangGraph users to plug in quickly.

comments.author: ColonistOne
comments.body:
Different shape worth flagging: not a CLI orchestration layer over many agents, but **single-host coordination of multiple agents that each need exclusive GPU access**. We run two agents — one Python/LangGraph, one TypeScript/ElizaOS, different LLMs — on a single 24 GB-VRAM machine, swapped on demand. The interesting failure modes here aren't graph-side (checkpointer, retry queue — those are well-covered above) but process-level:

1. **Mutual exclusion via a shared `flock`.** Each agent's launcher takes the same lock before importing the LLM client; if held, the launcher exits gracefully. Accidental concurrency is impossible by construction; if one crashes mid-tick, the lock releases and a supervisor brings up the default agent.

2. **Supervisor as a separate systemd unit, not part of either agent.** Polls the parked agent's pending-work count via the platform API once a minute. When work crosses a threshold OR a scheduled-wakeup interval elapses, it stops the running agent, waits for the LLM to unload (`OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=0` + a follow-up `/api/generate` no-op), confirms VRAM is free, then starts the other.

3. **Minimum-window guarantee.** Once swapped in, the new agent gets at least N seconds before the supervisor will consider swapping back, regardless of idle signal. We landed on 1200 s — anything shorter killed multi-step react-then-comment chains mid-tick on the heavier model. This is also the answer to @m13v's "stuck-looking-productive" point on the failure-recovery side: single-tick timeouts misclassify slow inference as stuck. Idle detection has to be `consecutive idle polls past the minimum window`, not single-tick.

4. **Scheduled wakeup interval as a fallback.** Agents that mostly do engagement loops (browsing, reacting, posting on a schedule) never get scheduled in by inbound traffic on quiet days. A ~2 h scheduled wakeup keeps them alive even when there's zero work to react to.

5. **Heavy-process cold-load reality.** End-to-end swap is ~30–40 s on our hardware (poll detect → stop → Ollama unload → VRAM probe → start → cold model load on the new agent). Worth budgeting for explicitly — under the hood, the swap is dominated by the cold load of the next model into VRAM.

This is closer to a "Kubernetes-style controller for one resource" than a task queue — on a single host with one GPU, the bottleneck isn't task scheduling, it's exclusive resource ownership. Worth flagging because most CLI-orchestrator patterns assume resources are shared / cheap; local-LLM single-host deployment inverts that and the design surface changes accordingly.

To @oxgeneral's specific question — yes, there's interest in a more formal LangGraph adapter, and the shape that matters most for our use case is `start` / `heartbeat` / `checkpoint` / `finalize` / `abort` exactly as @pandego described, plus an explicit hook for the "I need exclusive `<resource>` before I can `start`" precondition. Without that, a multi-resource scheduler can't coexist with a constrained-resource one.

title: Background runs re-executed after ~180s despite BG_JOB_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS being set higher
body: This issue has been superseded by #7417 with a cleaner write-up. Closing and clearing content.

comments.author: mykolademyanov
comments.body:
This looks like duplicate re-entry of a long-running step.

If the runtime sweeps or retries the job before the original execution finishes, the same node can be invoked again even though the first run is still progressing. Without an execution boundary this ends up repeating the side effect and doubling the cost.

One pattern we've been using is guarding local agent/tool side effects with an execution lease so retries or sweeps can't re-run the same effect once the first execution has claimed ownership.

Closest example:
https://github.com/OnceOnly-Tech/onceonly-python/blob/main/examples/ai/agent_action_local.py

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)


### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell

```

### Description

AsyncPostgresStore.abatch currently acquires a connection via _ainternal.get_connection(self.conn) but does not actually use that connection for I/O. Instead, _execute_batch calls _cursor(pipeline=True), and _cursor performs a second _ainternal.get_connection(self.conn) and uses that connection to run all queries.

This results in:

- Redundant connection acquisition.
- With AsyncConnectionPool, two connections can be checked out from the pool per abatch call, although only one is used for real work.

comments.author: gitbalaji
comments.body:
Hi, I've investigated this bug and have a fix ready. The root cause is in `AsyncPostgresStore.abatch` ([aio.py:163](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/checkpoint-postgres/langgraph/store/postgres/aio.py#L163)) — it wraps `_execute_batch` in `_ainternal.get_connection()`, but `_execute_batch` immediately calls `self._cursor(pipeline=True)` which calls `_ainternal.get_connection()` again internally. The `conn` argument passed to `_execute_batch` is never used. With `AsyncConnectionPool` this checks out two connections per `abatch` call while only one does any work.

Fix is two lines:
1. Remove the `get_connection` wrapper in `abatch`
2. Drop the unused `conn` parameter from `_execute_batch`

Also adding a regression test using `max_size=1, timeout=2.0` — the pre-fix code deadlocks within 2s since `abatch` holds the only pool connection while `_cursor` waits for a second. Could a maintainer please assign this issue so I can open the PR?

title: Calling .invoke() as standalone on a StructuredTool requires a ToolRuntime object
body:
### Checked other resources

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.
- [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.

- [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package).
- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
@tool
def tool_test_one(runtime: ToolRuntime):
     pass

tool_test_one.invoke({})


@tool
def tool_test_two(runtime: Optional[ToolRuntime]):
     pass

tool_test_two.invoke({'runtime': None})
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
I am not allowed to provide the stack trace due to operating on corporate hardware, but the error for the first case stems from Pydantic saying the 'runtime' input is missing. The error for the second case is from Pydantic saying it can't evaluate the Optional[ToolRuntime] type and tool input parameters need to be JSON serializable.
```

### Description

My question is what is the proper way to call invoke on a previously created tool function when there is no ToolRuntime since the tool function is being called standalone as part of a unit test via invoke() on the StructuredTool? Does the source code need to be changed to allow Optional[ToolRuntime] as an input to the tool or change the invoke function to not be required to provide a ToolRuntime object?

### System Info

I am not allowed to share this due to operating on corporate hardware.

comments.author: morehardy
comments.body:
This looks like an usage mismatch rather than a execution bug. ToolRuntime is not a normal tool input. It is a special injected argument that LangGraph provides during tool execution, not when calling the underlying `StructuredTool.invoke()` standalone.

The correct usage is to execute the tool through ToolNode or a graphthat uses ToolNode, for example:
```
from unittest.mock import Mock
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode, ToolRuntime

@tool
def my_tool(query: str, runtime: ToolRuntime) -> str:
    return f"query={query}, tool_call_id={runtime.tool_call_id}"

tool_node = ToolNode([my_tool])

mock_runtime = Mock()
```

title: Proposal: Identity-Aware Agent Nodes for Multi-Agent Graphs
body:
## Summary

LangGraph graph nodes can represent different agents, including dynamically spawned subagents. When a supervisor node delegates to a subagent, or agents communicate across graph boundaries, there is no built-in mechanism to verify agent identity.

## Problem

- No identity verification when state passes between agent nodes
- Dynamically spawned subagents have no verifiable credentials
- Multi-tenant deployments on LangGraph Platform need agent isolation

## Proposal

An identity-aware AgentNode wrapper. When a graph edge passes state from one agent node to another, the receiving node can verify the sender's identity:

```python
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph

def identity_check(state, sender_credential):
    # Verify sender's AgentID certificate
    result = agentid.verify(sender_credential)
    return result["verified"]

graph = StateGraph(State)
graph.add_node("researcher", researcher_agent)
graph.add_node("writer", writer_agent)
graph.add_edge("researcher", "writer", guard=identity_check)
```

## Reference Implementation

[AgentID](https://getagentid.dev) provides ECDSA P-256 certificates, verification API, and trust scores. We have a LangChain integration already built:

[agentid-langchain on GitHub](https://github.com/haroldmalikfrimpong-ops/getagentid/tree/main/integrations/langchain)

Happy to contribute a LangGraph-specific example using StateGraph with identity checks on inter-agent edges.

comments.author: internet-dot
comments.body:
For the identity layer, consider a public registry for cross-graph agent verification. When agent nodes span organizations, local-only credentials are not enough.

[HCS-14 UAIDs](https://hol.org/docs/standards/hcs-14) (Hashgraph Online) could be attached to LangGraph nodes — a deterministic, protocol-neutral identifier that any external agent can verify via the public registry. Cross-graph verification becomes a simple UAID resolution step. The [Python SDK](https://github.com/hashgraph-online/standards-sdk-py) handles resolution.

title: AsyncPostgresSaver enforces instance-level threading.Lock() during asynchronous execution
body:
### **Problem Description**
When deploying `langgraph-checkpoint-postgres` in high-concurrency environments, the `AsyncPostgresSaver` utilizes an instance-level Python `threading.Lock()` across its internal cursor execution methods (such as `get_tuple` and `put`). 

While this prevents race conditions locally, it restricts concurrent `asyncio` tasks within the same process from fully utilizing the underlying `psycopg_pool.AsyncConnectionPool`. This constraint serializes asynchronous database multiplexing and increases latency ceilings under heavy payload.

### **Context & Repro**
We deployed a FastAPI LangGraph application (`builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)`) to a 3-node GKE cluster backed by Cloud SQL PostgreSQL. An `AsyncConnectionPool` was configured with `max_size=100`. 

We executed a 500-user concurrent 60-second load test against two identical endpoints to isolate the checkpointer's impact:

```python
# 1. The Locked LangGraph Implementation
@app.post("/chat")
async def chat_endpoint(thread_id: str):
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}}
    # Interfacing with agent.ainvoke funnels the state downward into the AsyncPostgresSaver `put` lock
    await agent_app.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Test"}]}, config)


# 2. The Unlocked Control Baseline
@app.post("/baseline")
async def baseline_endpoint(thread_id: str):
    # Intercepts the EXACT SAME pool instance, but bypasses the LangGraph logic lock entirely
    async with pool.connection() as conn:
        await conn.execute("SELECT 1;")
```

**Telemetry Output Data:**
The benchmark demonstrates that throughput and latency are severely bottlenecked locally by the Python `threading.Lock()`, rather than the maximum pool or database capacity.

*1. Unlocked Baseline Output (Raw `psycopg_pool` execution):*
```text
Type     Name        # reqs  # fails |  Avg   Min   Max   Med |  req/s  
--------|-----------|-------|--------|-------|-----|-----|----|---------
POST     /baseline    38044    0     |   88    47   717    73 | 1295.10
```

*2. Locked Output (`AsyncPostgresSaver` execution):*
```text
Type     Name        # reqs  # fails |  Avg   Min   Max   Med |  req/s  
--------|-----------|-------|--------|-------|-----|-----|----|---------
POST     /chat         9786    0     | 1923    75  3558  2000 |  199.90
```

### **System Info**
* **LangGraph Version:** `0.2.x`
* **LangGraph Checkpoint Postgres:** Latest
* **Testing Infrastructure:** GKE, Cloud SQL for Postgres 15, FastAPI, `psycopg_pool`

```python
import sqlite3
  from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver

  conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", check_same_thread=False)
  saver = SqliteSaver(conn)
  saver.setup()

  # Insert 100 checkpoints with writes
  for i in range(100):
      checkpoint_id = f"{i:032}.0"
      config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1", "checkpoint_ns": "", "checkpoint_id": checkpoint_id}}
      conn.execute(
          "INSERT INTO checkpoints (thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, type, checkpoint, metadata) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
          ("1", "", checkpoint_id, "json", b'{}', b'{}'),
      )
      conn.execute(
          "INSERT INTO writes (thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, task_id, idx, channel, type, value) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
          ("1", "", checkpoint_id, "task1", 0, "messages", "json", b'[]'),
      )
  conn.commit()

  # This triggers 101 queries (1 for checkpoints + 100 for writes)
  # Enable SQLite tracing to observe:
  queries = []
  conn.set_trace_callback(lambda q: queries.append(q))
  list(saver.list({"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}}))
  print(f"Total queries executed: {len(queries)}")
  # Output: Total queries executed: 101
  # Expected: 2
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell

```

### Description

 Description:                                                                                                                                                                 
  `SqliteSaver.list()` and `AsyncSqliteSaver.alist()` execute a separate                                                                                                       
  writes query for every checkpoint row returned. This is a classic N+1                                                                                                        
  query pattern.                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                               
  - I'm listing checkpoints via `SqliteSaver.list()` on a thread with N checkpoints.                                                                                           
  - I expect the number of database queries to be constant (2: one for checkpoints, one for all writes).                                                                       
  - Instead, it executes N+1 queries (1 for checkpoints + 1 per checkpoint for writes), which degrades linearly.                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                               
  **Affected files:**                                                                                                                                                          
  - `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/__init__.py` — `SqliteSaver.list()` (line 335)                                                                         
  - `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/aio.py` — `AsyncSqliteSaver.alist()` (line 431)

*(Note: Using this required field to describe a Feature Proposal, as the feature template is unavailable. I already have a fully tested PR ready for review: #7239)*

I have implemented a `langgraph.graph.reducers` module (including `smart_merge_dict`, `combine_distinct`, and `first_wins`) that intelligently deep-merges dictionaries, extends lists, and upgrades conflicting scalars to lists to preserve all historical signals.

- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Related Issues / PRs

#7273

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, AIMessage
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages

# 1. Message IDs are lost
left = [HumanMessage(content="hello", id="msg-1")]
right = [AIMessage(content="world", id="msg-2")]

result = add_messages(left, right, format="langchain-openai")

print(result[0].id)  # None — expected "msg-1"
print(result[1].id)  # None — expected "msg-2"

# 2. Custom additional_kwargs are lost
msg = AIMessage(
    id="msg-1",
    content="hello",
    additional_kwargs={"widgets": [{"type": "carousel"}]},
)
result = add_messages([], [msg], format="langchain-openai")
print(result[0].additional_kwargs)  # {} — expected {"widgets": [{"type": "carousel"}]}
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
No error raised. Message IDs are silently set to None and custom additional_kwargs are silently dropped.
```

### Description

`add_messages(format="langchain-openai")` loses message IDs and custom `additional_kwargs` during the OpenAI format round-trip.

  `_format_messages()` in `langgraph/graph/message.py` calls `convert_to_openai_messages()` without `include_id=True`. The round-trip `BaseMessage → OpenAI dict → BaseMessage` strips all IDs to
   `None`. Additionally, any custom `additional_kwargs` (e.g. UI widgets, metadata) are dropped because `convert_to_openai_messages` only outputs standard OpenAI fields.

  **Impact:**
  1. Every subsequent reducer call assigns new random UUIDs to all existing messages, breaking ID-based deduplication and update logic.
  2. Custom data stored in `additional_kwargs` is silently lost after each reducer invocation.

  **Proposed fix:** Pass `include_id=True` to preserve IDs. Save `additional_kwargs` by message ID before conversion and restore lost fields after.

title: Suggest: generate random Postgres password instead of hardcoded default in Docker Compose
body:
## Suggest: generate random Postgres password instead of hardcoded default in Docker Compose

### Summary

The LangGraph CLI generates Docker Compose configurations with a hardcoded `postgres:postgres` password for the internal PostgreSQL service. If users deploy this configuration without changing the default, the database is accessible with a predictable credential. Generating a random password at `langgraph up` time would prevent accidental production use of the default.

**Affected files**:
- `libs/cli/langgraph_cli/docker.py` (line 12)
- `libs/cli/langgraph_cli/config.py` (line 1425)

### Current Behavior

**`docker.py:11-13`**:
```python
DEFAULT_POSTGRES_URI = (
    "postgres://postgres:postgres@langgraph-postgres:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable"
)
```

**`config.py:1425`**:
```python
postgres_uri = "postgres://postgres:postgres@langgraph-postgres:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable"
```

Both locations hardcode `postgres:postgres` as the database credential. This URI is injected into the Docker Compose environment for the orchestrator, API, and executor services.

### Proposed Behavior

When `langgraph up` generates a Docker Compose configuration and the user has not provided a custom `DATABASE_URI`:

1. Generate a random password (e.g., 24-character alphanumeric)
2. Use this password in both the Postgres service and the connecting services
3. Optionally persist the generated password in a `.env` file so it remains stable across restarts

### Suggested Implementation

```python
import secrets
import string

def _generate_postgres_uri() -> str:
    """Generate a Postgres URI with a random password for Docker Compose."""
    alphabet = string.ascii_letters + string.digits
    password = ''.join(secrets.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(24))
    return f"postgres://postgres:{password}@langgraph-postgres:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable"
```

In `config.py` and `docker.py`, replace the hardcoded URI:

```python
# Before:
postgres_uri = "postgres://postgres:postgres@langgraph-postgres:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable"

# After:
postgres_uri = user_provided_uri or _generate_postgres_uri()
```

### Why This Matters

- Docker Compose deployments are often used as staging or even production environments
- Users frequently deploy defaults without modification, especially during initial setup
- A predictable password combined with an accidentally exposed port (e.g., Postgres port-forwarded or network misconfigured) creates a direct database access risk
- Generating a random password is a zero-cost improvement that eliminates this class of risk entirely

### Alternatives Considered

- **Documentation-only fix**: Add a warning comment in the generated Docker Compose. Less effective — users skip comments.
- **Startup validation**: Check if the default password is in use and warn at runtime. Better than nothing, but still relies on users acting on warnings.
- **Random generation (proposed)**: Eliminates the problem by default. No user action required.

title: Collaboration: Trust-gated checkpoints and governance nodes for LangGraph
body:
## Summary

We've built a trust-aware governance integration for LangGraph in the [Agent Governance Toolkit](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-governance-toolkit) (MIT, 6,100+ tests). The adapter lives at [packages/agentmesh-integrations/langgraph-trust/](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-governance-toolkit/tree/main/packages/agentmesh-integrations/langgraph-trust).

## What it provides

| Capability | Description |
|---|---|
| **Trust-gated checkpoint nodes** | Graph nodes that enforce trust thresholds before proceeding |
| **Governance policy nodes** | Inline policy evaluation within graph execution |
| **Trust routing** | Route execution paths based on agent trust scores |
| **Audit trail** | Every graph transition logged with tamper-proof hash chain |

## Integration approach

LangGraph's graph-based execution model maps naturally to governance — policy checks become nodes, trust gates become conditional edges.

\\\python
pip install langgraph-trust
\\\

## Why this matters for LangGraph users

- **Multi-agent governance** — trust scoring becomes critical when agents collaborate in graphs
- **Conditional safety** — route to human review when trust drops below threshold
- **Compliance** — audit trail captures every state transition

## Open questions

1. Would you consider trust/governance as a first-class concept in LangGraph's checkpoint system?
2. Is there a preferred extension point for middleware nodes?

Happy to discuss or submit a PR.

comments.author: pshkv
JohnnyTarrr
comments.body:
Interesting approach mapping governance to graph nodes. For the factual verification gate — checking that agent outputs are grounded before proceeding to the next node — VeroQ Shield returns a 0-1 confidence score you could use directly as a trust signal for conditional edges.

We already have a LangChain integration (`pip install langchain-veroq`) with 40 tools. The `verify_output` method checks every claim in a text block, which maps cleanly to your trust-gated checkpoint pattern: if trust_score < threshold, route to review node instead of proceeding.

Also has a private knowledge base mode for verifying against internal docs.

comments.author: imran-siddique
comments.body:
Update: we shipped the \langgraph-trust\ integration package with trust-gated checkpoint verification. It's at \packages/agentmesh-integrations/langgraph-trust/\ on PyPI.

@JohnnyTarrr — factual verification as a conditional edge signal is exactly the right pattern. Our \ContentQualityEvaluator\ provides dimension-based scoring (accuracy, completeness, etc.) that could drive LangGraph conditional edges alongside external verification tools. comments.author: pshkv
imran-siddique
comments.body:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/contributor-check.yml
on:

    types: [opened]

jobs:

```

**What it does:**

- Detects credential-spray patterns (merged PRs cited across other repos)

- Zero external dependencies (Python stdlib only)
