comments.author: hanselhansel
comments.body:
The scheduling interface proposal addresses compile-time configuration well. The gap I'd flag from a production ops angle: the cases that hurt most are when you need to adjust scheduling policy at runtime without redeploying the graph.

In practice, priority needs change based on system load, SLA windows, or upstream incidents. A guardrail-check node that's low priority during normal operation needs to become blocking during a compliance review window. Encoding that into a static `NodePriorityScheduler` at compile time means redeployment every time operational conditions shift.

The question for the proposal: is the scheduling policy object intended to be injectable at runtime (passed in at invocation time alongside input), or is it fixed at compile time? If it's compile-time only, operators in production will end up maintaining multiple compiled graph variants and routing between them, which is workable but adds a layer of operational complexity the framework could absorb.

comments.author: karimluna
comments.body:
Good catch @hanselhansel, for system owned signals (load, incidents, compliance windows) the policy object itself is the right place. It's compiled once and can poll Redis, a feature flag SDK, or any external source internally so no redeployment needed. That works with the proposed hook as-is.

For caller-owned signals (request tier, tenant id, SLA class) the natural LangGraph pattern is `config["configurable"]`, which is the standard per-invocation slot already used for thread ids, user ids, and similar runtim context. To make this work,`SchedulerContext` would need to expose `configurable` alongside the already-proposed `metadata` field:

```python
@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
class SchedulerContext:
    step: int
    tasks: Sequence[PregelExecutableTask]
    graph_id: str | None = None
    metadata: dict[str, Any] = dataclasses.field(default_factory=dict)
    configurable: dict[str, Any] = dataclasses.field(default_factory=dict)  # proposed addition
```
Which would allow

```python
class TieredScheduler:
    def prioritize(self, ctx: SchedulerContext):
        tier = ctx.configurable.get("tier", "standard")
        priorities = PREMIUM_PRIORITIES if tier == "premium" else STANDARD_PRIORITIES
        return sorted(ctx.tasks, key=lambda t: priorities.get(t.name, 5))

graph.compile(scheduler_policy=TieredScheduler())

# standard LangGraph invocation and no redeployment:
graph.invoke(input, config={"configurable": {"tier": "premium"}})
```

The implementation cost is small: one field on `SchedulerContext`, one line in the loop populating it from the existing `config` dict that already flows through at every superstep. If maintainers consider this in scope I'd include it in the same PR, which would make the hook fully runtime-injectable through the standard LangGraph config pattern.

comments.author: kinthaiofficial
comments.body:
Good proposal — graph-level task scheduling is essential once you move beyond simple sequential chains.

From building scheduling policies for multi-agent graph execution:

**Three scheduling dimensions**: A useful scheduling policy needs to address:
1. **Priority** — Which graph nodes execute first when resources are constrained? We use three tiers: interactive (human-facing, sub-second latency), background (autonomous, tolerates 5-10s delay), batch (analytics/consolidation, schedule during low utilization)
2. **Concurrency** — How many nodes can execute in parallel? This should be configurable per-graph and respect resource limits. Unbounded parallelism causes model API rate limit storms
3. **Budget** — How much can a graph execution cost in total? Per-node cost ceilings with pessimistic allocation on node creation prevent runaway spending

**Cost-aware node scheduling**: Not all nodes in a graph have equal cost. A node that calls an expensive model should be scheduled only when its inputs are validated and the remaining budget is sufficient. We estimate cost at scheduling time: `(model_price × expected_input_tokens) + (model_price × expected_max_output)`. If estimated cost exceeds remaining budget, the scheduler blocks the node and returns a structured error rather than letting it fail mid-execution.

**Dynamic graph modification based on runtime signals**: The most powerful scheduling pattern is adjusting the graph structure at runtime. If a reasoning node determines the task is simpler than expected, it should be able to skip subsequent analysis nodes. If a node fails, the scheduler should support fallback paths without requiring pre-defined error edges for every possible failure.

**Checkpoint-based resumability**: Long-running graph executions need checkpoint support at the scheduling level. If a graph execution is interrupted (timeout, budget exhaustion, node failure), it should be resumable from the last successful checkpoint rather than re-executing from the start.

Architecture on multi-agent scheduling and cost governance: https://blog.kinthai.ai/openclaw-multi-tenancy-why-vm-per-user-doesnt-scale
Coordination patterns for parallel execution: https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons

comments.author: hanselhansel
comments.body:
The compile step is where I would slow down. "Compiled once" sounds clean, but in practice the policy compile has an owner question that is easy to skip. Who reloads it when the underlying signal source changes shape, who validates that the compiled policy is still safe against the new signal schema, and what happens to in-flight runs that were scheduled against the old compile.

In a system I deployed, we treated the compiled policy as a versioned artifact tied to a run, not a process-global. New runs picked up new compiles; in-flight runs ran against the compile they were dispatched with. That gave us a clean rollback path when a compliance window definition changed and we needed to honor the old window for sessions already in motion. Curious how you are thinking about that boundary, since the polling source you mention (Redis, flag SDK) implies the compile output can change under a running graph.

title: TypeError collecting serde allowlist for collections.abc generic containers
body:
### Checked other resources

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.
- [x] I used GitHub search to find a similar issue and did not find one for this serde allowlist path.
- [x] I included a self-contained minimal reproducible example.

### Example Code

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from collections.abc import Sequence

from langgraph._internal._serde import collect_allowlist_from_schemas


@dataclass
class Item:
    x: int


@dataclass
class State:
    items: Sequence[Item]


allowlist = collect_allowlist_from_schemas(schemas=[State])
print(allowlist)
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace

On Python 3.10, this raises:

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 17, in <module>
  File ".../langgraph/_internal/_serde.py", line 112, in collect_allowlist_from_schemas
    _collect_from_type(schema, allowlist, seen, seen_ids)
  File ".../langgraph/_internal/_serde.py", line 191, in _collect_from_type
    _collect_from_type(field_type, allowlist, seen, seen_ids)
  File ".../langgraph/_internal/_serde.py", line 174, in _collect_from_type
    if _is_pydantic_model(typ):
  File ".../langgraph/_internal/_serde.py", line 237, in _is_pydantic_model
    return issubclass(typ, BaseModelV1)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/abc.py", line 123, in __subclasscheck__
    return _abc_subclasscheck(cls, subclass)
TypeError: issubclass() arg 1 must be a class
```

### Description

`collect_allowlist_from_schemas()` recurses through built-in containers such as `list[T]`, `dict[K, V]`, and `deque[T]`, but it does not currently handle abstract containers from `collections.abc`, such as `Sequence[T]`, `Mapping[K, V]`, and `Iterable[T]`.

For `collections.abc.Sequence[Item]` on Python 3.10, `isinstance(typ, type)` returns `True`, but passing that object to `issubclass()` can raise `TypeError`. That means allowlist collection can fail before it has a chance to collect nested custom types.

I would expect abstract containers to be treated similarly to the supported built-in containers, so the example above should return an allowlist containing both `State` and `Item`.

### Proposed fix

I have a draft PR with a small regression test and fix here:

https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/7600

The change:

- recurses into common `collections.abc` generic containers
- guards pydantic model detection against `TypeError` from `issubclass()`
- extends `test_serde_allowlist.py` to cover `Sequence`, `Mapping`, and `Iterable`

### System Info

Reproduced against `main` at `45246f6c`.

```text
Python: 3.10.12
langgraph source checkout: langchain-ai/langgraph main
```

I’d like to work on this issue. I opened the original draft PR with a minimal fix and regression test in #7600 before creating this issue. Could a maintainer assign this issue to me?

Hey, what version of LangGraph are you running this on? Just curious 'cause we've hit something super similar with the `collect_allowlist_from_schemas()` function when dealing with generic container types like `Sequence` on Python 3.10. Honestly, the error in `issubclass()` tripping on non-class types is a pain, and it seems like the serde logic doesn't handle ABC generics gracefully yet. Turns out, we had to patch around this in one of our pipelines by explicitly avoiding the recursion on abstract base classes — took us a few tries to nail it.

Here's a quick workaround we used to bypass the check for non-class types before it hits the `issubclass()` call:

```python
def _is_pydantic_model(typ):
    if not isinstance(typ, type):
        return False
    return issubclass(typ, BaseModelV1)
```

We’ve been running this in prod with a custom fork for a few weeks now across a couple hundred schemas, and it’s held up fine. The thing is, if LangGraph upstream hasn’t addressed this yet, you might need to raise a PR or pin to a specific commit until it’s fixed. Not gonna lie, digging into their serde internals was a bit of a rabbit hole.

title: PostgresSaver.setup() fails when called inside a transaction due to CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
body:
> Targets the `libs/checkpoint-postgres` subpackage (langgraph-checkpoint-postgres 3.0.5).

### Bug description

`PostgresSaver.setup()` (and equivalently `PostgresStore.setup()`, same root cause) raises
`psycopg.errors.ActiveSqlTransaction: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block`
whenever the call site wraps it in an explicit transaction. `MIGRATIONS` contains three
`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` statements (`base.py` L76/L79/L82), and Postgres rejects
`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` inside any open transaction block — even an empty one on
a fresh table.

This is distinct from the closed issues #2887 and #5327, which were resolved with
"set `autocommit=True`." That guidance works for callers that *only* run `setup()`,
but it conflicts with two legitimate scenarios:

1. **Atomic provisioning flows** that need `setup()` to roll back together with sibling
   DDL — e.g., schema-per-tenant onboarding where tenant schema creation, checkpoint
   table provisioning, and external-system bookkeeping must commit-or-rollback as a
   single unit. `autocommit=True` defeats atomicity by design.
2. **Implicit transaction contexts** opened by upstream LangGraph itself, e.g. anywhere
   a checkpointer is exercised via `graph.compile(checkpointer=...)` against a
   non-autocommit `Connection`/`ConnectionPool` configured by the application.

### Reproduction

Pytest-style minimal repro, drop-in compatible with `libs/checkpoint-postgres/tests/`
(uses `testcontainers` so it is runnable without the in-tree `compose-postgres.yml`;
the same assertion holds when swapped to the existing `DEFAULT_POSTGRES_URI` fixture):

```python
"""Reproduction: PostgresSaver.setup() fails when called inside a transaction.

Drop into libs/checkpoint-postgres/tests/. Self-contained — uses the
testcontainers fixture pattern instead of the in-tree compose-postgres.yml so
contributors without docker-compose infra can still execute it. Swap to
``DEFAULT_POSTGRES_URI`` from ``conftest`` if matching the existing fixture
style is preferred; the bug reproduces under either harness.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import pytest
from psycopg import Connection
from psycopg.errors import ActiveSqlTransaction
from psycopg.rows import dict_row
from testcontainers.postgres import PostgresContainer

from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres import PostgresSaver


@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def pg_dsn():
    with PostgresContainer("postgres:16") as pg:
        yield str(pg.get_connection_url()).replace(
            "postgresql+psycopg2://", "postgresql://"
        )


def test_setup_fails_inside_explicit_transaction(pg_dsn: str) -> None:
    """PostgresSaver.setup() must not be called inside a transaction.

    Callers that wrap the checkpoint scaffolding in an explicit transaction
    for atomicity (e.g. multi-tenant onboarding flows that provision tenant
    schema + checkpoint tables together) hit psycopg's ActiveSqlTransaction
    because MIGRATIONS contains CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY statements.
    """
    # autocommit=False is psycopg's default; this mirrors any caller that
    # uses ``with conn.transaction(): ...`` or relies on implicit txn open.
    with Connection.connect(pg_dsn, autocommit=False, row_factory=dict_row) as conn:
        saver = PostgresSaver(conn)
        with pytest.raises(ActiveSqlTransaction) as exc_info:
            with conn.transaction():
                saver.setup()
        assert "CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY" in str(exc_info.value)
```

Verified passing against `langgraph-checkpoint-postgres==3.0.5`, `psycopg==3.x`,
`postgres:16`, Python 3.13.

### Expected behaviour

Two possible directions (no preference expressed; this is for upstream to design):

- **(a)** Detect a live transaction in `setup()` and skip `CONCURRENTLY` for fresh
  empty tables (where there are no concurrent writers, the locking distinction is
  moot), or
- **(b)** Split `MIGRATIONS` into "in-txn-safe" and "must-run-outside-txn" buckets
  and let the caller orchestrate, so atomic provisioning flows can opt into running
  the in-txn-safe portion under their transaction and the index step afterwards.

### Local workaround

Subclass `PostgresSaver` and strip `CONCURRENTLY` before the parent migrates:

```python
class _TxnSafePostgresSaver(PostgresSaver):
    # Strip CONCURRENTLY so setup() can run inside an explicit transaction.
    # Acceptable because target tables are fresh and have no concurrent writers
    # at provisioning time.
    MIGRATIONS = tuple(
        sql.replace("CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY", "CREATE INDEX")
        for sql in PostgresSaver.MIGRATIONS
    )
```

This is functionally fine for the provisioning use case but obviously diverges from
the upstream migration list, which is why we'd prefer a first-class story.

### Environment

- Python: 3.13
- Postgres: 16
- `langgraph-checkpoint-postgres`: 3.0.5
- `psycopg`: 3.x with `psycopg-pool`
- OS: macOS 25.4 (also reproduced on Linux CI)

comments.author: Alexxigang
comments.body:
I traced this to the current `setup()` migration loop in `libs/checkpoint-postgres`: both `PostgresSaver.setup()` and `PostgresStore.setup()` execute their migration lists through a single cursor/context, so the `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` migrations inherit any caller transaction and hit `ActiveSqlTransaction`.

I'd like to take this on with a fix that keeps the transaction-safe setup path explicit and adds regression tests for both saver and store setup under an explicit transaction. If that direction sounds good, could I be assigned?

comments.body: Friendly follow-up: I finished a patch for this on my fork and pushed it on branch `fix/postgres-setup-transactional-migrations`. The change handles `setup()` migrations safely when the connection is already inside a transaction, and I added regression coverage for saver/store setup under explicit transactions plus sync/async migration utility coverage. Since LangGraph often prefers assigned issues before opening a PR, I held off on creating one unprompted, but I'm happy to open it immediately if you'd like me to proceed.

title: [Feature] Add delete_for_runs support for SQLite checkpoint savers
body:
### Privileged issue

- [ ] I am a LangGraph maintainer.

### Issue Content

Opening this issue per maintainer request in this forum thread: [Proposal: implement delete_for_runs for SQLite checkpoint savers](https://forum.langchain.com/t/proposal-implement-delete-for-runs-for-sqlite-checkpoint-savers/3621)

## Problem

While building with LangGraph + SQLite, I wanted to delete checkpoints associated with a few specific runs. I noticed that `BaseCheckpointSaver` already exposes `delete_for_runs` / `adelete_for_runs`, and checkpoint metadata already includes `run_id`, but the SQLite checkpoint savers do not currently implement these methods.

Relevant code:
- `BaseCheckpointSaver.delete_for_runs` / `adelete_for_runs`: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/checkpoint/langgraph/checkpoint/base/__init__.py
- SQLite saver: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/__init__.py
- Async SQLite saver: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/aio.py

Related existing work:
- Existing conformance tests for `delete_for_runs`: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/checkpoint-conformance/langgraph/checkpoint/conformance/spec/test_delete_for_runs.py
- Open PostgreSQL implementation PR: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/6883

## Proposal

Implement `delete_for_runs` support for the SQLite checkpoint savers:

- Add `delete_for_runs` to `SqliteSaver`.
- Add `adelete_for_runs` to `AsyncSqliteSaver`.
- Delete checkpoints whose metadata `run_id` is in the provided run IDs.
- Delete associated pending writes for those checkpoints.
- Preserve checkpoints from unrelated runs.
- Treat an empty list or unknown run IDs as no-op.
- Support deletion across checkpoint namespaces, matching the existing conformance behavior.

## Testing

I plan to implement this so SQLite passes the existing `delete_for_runs` conformance tests.

If needed, I can also add SQLite-specific tests in `libs/checkpoint-sqlite/tests` to make sure both `SqliteSaver` and `AsyncSqliteSaver` are covered.

## Scope

I do not plan to touch the Postgres implementation, base interfaces, lockfiles, or add new dependencies.

title: Visualization disconnected when using Command(graph=Command.PARENT, goto=...) from a subgraph
body:
### Checked other resources

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.
- [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code.
- [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package).
- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Related Issues / PRs

_No response_

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
import operator
import random
from typing_extensions import Annotated, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START
from langgraph.types import Command

class State(TypedDict):
    foo: Annotated[str, operator.add]

def node_a(state: State):
    value = random.choice(["a", "b"])
    # Dynamic routing to parent nodes
    return Command(
        update={"foo": value},
        goto="node_b" if value == "a" else "node_c",
        graph=Command.PARENT,
    )

inner_graph = StateGraph(State).add_node(node_a).add_edge(START, "node_a").compile()

def node_b(state: State): return {"foo": "b"}
def node_c(state: State): return {"foo": "c"}

builder = StateGraph(State)
builder.add_node("my_subgraph", inner_graph)
builder.add_node(node_b)
builder.add_node(node_c)
builder.add_edge(START, "my_subgraph")

graph = builder.compile()

# The graph runs perfectly, but the visualization is broken (node_b and node_c are isolated).
print(graph.get_graph(xray=True).draw_mermaid())
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell

```

### Description

When using the Command object inside a subgraph to dynamically route to nodes in the parent graph (graph=Command.PARENT), the static graph visualization (get_graph().draw_mermaid() or draw_png()) fails to capture these routing paths.

As a result, the target nodes in the parent graph appear as completely disconnected/orphaned in the generated diagram, and the subgraph appears to route directly to __end__.

While this is understandable since Command routing is evaluated at runtime, it creates a frustrating developer experience. To fix the visualization, developers are forced to write dummy add_conditional_edges, which duplicates the routing logic and defeats the purpose of the elegant Command pattern.

### Current Workaround & Its Drawbacks

To make the visualization work, we have to add a dummy conditional edge:
```python
def dynamic_routing_hack(state):
    # We must explicitly handle the Command object bubbling up, 
    # otherwise it raises a KeyError during execution!
    if isinstance(state, Command):
        return state.goto
    return "node_b"

builder.add_conditional_edges("my_subgraph", dynamic_routing_hack, ["node_b", "node_c"])
```

### Drawbacks of this workaround:

1. Logic Duplication: We have to maintain the list of possible targets ["node_b", "node_c"] twice.

2. Hidden Traps (KeyError): Because the parent graph evaluates the conditional edge by passing the bubbled-up Command object as the state, developers must check isinstance(state, Command). Missing this leads to a runtime KeyError.

### Expected Behavior / Feature Request

It would be great if there was a way to declare "visual routing hints" natively when using Command, without affecting the runtime execution or writing dummy conditional edges.

Perhaps something like:

1. Allowing static path declarations on the node/subgraph registration (e.g., builder.add_node("my_subgraph", inner_graph, expected_routes=["node_b", "node_c"])).

2. Or a dedicated method like builder.add_visual_edge("my_subgraph", ["node_b", "node_c"]) purely for the static analyzer.

comments.body:
Thanks for the clear repro. I checked this locally using the example from the issue, and `destinations` seems to cover this visualization-only case. Without `destinations`, the xray Mermaid output shows the subgraph node going to `__end__`, while `node_b` and `node_c` appear disconnected on the side.

> For same-graph `Command(goto=...)`, the main docs already mention using a return annotation like `Command[Literal["node_b", "node_c"]]` so graph rendering can infer possible routes. But this cross-subgraph case appears to need a different pattern: declare the parent-level visual destinations when registering the subgraph node.


With:

  ```python
  builder.add_node(
      "my_subgraph",
      inner_graph,
      destinations=("node_b", "node_c"),
  )
```

The Mermaid output renders dotted visual edges from the subgraph node to node_b and node_c:

  ```
  my_subgraph\3anode_a -.-> node_b;
  my_subgraph\3anode_a -.-> node_c;
  node_b --> __end__;
  node_c --> __end__;
```

The destinations parameter is documented in the StateGraph.add_node API reference as rendering-only, but I couldn’t find an example in the main Graph API docs for using it together with Command(graph=Command.PARENT, goto=...).

If maintainers agree, I’d be happy to open a docs PR adding a small example for this subgraph-to-parent routing visualization pattern.

Relevant docs :

- `StateGraph.add_node(..., destinations=...)` reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/graph/state/StateGraph/add_node
- Main `Command` / `Command.PARENT` docs: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#command

title: ToolNode wrapper callbacks can return unsupported values without a clear boundary error
body:
### Checked other resources

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.
- [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code.
- [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package).
- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Related Issues / PRs

Related PR: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/7654

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
from collections.abc import Callable

from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, ToolMessage
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode
from langgraph.prebuilt.tool_node import ToolCallRequest
from langgraph.types import Command


@tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two numbers."""
    return a + b


def bad_wrapper(
    request: ToolCallRequest,
    execute: Callable[[ToolCallRequest], ToolMessage | Command],
) -> ToolMessage | Command:
    # User bug: the wrapper accidentally returns an unsupported value.
    return None  # type: ignore[return-value]


tool_node = ToolNode([add], wrap_tool_call=bad_wrapper)

result = tool_node.invoke(
    {
        "messages": [
            AIMessage(
                "adding",
                tool_calls=[
                    {
                        "name": "add",
                        "args": {"a": 1, "b": 2},
                        "id": "call_1",
                    }
                ],
            )
        ]
    }
)

print(result)
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
There is no clear boundary error from the wrapper callback itself. The unsupported wrapper return value is trusted by the wrapper path and can be returned from the node / fail later depending on the call path.
```

### Description

`ToolNode` documents `wrap_tool_call` / `awrap_tool_call` as callbacks that return `ToolMessage` or `Command`.

If a custom wrapper accidentally returns `None` or another unsupported value, I would expect `ToolNode` to fail at the wrapper boundary with a clear `TypeError`, similar to the existing normalization path for direct tool outputs.

Instead, the wrapper return value is accepted directly in the wrapper path. This makes wrapper bugs harder to diagnose because the invalid value is no longer reported at the callback boundary.

Would the project accept a small PR that validates wrapper return values with the same normalization behavior used for direct tool output? I have a focused patch and tests covering sync and async wrappers in https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/7654, but that PR was auto-closed because it needs an approved issue link / assignment first. If this is considered a valid bug, please assign me and I can update or reopen the PR with `Fixes #...`.

title: Allow invoke API with command to update subGraph state
body:
### Privileged issue

- [x] I am a LangGraph maintainer.

### Issue Content

invoke API with command today can only update parent state.
But sometimes user need to update the subGraph state. 

The workaround is to use update_state to update subGraph state and then invoke, which is not ideal.

This is to add the native support to invoke API.

comments.author: theiconik
comments.body:
I spent some time reading through the relevant code paths and reproduced the current behavior locally. The issue makes sense: when `invoke(Command(update=..., resume=...), subgraph_config)` is called,
  the `Command.update` currently gets treated as input to the root graph loop, so it does not update the subgraph checkpoint state.

  I see two possible directions:

  1. Internalize the current workaround in `stream` / `astream`

     If the input is a `Command` with `update`, and the config points to a subgraph checkpoint via `checkpoint_ns`, LangGraph could first call `bulk_update_state` / `abulk_update_state` with that same subgraph config, then continue the run with the same command but with `update=None`.

     Roughly:

     ```python
     if (
         isinstance(input, Command)
         and input.graph is None
         and input.update
         and config["configurable"].get("checkpoint_ns")
     ):
         config = self.bulk_update_state(config, [[StateUpdate(input.update)]])
         input = replace(input, update=None)

  This seems low risk because bulk_update_state already delegates to the matching subgraph based on checkpoint_ns, so it reuses the existing workaround behavior and should cover nested subgraphs too.

  2. Add a more explicit API for targeting graph state updates

     Another direction would be adding/clarifying an explicit target, for example using Command(graph=...) or a new parameter to say which graph’s state the update should apply to. This might be cleaner
     long-term, but it feels like a larger API design question and would need docs/spec clarification.

  I’m curious which direction the team would prefer here: internalizing the existing workaround in stream / astream, or designing a more explicit command target API?

  Also, is this issue open for an external contributor to work on, or is it intended to be handled by the LangGraph team internally?

title: Bug: PostgresStore numeric filter operators ($gt, $gte, $lt, $lte) use lexicographic (text) comparison instead of numeric comparison
body:
### Checked other resources

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.
- [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code.
- [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package).
- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Related Issues / PRs

_No response_

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
from langgraph.store.postgres.base import BasePostgresStore

class _MockStore(BasePostgresStore):
    pass

store = object.__new__(_MockStore)

for op in ["$gt", "$gte", "$lt", "$lte"]:
    sql, params = store._get_filter_condition("score", op, 10)
    print(f"{op}: sql={sql!r}, params={params}")

# Output (all four use text extraction with str param):
# $gt:  sql='value->>%s > %s',  params=['score', '10']
# $gte: sql='value->>%s >= %s', params=['score', '10']
# $lt:  sql='value->>%s < %s',  params=['score', '10']
# $lte: sql='value->>%s <= %s', params=['score', '10']

# In PostgreSQL: '9' >= '10' is True (text ordering) — items with score=9
# incorrectly pass a {"score": {"$gte": 10}} filter.
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell

```

### Description

`PostgresStore._get_filter_condition()` uses `value->>key` (text extraction)
with `str(value)` for `$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte` operators.
Since `->>` returns TEXT in PostgreSQL, numeric comparisons use lexicographic
ordering instead of numeric ordering, producing silently wrong query results.

Expected: `filter={"score": {"$gte": 10}}` returns only items where score >= 10.
Actual:   Items with score=2..9 are incorrectly included ('9' >= '10' in text ordering).

Note: `SqliteStore._get_filter_condition()` already handles this correctly with
`CAST(... AS REAL)` — the fix was not propagated to `PostgresStore`.

comments.author: awesome-pro
comments.body:
I have a fix with unit tests ready on my fork (PR #7983, auto-closed because I wasn't assigned first).

One detail worth noting on the cast choice: `SqliteStore` uses `CAST(... AS REAL)` (float64). For PostgreSQL I used `(value->>%s)::numeric` rather than `::float8` because `numeric` is arbitrary-precision — it handles exact integer comparisons at the edges of float64 range correctly (e.g. `score = 1000000000000001` would be miscompared under float64 rounding). `::numeric` also matches PostgreSQL's own recommendation for JSONB numeric field extraction.

Worth noting what's *not* changed: `$eq` and `$ne` already use `value->%s = %s::jsonb` comparison, which is correctly type-aware and handles both `"score": 10` and `"score": 10.5` without needing a cast. Only the four range operators needed the fix.

The PR includes 13 unit tests for `_get_filter_condition()` that run without a live Postgres connection, covering numeric cast presence, param types, string fallback, jsonb equality/inequality, and an unknown-operator ValueError.

Could a maintainer assign me to this issue so PR #7983 can be reopened?

### Related Issues / PRs

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

def node_a(state): return {"a": interrupt("question A")}
def node_b(state): return {"b": interrupt("question B")}

g = StateGraph(dict)
g.add_node("a", node_a)
g.add_node("b", node_b)
g.add_edge(START, "a")
g.add_edge(START, "b")
g.add_edge("a", END)
g.add_edge("b", END)
graph = g.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}}
graph.invoke({}, cfg)
# Resume with a single value while two interrupts are pending -> raises:
graph.invoke(Command(resume="answer"), cfg)
```

```shell
RuntimeError: When there are multiple pending interrupts, you must specify the
interrupt id when resuming. Docs:
https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/add-human-in-the-loop#resume-multiple-interrupts-with-one-invocation.
```

### Description

The docs URL embedded in this RuntimeError points to a page that no longer exists
and returns HTTP 404:

  https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/add-human-in-the-loop#resume-multiple-interrupts-with-one-invocation

The actual section explaining how to resume multiple interrupts in a single
invocation (using a `{interrupt_id: resume_value}` map passed to `Command(resume=...)`)
now lives at:

  https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts#handling-multiple-interrupts

  libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_loop.py:771

the content but did not update this in-source reference. There is also no entry in
docs/redirects.json mapping the old path to the new one.

Expected: the URL in the error message points users to a real page that documents
the fix (using `interrupt_id` keyed resume map).

comments.author: hanselhansel
comments.body: Worth anchoring this on what the audit artifact looks like at the moment of human approval, before deciding the API shape. comments.body:

comments.author: giskard09
comments.body:
Following up on the compliance gate + audit trail thread — we now have a working example that wires a `MyceliumTrailCallback` into a LangGraph compliance pipeline.

The callback handler posts a tamper-evident trail after every tool call, fire-and-forget, non-blocking:

```python
class MyceliumTrailCallback(BaseCallbackHandler):
    """Post a tamper-evident trail after every tool call."""

    def on_tool_end(self, output: str, *, run_id, parent_run_id=None,
                    tags=None, **kwargs) -> None:
        tool_name  = kwargs.get("name", "unknown_tool")
        ts_ms      = int(time.time() * 1000)
        action_ref = derive_action_ref(AGENT_ID, "BUILD", tool_name, ts_ms)

        try:
            with httpx.Client(timeout=3.0) as client:
                client.post(f"{ARGENTUM_API}/action/submit", json={
                    "entity_id":   AGENT_ID,
                    "entity_type": "agent",
                    "action_type": "BUILD",
                    "description": f"Tool: {tool_name}",
                    "nonce":       action_ref,
                    "timestamp":   ts_ms // 1000,
                })
        except Exception:
            pass  # trail failure never interrupts the graph
```

The canonical `action_ref` derivation (shared across LangGraph, SafeAgent, and DashClaw):

```python
def derive_action_ref(agent_id: str, action_type: str, scope: str, ts_ms: int) -> str:
    payload = (
        agent_id.encode("utf-8")
        + action_type.encode("utf-8")
        + scope.encode("utf-8")
        + struct.pack(">q", ts_ms)   # int64 big-endian
    )
    return hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()
```

Full working example (compliance gate node → execute node → callback, ~80 lines):

```python
graph = StateGraph(dict)
graph.add_node("compliance_gate", compliance_gate_node)
graph.add_node("execute",         execute_node)
graph.set_entry_point("compliance_gate")
graph.add_conditional_edges(
    "compliance_gate",
    lambda s: "execute" if s["approved"] else END,
    {"execute": "execute", END: END}
)
graph.add_edge("execute", END)
app = graph.compile(callbacks=[MyceliumTrailCallback()])
```

The key property for regulated environments: `action_ref` is derived from tool arguments *before* execution, so the same tool call always produces the same identifier — deterministic retry detection and audit trail linkage across the full stack.

comments.author: giskard09
comments.body:
@priyanka25aug — following up on the callback handler thread from the 15th.

One dimension worth surfacing for the UBS context specifically: the audit question for regulated workloads isn't just "did this agent act correctly" — it's "can an external auditor verify what happened without going through the operator's infrastructure."

A signed log or hashed database answers the first question. It doesn't answer the second: verification still requires trusting whoever runs the system.

The pattern we've been building toward in this thread (tamper-evident records, callback handlers with verifiable output hashes) becomes regulator-grade when the anchor is on-chain — meaning an FCA or MiFID II auditor can verify the record directly against a public chain without contacting UBS, without API keys, without the system being online.

That's what Mycelium Trails adds to the architecture you're describing: `tx_hash` on Arbitrum, publicly verifiable, independent of the operator. The conformance spec is at [action-ref-v1.0](https://github.com/giskard09/argentum-core/blob/action-ref-v1.0/docs/spec/action-ref.md) — five independent implementations running the same derivation.

Happy to map the interface to the LangGraph callback structure if that's useful for the compliance layer.

comments.author: atensecurity-bot
comments.body:
+1 on this gap. I can contribute a production-oriented example (docs/example) that stays framework-native:

- flow: `analyze -> classify_risk -> policy_gate -> execute`
- decision states: `ALLOW | STEP_UP | BLOCK`
- auditable receipt per action:
  - `thread_id`, `run_id`, `tool_call_id`
  - `policy_id`, `decision`, `reason`
  - timestamp + hash-chained receipt id for tamper evidence
- default low-noise behavior:
  - approved tool/vendor path = pass-through
  - unknown path = step-up or block (configurable)

If that shape is useful, I'll open a PR with minimal dependencies and runnable sample code.

comments.author: chopmob-cloud
comments.body:
The compliance gate in a regulated environment needs one property beyond hash-chaining and callback handlers: the receipt format needs to be IETF-specified to be citable in an FCA, MiFID II, or DORA compliance filing.

AlgoVoi has this live:

**Compliance receipt** -- `draft-hopley-x402-compliance-receipt-02` ([datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-hopley-x402-compliance-receipt/)). Closed three-state verdict: `ALLOW` / `REFER` / `DENY`. The `REFER` state maps directly onto the human-in-the-loop checkpoint this thread is building -- it is a first-class categorical outcome for "escalate for human review" rather than a DENY with a note. JCS (RFC 8785) canonical form, SHA-256 content-binding. No on-chain gas dependency -- verifiable offline by any auditor against the IETF spec without a chain connection.

**ATB -- adversarial behavioral testing above the gate**

The compliance gate prevents the wrong action. The [Agent Trust Bench](https://agent-trust-bench.algovoi.co.uk) (166 adversarial profiles, 36 categories) tests whether the agent handles the gate correctly under adversarial conditions -- bait-and-switch challenges, injection, mandate expiry replay. An ATB-certified agent presents an `X-ATB-ZK-Credential` header (Pedersen commitment + Bulletproofs range proof, Falcon-1024 signed, no score disclosed) that a compliance gate can verify in a single header check.

For a LangGraph integration: compliance gate node emits a `draft-hopley-x402-compliance-receipt-02` receipt; ATB credential check is a pre-node hook. The receipt proves the policy ran; the ATB credential proves the agent can be trusted to handle it correctly under adversarial conditions.

*AlgoVoi (chopmob-cloud) -- [docs.algovoi.co.uk/compliance-gate-v1](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/compliance-gate-v1)*

body:
### Checked other resources

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.
- [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.

- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Related Issues / PRs

_No response_

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
- Run langgraph dev
- Open langgraph studio and connect, or agent-chat-ui and send a message
- Hit Ctrl + C on langgraph dev to stop it
- Try to restart langgraph dev immediately
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
File ".../bin/langgraph", line 8, in <module>
    sys.exit(cli())
             ^^^^^

    return self.main(*args, **kwargs)

         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

                           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    run_server(
  File ".../lib/python3.12/site-packages/langgraph_api/cli.py", line 202, in run_server
    port = _resolve_port(host, port)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File ".../lib/python3.12/site-packages/langgraph_api/cli.py", line 155, in _resolve_port
    raise OSError(
OSError: Port 2024 is already in use. Please specify a different port or omit the port argument to auto-discover an available one.
```

### Description

`langgraph dev` fails to start with `OSError: Port 2024 is already in use` for ~60 seconds after a Ctrl+C, even though no process is `LISTEN`-ing on the port. The only workaround appears to be waiting out the TCP TIME-WAIT timer or rebooting.

The error is in langgraph_api, in _resolve_port(). I fixed it locally by trying and bind the port with SO_REUSEADDR, then closing it: 

**langgraph_api/cli.py**
```python
def _resolve_port(host: str, port: int) -> int:
    """Resolve the port to use for the server."""
    if port is not None:
        s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
        s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        try:
            s.bind((host, port))
        except OSError:
            s.close()
            raise OSError(
                f"Port {port} is already in use. Please specify a different port "
                f"or omit the port argument to auto-discover an available one."
            )
        s.close()
        return port
    # function continues...
```

title: draw_graph: TypeError sorting edges with None data from conditional edges
body:
### Description

When a `StateGraph` has a node that returns `Command[Literal[...]]` AND also uses `add_conditional_edges` from the same node, calling `graph.get_graph()` fails with:

```
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'str'
```

The bug is in `libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_draw.py` and exists in versions **1.1.10 through 1.2.0a5** (as of May 2026).

### Root Cause

Two `sorted()` calls sort `NamedTuple` types (`TriggerEdge` and `Edge`) whose `data` field is `str | None`. When tuples share identical fields before `data` but have mixed `None`/`str` in `data`, Python's default tuple comparison fails.

The specific trigger: `_control_static()` at `state.py:1575-1577` produces entries with `label=None` when `ends` is a tuple (which happens when a node returns `Command[Literal[...]]`). These collide with string-labeled entries from `add_conditional_edges` via `branch.run()`.

**Location 1 — `TriggerEdge` sort (~line 203):**
```python
for src, cond, label in sorted(trigger_to_sources[trigger]):
```

**Location 2 — `Edge` sort (~line 238):**
```python
for src, dest, is_conditional, label in sorted(edges):
```

### Minimal Reproduction

Requires `langgraph >= 1.1.10`:

```python
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from typing import Annotated, Literal
from typing_extensions import TypedDict
from langgraph.types import Command

class State(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list, lambda x, y: x + y]

def node_a(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"messages": []}

# node_b returns Command[Literal["node_a"]] → sets ends=("node_a",) tuple
# → _control_static produces (branch:to:node_a, None, None) with label=None
def node_b(state: State) -> Command[Literal["node_a"]]:
    return Command(goto="node_a")

builder = StateGraph(State)
builder.add_node("node_a", node_a)
builder.add_node("node_b", node_b)
builder.add_edge(START, "node_a")
builder.add_edge("node_a", "node_b")

# add_conditional_edges produces entries with label="node_a" (string)
# this collides with the label=None from node_b's return type
def route_to_a(state: State) -> Literal["node_a"]:
    return "node_a"
builder.add_conditional_edges("node_b", route_to_a)

builder.add_edge("node_b", "node_a")
builder.add_edge("node_a", END)

graph = builder.compile()
graph.get_graph()  # TypeError
```

### Proposed Fix

Add a key function to both `sorted()` calls that normalizes `data`:

```python
# Line ~203 — TriggerEdge sort:
sorted(trigger_to_sources[trigger],
       key=lambda x: (x.source, x.conditional, x.data or ""))

# Line ~238 — Edge sort:
sorted(edges,
       key=lambda x: (x.source, x.target, x.conditional, x.data or ""))
```

### Environment

- langgraph: 1.1.10 through 1.2.0a5
- Python: 3.12+
- OS: Linux

comments.body:

```python
# Monkey-patch the sort key to handle None data

comments.author: nogueira-raphael
comments.body:
I don’t think this is exactly a bug.

In this case, we are mixing two different ways of defining the next node:

1. `Command[Literal["node_a"]]`, where the node itself explicitly defines the next node through `goto`.
2. `add_conditional_edges`, where the graph decides the next node through a conditional routing function.

If `node_b` already returns `Command(goto="node_a")`, then the conditional edge is unnecessary. Also, the return type annotation is mainly used by LangGraph to infer/render the graph structure, for example in the Mermaid diagram.

So the example can be simplified by removing the explicit `Command[Literal["node_a"]]` annotation:

```python
def node_b(state: State):
    return Command(goto="node_a")
```

Or alternatively, keep the annotation and remove `add_conditional_edges`.

In other words, we should avoid using both `Command[Literal[...]]` and `add_conditional_edges` from the same node, because they both describe routing from that node.

The code below works for generating the mermaid diagram, but if you notice, you have a looping graph, which will result in a recursion exception when you invoke the graph.

```python
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from typing import Annotated, Literal
from typing_extensions import TypedDict
from langgraph.types import Command

class State(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list, lambda x, y: x + y]

def node_a(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"messages": []}

def node_b(state: State) -> Command[Literal["node_a"]]:
    return Command(goto="node_a")

builder = StateGraph(State)
builder.add_node("node_a", node_a)
builder.add_node("node_b", node_b)
builder.add_edge(START, "node_a")
builder.add_edge("node_a", "node_b")

builder.add_edge("node_b", "node_a")
builder.add_edge("node_a", END)

graph = builder.compile()

display(Image(graph.get_graph().draw_mermaid_png()))
```

comments.author: hanselhansel
comments.body: Operator question: when this fires in your setup, are the conditional edges fanning out across parallel branches, or single-branch? We hit a near-identical sort crash in a multi-agent graph the moment a router started returning `None` for one of its branches under a specific tenant config, and the failure mode was nondeterministic (order of branch resolution decided whether the bad tuple ever reached the sort). A stable tiebreak on the sort key (e.g., `(source, target, "" if data is None else data)`) would at least make the crash deterministic across runs, which matters more than the crash itself when you are debugging from CI logs. Has anyone tried pinning a repro with a fixed-seed router? Curious whether the bug surfaces at graph-construction time or only at render time in your repros.

comments.author: WatchTree-19
comments.body:
fair point - mixing the two routing styles is anti-pattern. but two reasons to keep this open:

1. the fix is `key=` on the existing `sorted()` calls, ~10 lines, no API change, no behaviour change for users who don't mix the patterns. negligible cost.

2. as @hanselhansel noted upthread, the current failure mode is order-dependent (depends on which tuple reaches the sort first), which is much harder to debug from CI logs than a deterministic outcome. users hit this from third-party integrations where they don't control both patterns, and "don't mix them" isn't enforceable from outside the user's own code.

the fix turns an order-dependent TypeError into a deterministic render. happy to PR if a maintainer agrees with that framing.

comments.author: pragnyanramtha
comments.body:
Thanks for the clear repro. I have a minimal patch locally that normalizes the two `_draw.py` edge sort keys for `None` labels and adds a regression test for the `Command[Literal[...]]` + `add_conditional_edges` graph-rendering case.

Validated locally in `libs/langgraph` with:
- `NO_DOCKER=true make test TEST='tests/test_pregel.py::test_get_graph_sorts_mixed_none_and_string_edge_labels'`
- `make lint_package`
- `make lint_tests`

I see @WatchTree-19 already volunteered above, so I am happy to defer to them. If maintainers would like me to submit the patch, please assign/approve and I can open a focused PR linked to this issue.

comments.author: WatchTree-19
comments.body: Happy to defer. Your regression case (`Command[Literal[...]]` + `add_conditional_edges` graph-rendering) is the right spec to pin, and you've already run the lint/test gauntlet locally — please ship it. Thanks for picking this up.

comments.author: awesome-pro
comments.body:
I have a fix with a regression test ready on my fork (PR #7984, auto-closed because I wasn't assigned first). Want to address the "is this actually a bug?" discussion.

@nogueira-raphael's point is correct at *execution* time: mixing `Command[Literal[...]]` routing with `add_conditional_edges` on the same node is an anti-pattern. But the crash happens at *render* time — in `get_graph()`, which is a static inspection/visualization tool. The two concerns are separable:

1. Whether the graph *runs correctly* — that's the execution question, and yes, mixing routing styles there is undefined behavior.
2. Whether `get_graph()` *crashes* on a valid Python type combination (`str | None` in a sort key) — that's the visualization question, and crashing is wrong regardless.

Users call `get_graph()` for debugging, often *because* something looks off in their graph structure. Making the debug tool crash on the exact case where users need it most defeats the purpose. The fix is two `key=` lambdas, ~10 lines, zero behavior change for graphs with all-string labels.

Also worth noting @hanselhansel's CI point: the crash is currently **order-dependent** — whether the `None` and string labels collide in the sort depends on dict insertion order, which varies across Python versions and invocations. The `key=` fix makes even the pathological case deterministic across runs, which matters when triaging flaky CI.

Could a maintainer assign me to this issue so PR #7984 can be reopened?

builder.add_edge("node_b", "node_a")

Operator question: when this fires in your setup, are the conditional edges fanning out across parallel branches, or single-branch? We hit a near-identical sort crash in a multi-agent graph the moment a router started returning `None` for one of its branches under a specific tenant config, and the failure mode was nondeterministic (order of branch resolution decided whether the bad tuple ever reached the sort). A stable tiebreak on the sort key (e.g., `(source, target, "" if data is None else data)`) would at least make the crash deterministic across runs, which matters more than the crash itself when you are debugging from CI logs. Has anyone tried pinning a repro with a fixed-seed router? Curious whether the bug surfaces at graph-construction time or only at render time in your repros.

fair point - mixing the two routing styles is anti-pattern. but two reasons to keep this open:

1. the fix is `key=` on the existing `sorted()` calls, ~10 lines, no API change, no behaviour change for users who don't mix the patterns. negligible cost.

2. as @hanselhansel noted upthread, the current failure mode is order-dependent (depends on which tuple reaches the sort first), which is much harder to debug from CI logs than a deterministic outcome. users hit this from third-party integrations where they don't control both patterns, and "don't mix them" isn't enforceable from outside the user's own code.

the fix turns an order-dependent TypeError into a deterministic render. happy to PR if a maintainer agrees with that framing.

Thanks for the clear repro. I have a minimal patch locally that normalizes the two `_draw.py` edge sort keys for `None` labels and adds a regression test for the `Command[Literal[...]]` + `add_conditional_edges` graph-rendering case.

Validated locally in `libs/langgraph` with:
- `NO_DOCKER=true make test TEST='tests/test_pregel.py::test_get_graph_sorts_mixed_none_and_string_edge_labels'`
- `make lint_package`
- `make lint_tests`

I see @WatchTree-19 already volunteered above, so I am happy to defer to them. If maintainers would like me to submit the patch, please assign/approve and I can open a focused PR linked to this issue.

Happy to defer. Your regression case (`Command[Literal[...]]` + `add_conditional_edges` graph-rendering) is the right spec to pin, and you've already run the lint/test gauntlet locally — please ship it. Thanks for picking this up.

I have a fix with a regression test ready on my fork (PR #7984, auto-closed because I wasn't assigned first). Want to address the "is this actually a bug?" discussion.

@nogueira-raphael's point is correct at *execution* time: mixing `Command[Literal[...]]` routing with `add_conditional_edges` on the same node is an anti-pattern. But the crash happens at *render* time — in `get_graph()`, which is a static inspection/visualization tool. The two concerns are separable:

1. Whether the graph *runs correctly* — that's the execution question, and yes, mixing routing styles there is undefined behavior.
2. Whether `get_graph()` *crashes* on a valid Python type combination (`str | None` in a sort key) — that's the visualization question, and crashing is wrong regardless.

Users call `get_graph()` for debugging, often *because* something looks off in their graph structure. Making the debug tool crash on the exact case where users need it most defeats the purpose. The fix is two `key=` lambdas, ~10 lines, zero behavior change for graphs with all-string labels.

Also worth noting @hanselhansel's CI point: the crash is currently **order-dependent** — whether the `None` and string labels collide in the sort depends on dict insertion order, which varies across Python versions and invocations. The `key=` fix makes even the pathological case deterministic across runs, which matters when triaging flaky CI.

Could a maintainer assign me to this issue so PR #7984 can be reopened?

- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Related Issues / PRs

_No response_

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
import asyncio
from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite.aio import AsyncSqliteSaver
from langgraph.graph import END, StateGraph
from langgraph.types import interrupt
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing_extensions import TypedDict
from langgraph.checkpoint.serde.jsonplus import JsonPlusSerializer
from langgraph.types import Command

# framework integrator types (e.g. UiPath-Langchain interrupt models)
class FrameworkInterrupt(BaseModel):
    some_value: str

# user-defined models
class UserModel(BaseModel):
    value: int
    label: str

class AgentState(TypedDict):
    payload: UserModel | None

def populate_payload(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    return {
        "payload": UserModel(
            value=100,
            label="test_label",
        )
    }

def suspend_and_read_label(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    interrupt(FrameworkInterrupt(some_value="waiting for external event"))
    state["payload"].label
    return state

def build_graph() -> StateGraph:
    graph = StateGraph(AgentState)
    graph.add_node("populate", populate_payload)
    graph.add_node("suspend_and_read_label", suspend_and_read_label)
    graph.set_entry_point("populate")
    graph.add_edge("populate", "suspend_and_read_label")
    graph.add_edge("suspend_and_read_label", END)
    return graph

async def main() -> None:
    thread = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "demo-thread"}}

    async with AsyncSqliteSaver.from_conn_string(":memory:") as memory:
        await memory.setup()

        # custom framework registers its own modules to suppress deserialization warnings for first-party types.
        memory.serde = JsonPlusSerializer(
            # setting this flips JsonPlusSerializer into strict mode → on resume, UserModel
            # is degraded to dict and line 32 raises AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'label'.
            allowed_msgpack_modules=[(FrameworkInterrupt.__module__, FrameworkInterrupt.__name__)],
        )

        graph = build_graph().compile(checkpointer=memory)
        await graph.ainvoke( {"payload": None}, config=thread)
        await graph.ainvoke(Command(resume="interrupt result"), config=thread)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
Blocked deserialization of __main__.UserModel - not in allowed_msgpack_modules. Add to allowed_msgpack_modules to allow: [('__main__', 'UserModel')]
AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'label'
During task with name 'suspend_and_read_label' and id 'bf3ba4b4-ee1e-32cc-d30e-fbecab891e2f
```

### Description

Cross posting for visibility.
Related langchain community forum post [here](https://forum.langchain.com/t/feature-request-wire-allowed-msgpack-modules-in-langgraph-json/3624).

## Core problem
There’s no way for a framework integrator (that owns the checkpointer configuration) to register a few first-party types without changing what happens to user types.

## Suggested improvements
1. Expose a way to register library types to msgpack allow list without enabling strict mode (supress `Deserializing unregistered type ... from checkpoint. This will be blocked in a future version` warnings).
2. Allow registering `allowed_msgpack_modules` in langgraph.json so users can whitelist their custom types (example usage https://github.com/UiPath/uipath-langchain-python/pull/814/changes#diff-2f9f8576b44f57e45a2c0a6cc1317032554dcd536cc2c7d901a605ebb8df50b4R10) so the transition to a _langgraph integrator_ framework would be seamless.


If the above mentioned improvements are acceptable I am happy to work on the implementation.
Thanks.

N/A

title: [Feature] Add fetch() primitive — a typed, always-resuming variant of interrupt() for s2s data dependencies
body:
### Privileged issue

- [ ] I am a LangGraph maintainer.

### Issue Content

Opening this issue per maintainer guidance in this forum thread: 
https://forum.langchain.com/t/should-interrupt-be-split-into-two-primitives-one-for-human-input-one-for-s2s-data-fetching/3611

## Problem

`interrupt()` is intentionally human-in-the-loop only, but teams deploying 
agents as pure services (no credentials, no network access) need a 
pause/resume/checkpoint mechanism for s2s data dependencies. Using 
`interrupt()` for this is a semantic mismatch — no resume guarantee, no SLA, 
wrong endpoint surfaced by LangGraph Server.

The typed envelope workaround works mechanically but gives the framework no 
tooling to enforce or introspect the distinction.

## Proposal

- Add a `kind` field to `Interrupt` dataclass (`"human"` | `"fetch"`)
- Expose `task.fetches` alongside `task.interrupts` on `PregelTask`
- Add a `fetch()` convenience function (thin wrapper over `interrupt()` with `kind="fetch"`)
- LangGraph Server: surface fetch requests separately from human interrupts

## Testing

Existing interrupt tests cover the checkpoint/resume mechanics. New tests 
would cover:
- `task.fetches` vs `task.interrupts` separation
- `fetch()` returning the resume value correctly
- LangGraph Server routing fetch vs human interrupts to correct endpoints

## Scope

- No changes to checkpoint/resume mechanics
- No changes to existing `interrupt()` behavior
- Additive only — fully backwards compatible

title: LangGraph checkpoint serialization produces 85% storage bloat and 37.8% token overhead with no opt-out path - reproducible with drop-in fix
body:
### Checked other resources

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.
- [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code.
- [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package).
- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Related Issues / PRs

- langchain-ai/langchain #36764 - Token-efficient serialization for agent message passing (feature request, langchain-core)

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
import tiktoken
import json
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMessage, AIMessage, ToolMessage

# --- Build a minimal 4-turn ReAct state to demonstrate the overhead ---

def make_react_state(turns: int = 4) -> dict:
    messages = [SystemMessage(content="You are a helpful assistant.")]
    for i in range(turns):
        messages.append(HumanMessage(content=f"User turn {i}: what is the status of order {1000 + i}?"))
        messages.append(AIMessage(
            content="",
            tool_calls=[{"id": f"call_{i}", "name": "check_order", "args": {"order_id": 1000 + i}}]
        ))
        messages.append(ToolMessage(
            content=json.dumps({"order_id": 1000 + i, "status": "shipped", "eta": "2025-08-01"}),
            tool_call_id=f"call_{i}"
        ))
        messages.append(AIMessage(content=f"Order {1000 + i} has shipped and will arrive 2025-08-01."))
    return {"messages": messages, "thread_id": "repro-thread", "turn": turns}

state = make_react_state(turns=4)

# --- Measure what LangGraph actually serializes into the checkpoint ---

from langchain_core.load import dumpd

def langgraph_checkpoint_bytes(state: dict) -> int:
    serialized = json.dumps(
        {k: dumpd(v) if not isinstance(v, (str, int, bool)) else v
         for k, v in state.items()},
        default=str
    )
    return len(serialized.encode("utf-8"))

# --- Measure token overhead in the context window ---

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

def tokens_langgraph(state: dict) -> int:
    payload = json.dumps(
        {k: dumpd(v) if not isinstance(v, (str, int, bool)) else v
         for k, v in state.items()},
        default=str
    )
    return len(enc.encode(payload))

checkpoint_bytes = langgraph_checkpoint_bytes(state)
token_count = tokens_langgraph(state)

print(f"Checkpoint storage (4-turn, 13 messages) : {checkpoint_bytes:,} bytes")
print(f"Token count injected into context window  : {token_count:,} tokens")
print()
print("Expected: compact serialization proportional to semantic content")
print("Actual  : full Pydantic metadata, repeated key names, zero opt-out")
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
Checkpoint storage (4-turn, 13 messages) : ~6,800 bytes
Token count injected into context window  : ~1,450 tokens

Expected: compact serialization proportional to semantic content
Actual  : full Pydantic metadata, repeated key names, zero opt-out

No exception is raised. LangGraph silently accepts and forwards bloated
and structurally corrupt payloads to the LLM without any validation.

Corrupt payload example (orphaned tool result, no matching call):
  → LangGraph: PASSED (silent)
  → No error, no warning, payload reaches the LLM unchanged
```

### Description

### What is happening

LangGraph's checkpoint serialization path (`MemorySaver`, `SqliteSaver`, `PostgresSaver`) uses full Pydantic metadata serialization via `dumpd()` for every channel value on every checkpoint write. This creates two measurable and compounding problems:

**Problem 1: Storage bloat.**
A 16-turn ReAct agent with 65 messages produces a checkpoint of **21,850 bytes** under the default `MemorySaver`. The same state encoded with a binary pooling serializer compresses to **3,217 bytes**. That is an **85.3% storage overhead** (6.79x) that compounds directly into Postgres/Redis storage costs at scale and checkpoint write latency on every single graph turn.

**Problem 2: Token overhead in the context window.**
When LangGraph serializes agent state to inject into the LLM context, the full Pydantic metadata representation of a 16-turn agent produces **5,764 tokens (20,516 chars)**. The semantic content of those same messages requires **3,587 tokens (10,703 chars)**. That is a **37.8% token overhead** paid on every LLM call, every turn, compounding across the full agent loop.

**Problem 3: No structural validation.**
LangGraph's serialization layer silently accepts and forwards structurally corrupt agent payloads to the LLM. Tested against 4 categories of corruption:

| Scenario | LangGraph |
|---|---|
| Orphaned tool result (no matching call) | Silent pass |
| Backward step counter regression | Silent pass |
| Invalid record type enum | Silent pass |
| Missing required fields | Silent pass |

All 4 corrupt variants reach the LLM without any error, warning, or rejection.

**Problem 4: No opt-out path exists.**
There is currently no mechanism in LangGraph to plug in an alternative serializer at the checkpointer, store, stream, or subgraph boundary level.
Users cannot opt out of the JSON/pickle path without forking internal LangGraph classes.

---

### What I expect

LangGraph should expose a pluggable serialization interface at the `BaseCheckpointSaver` serde layer so that users can replace the default JSON/pickle path with an alternative serializer without modifying graph logic.

The interception point already exists structurally:
`serde.dumps_typed()` / `serde.loads_typed()` in `BaseCheckpointSaver`.

A minimal protocol would look like:

```python
class SerializerProtocol(Protocol):
    def dumps_typed(self, obj: Any) -> tuple[str, bytes]: ...
    def loads_typed(self, data: tuple[str, bytes]) -> Any: ...
```
This is sufficient to make the checkpointer backend-agnostic and serializer-pluggable without any changes to graph execution logic.

---
### Reproducible fix (drop-in, zero graph rewrites required)
I have implemented and benchmarked a drop-in extension that demonstrates the fix is viable today:

**Extension:** https://github.com/makroumi/ulmen/tree/main/ulmen/ext/langgraph

**Benchmark notebook (fully reproducible):**
https://github.com/makroumi/ulmen/blob/main/Notebooks/Benchmarks/extensions/langgraph/ulmen_langgraph_benchmarks.ipynb

The extension wraps `BaseCheckpointSaver` at the serde layer and requires zero changes to the user's graph definition:
```python
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
from ulmen.ext.langgraph import UlmenCheckpointer, make_ulmen_state

AgentState = make_ulmen_state(context_window=8000)
builder = StateGraph(AgentState)

# ... define nodes unchanged ...

checkpointer = UlmenCheckpointer(MemorySaver())
app = builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)
```
**Measured results on a 16-turn ReAct agent (65 messages, tiktoken cl100k_base, LangGraph 1.1.6, LangChain Core 1.2.28):

|**Metric** | **LangGraph Default** | **With Extension** | **Reduction**
|---|---|---|---|
|Checkpoint storage | 21,850 bytes | 3,217 bytes | **85.3%**
|LLM context tokens | 5,764 | 3,587 | **37.8%**
|Subgraph handoff (16 turns) | 13,404 bytes | 900 bytes | **93.3%**
|Stream egress per invocation | 19,126 bytes | 6,400 bytes | **66.5%**
|Round-trip fidelity | (50 cycles) | - | 100% PASS | -
|Firewall accuracy | 1/5 (20%) | 5/5 (100%) | -

**Financial projection (10M loops/year, GPT-4o at $2.50/1M tokens):**
|**System** | **Annual Cost**
|---|---|
LangGraph native JSON | $764,200.00
With structural savings | $565,000.00
With context compression | $391,600.00

Annual savings with compression: **$372,600 (48.8%)**
---
### What I am asking for
1. Expose a `SerializerProtocol` interface on BaseCheckpointSaver so that the serde layer is pluggable without forking internals.

2. Document the five serialization surfaces where pluggable serialization applies: checkpointer serde, context reducer, stream sink, store, and subgraph handoff.

3. Consider a structural validation hook at the serde boundary so that corrupt agent payloads can be caught before they reach the LLM.

I am ready to submit a PR implementing the `SerializerProtocol` interface once maintainers confirm the preferred integration point. The extension at `ulmen.ext.langgraph` serves as the reference implementation.

### System Info

Linux fedora 6.19.14-200.fc43.x86_64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Thu Apr 23 17:34:07 UTC 2026 x86_64 GNU/Linux

comments.author: hipvlady
comments.body:
The five-surface decomposition (checkpointer serde / context reducer / stream sink / store / subgraph handoff) is the part of this proposal I'd push on. Those aren't five independent surfaces — they're five points where the same state representation is read or written, and the "silent pass" failures in Problem 3 are inconsistencies between two of them, not serializer bugs per se. A pluggable SerializerProtocol cleanly addresses the cost axis; the validation hook is what keeps the correctness axis from regressing as those surfaces evolve at different rates.

The orphaned-tool-result case is the canonical version: nothing in the serializer models the call/result pairing as an invariant, so any surface that can drop or reorder messages silently breaks it. A boolean hook at the serde boundary catches it, but you'd probably want it parameterized by which invariants apply at that surface — checkpointer wants full message-graph integrity; stream sink may not.

The same broadcast-overhead pattern surfaced on the AutoGen side recently ([microsoft/autogen#7588](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/discussions/7588)), which strengthens the case — given your link to langchain/#36764 — that the protocol belongs in langchain-core rather than langgraph alone. One contract, every framework that does multi-turn agent state.

Happy to compare notes offline. I've been working on the cross-agent state-coordination problem from a coherence angle and the validation-at-serde-boundary point generalizes cleanly to the layer above.
